The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

fundamental.thesis: Kotak Mahindra Bank is one of India's largest private-sector banks, with a strong capital base (CET1 22.1%) and growing wealth and asset-management arms (customer AUM ₹8.14L cr, +8% YoY). Profit growth has picked up sharply: consolidated PAT rose 26.3% YoY to ₹5,645 cr in Q2FY27, up from +23.0% in Q1FY27 and +5.0% in Q3FY26, and standalone NII rose 16% to ₹8,459 cr. Asset quality has improved steadily, with GNPA falling from 1.39% to 1.04% over five periods and slippages down 24%, but this quarter's growth comes partly off a weak base (Q2FY26 PAT was -2.7%), and NIM fell 23bps YoY to 4.31% as costlier FCNR(B) deposits came in. On the bank yardstick (P/B plus ROE, not P/E), a P/B of 2.08x against an ROE of only 11.4-11.7% is fair, not cheap; it sits at the 86th percentile among bank peers on both P/B and forward P/E (13.6x), so it already carries a premium that its current ROE does not clearly earn. The biggest risk is margin squeeze: falling NIM, CASA slipping from 42.3% to 41.8%, a 4.52% cost of funds and an 8.1% cut to next-FY EPS estimates while 32 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower.

Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq), with watches, eyecare and the newly consolidated Damas (Gulf) business, and it gains from the premiumisation trend. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 19.1% YoY to ₹41,970 cr and reported PAT rose 88.6% to ₹4,170 cr (9.9% margin). That profit includes a ₹671 cr one-off fair-value gain on the Damas put option, so underlying PAT is about ₹3,499 cr: +58% YoY on an 8.3% margin. Part of the revenue growth comes from the Damas acquisition rather than the existing business. We only have this one half-year period with no standalone Q2 or prior-quarter rows, so the quarter-by-quarter trend cannot be checked. We used peer P/E and EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for premium discretionary names, and the stock is expensive on both: trailing P/E 74.3x (forward 49.4x) is inside the card's 60-100x range for premium names but 87% above the sector median of 39.7x, and EV/EBITDA of 48.1x sits at the 94th percentile, more than double the 21.9x peer median. Sell-side estimates have been raised 7% over 90 days, which supports earnings delivery but leaves little room for disappointment at around 72% of the 52-week range. The biggest worry is cash: operating cash flow was -₹11,177 cr against positive PAT, borrowings rose 2.5x to ₹24,265 cr, and inventory reached ₹50,861 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Hindalco is a global aluminium and copper group. Its earnings come mainly from the Indian upstream aluminium business (53.8% segment margin in H1FY27) and Novelis, its wholly owned rolled-products subsidiary (8.7% segment margin), with copper as a lower-margin third leg (6.7% margin). Consolidated H1FY27 revenue rose 35.5% YoY to ₹176,533 cr and PAT rose 66.4% to ₹14,546 cr (PAT margin 8.2%, EBITDA margin 15.2%), compared with Q1FY27 revenue growth of +32.0% and 9MFY26 growth of +13.3%. That looks like acceleration, but the trend table mixes periods (FY26 revenue is shown below 9MFY26, Q2FY27 has no separate row, and the Q1 figure of ₹84,825 cr does not match yfinance's ₹56,054 cr), and H1 profit includes ₹819 cr of Oswego business-interruption insurance recoveries, so the underlying growth rate is less clear than it appears. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive metals cyclical, the stock is at 9.3×. That is P7 within the 16-stock Materials set (median 17.9×), but the peer median is inflated by paint and adhesive franchises, metals peers such as VEDL and TATASTEEL are cheaper, and 9.3× sits above the sector card's 5–8× mid-cycle range for cyclicals. Forward P/E of 10.3× vs trailing 18.2× and P/B of 1.8× with an H1 ROE of 18.2% support a 'fair' grade, but with the stock at 85% of its 52-week range, much of the good news looks priced in. The biggest risk is cash conversion: H1 CFO/PAT was only 0.19× and FCF was −₹16,519 cr after ₹19,344 cr of capex, against net debt of ₹97,500 cr (1.82× EBITDA), so a turn in LME aluminium prices or a capex overrun would hit a stretched balance sheet.

fundamental.thesis: Cipla is a large drugmaker ranked No. 3 in India, No. 2 in South Africa's pharma market and No. 2 in North American generics on its reported market ranks, with very little debt in the latest filing (about ₹699 cr against ₹35,522 cr of equity). Revenue growth slipped from +2.3% to -2.4% YoY in Q2 FY27 (₹7,404 cr), and PAT fell 35.0% to ₹878 cr after falling 39.1% in Q1, with PAT margin at 11.9% versus 13.7-13.8% for FY26; India grew a healthier 12% and revenue and PAT rose sequentially, but EBITDA margin is unclear because the table shows a fall from 19.7% to 18.7% while the extracted KPI shows a 200 bps gain. Using P/E, EV/EBITDA and peer rank, valuation is fair: trailing P/E of 28.9x sits at the low end of the 28-40x sector range and at P38 among peers (median 36.4x), EV/EBITDA of 17.9x is also P38, and the forward P/E of 22.0x (P15) assumes an earnings recovery that analysts are trimming, while ROE of 11.7% helps explain the discount. The biggest risk is that the expected recovery does not arrive, as FY EPS estimates have been cut 4.1% over 90 days and the latest periods show no management guidance; the snapshot's 1.78 debt/equity and 93% dividend yield look like data errors and were not used.

Dabur is a mid-sized Indian FMCG company with an ayurvedic and natural focus, selling home and personal care, healthcare and food and beverages, and about a fifth of its business is international. Growth has picked up: revenue growth rose from +5.0% in FY26 to +10.6% in Q1FY27 and +11.6% in Q2FY27 (₹3,563 cr). H1 revenue was ₹7,327 cr (+11.1%) and H1 PAT ₹1,096 cr (+13.4%). Q2 PAT, derived as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹505 cr, a 14.2% margin, compared with 12.1% in Q4FY26. India volume growth of 5.5% is real, but it is only about half of the 10.7% value growth, and healthcare is lagging at +6.9%. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 39.4x sits just below the 40–65x FMCG norm and at the 20th percentile of its peers (median 43.8x). Forward P/E is 31.8x and EV/EBITDA is 29.2x versus a 31.0x peer median, and the stock is near its 52-week low, so P/E against peers is graded cheap. The card warns that cheap FMCG often signals a structural problem, and the slow healthcare segment is the likely candidate here. The biggest risk is rising input costs, with crude near $91, squeezing gross margins while about half of growth still comes from price and mix rather than volume.

fundamental.thesis: Trent runs Westside, Zudio and Star, and is one of India's fastest-growing fashion and value retailers, with roughly 1,340–1,400 stores (the store-count figures in the data don't agree with each other). In Q2 FY27, revenue grew +24.3% YoY to ₹5,873 cr, faster than +18.0% in Q1, but PAT rose only +3.8% to ₹468 cr against +22.0% in Q1 and +33.0% in Q4 FY26. PAT margin slipped from 9.0% to 8.0% and EBITDA margin from 14.7% to 13.4%, so the pre-computed 'expanding' margin label is misleading, and same-store sales growth is only mid-single digits, meaning most of the growth comes from opening new stores. For a retailer the right yardsticks are EV/EBITDA plus store economics: Trent trades at 55.3x EV/EBITDA (the most expensive in its sector, about 152% above the 21.9x median) and 85.4x trailing P/E (P88 vs a 39.7x median), so the stock is expensive even after its fall, though the 55.8x forward P/E shows the market still expects strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that profit growth keeps lagging revenue while same-store sales stay weak, which could cut the high multiple sharply, a pattern the sector card warns about.

fundamental.thesis: Varun Beverages is PepsiCo's largest bottler outside the US, with 54 plants across 26 Indian states and 9 international markets, and is expanding in Africa (Twizza merger in South Africa, Kenya entry from 1 Aug 2026). Sales growth sped up in Q3 CY26: revenue rose 33.2% YoY to Rs 6,607.6 cr, lifting 9M growth to +23.3% (Rs 21,815 cr) from +19.4% in H1. Volume grew 28.7% in 9M, with India +22.5% and international +39.9%, but part of the Q3 jump is acquired (Twizza added 15.3 mn of 354.4 mn cases). Profit has lagged sales: 9M PAT rose only 15.5% to Rs 3,202 cr, PAT margin fell to 14.7% from 15.7% a year ago, and Q3 gross margin dropped 334 bps to 53.1% (about 300 bps from packaging costs) while EBITDA margin fell 140 bps to 21.6%. Using the card's FMCG yardstick (P/E plus EV/EBITDA vs peers), the stock is fair: trailing P/E 56x is inside the 40-65x norm and at P67 among peers, EV/EBITDA 34.6x matches the peer median, and forward P/E 43.6x prices in growth. However, the price sits at 89.5% of its 52-week range and next-year EPS estimates were cut 1.6% over 90 days, so upside looks limited unless margins recover.

fundamental.thesis: Samvardhana Motherson is a global auto-parts supplier, making wiring harnesses, polymer modules and vision systems, with 425 plants in 47 countries. About 35% of its revenue comes from Europe and 22% from North America, so its earnings follow the global car cycle more than Indian demand. In Q1FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹35,244 cr, faster than FY26's +10.9%, but profit is not keeping up: PAT was ₹1,032 cr, a 2.9% margin versus 3.4% in FY26, and EBITDA margin slipped from 9.5% to 8.8%. Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-05 but have not been extracted yet, so this view is one quarter stale. On the right yardstick for a capital-heavy global supplier, EV/EBITDA is 13.9×, about 27% below the peer median of 19.1× (P20), and forward P/E of 22.1× is below the trailing 39.3×, which points to expected earnings growth. Weighed against ROE of only 10.1%, a stock sitting at 88% of its 52-week range and analyst targets just 4% above the price, overall valuation is fair. The biggest risks are a weakening European car cycle (VW, Mercedes and Audi are about 23% of revenue) and further margin pressure from acquisition-led growth.

fundamental.thesis: Bank of Baroda is one of India's largest public-sector banks, with about ₹15L cr of advances. Domestic loans grew 13.5% and international loans grew 39.7%. Q2FY27 total income rose 19.8% YoY to ₹41,966 cr and net profit rose 35.8% YoY to ₹6,532 cr, a PAT margin of 15.6%. The jump came after a very weak Q1FY27 (PAT of ₹1,278–1,783 cr; the sources disagree), so H1FY27 profit is still down 16.5% YoY. The underlying picture is mixed: asset quality is improving (GNPA fell from 1.99% to 1.78%, NNPA from 0.50% to 0.37%, provision coverage is 94.7%), but net interest margin keeps slipping (2.89% in FY26, 2.77% in Q1, 2.74% in Q2), CASA fell to 36.4% and fee income fell 8.5%. That suggests treasury gains and lower costs drove part of the Q2 beat, not core lending spread. For a lender I graded valuation on price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E: at 0.81x book with a 12.7% trailing ROE (19.3% annualised in Q2), the stock is cheap in absolute terms and against peers. It ranks P7 on P/B (median 1.5x) and P21 on trailing P/E (6.8x vs a 16.8x peer median). Part of that discount is the usual PSU-bank discount, so cheap here does not mean mispriced. The biggest risk is that margins keep sliding while credit costs rise (0.55% vs 0.29% a year ago), making the Q2 profit spike a one-off rather than the new run-rate. Data caveats: the Q3FY26 and H1FY26 rows in the trend table look like a much smaller entity (deposits ₹1.5L cr), so the pre-computed trajectory signals are unreliable. Live data also has errors (a 322% dividend yield, and the 52-week position does not match the price implied by the analyst target), so I lowered conviction.

fundamental.thesis: HAL is India's main state-owned maker of military aircraft and helicopters, with a Q4FY26 order book of about ₹2.55 lakh cr, or 7.7x revenue, and FY26 order inflow of about ₹97,028 cr (period label inferred), giving multi-year visibility. Q1FY27 revenue rose 14.4% YoY to ₹5,515 cr and PAT rose 14.9% to ₹1,590 cr (28.8% margin), an apparent acceleration from about +7% in FY26, but this is one seasonally small quarter and the pre-computed trend signals rely on inconsistent rows (for example, Q4FY26 revenue of ₹33,050 cr looks like the full year, and Q1FY26 PAT of ₹138 cr conflicts with the +14.9% growth), so I do not treat the margin expansion as proven. On EV/EBITDA, supported by order-book cover as the sector card directs, valuation is fair rather than the 'cheap' peer verdict: 29.0x is 14.7% below the 34.0x sector median but only P35, and while trailing P/E of 31.1x is P6 among peers, it sits within the 28-45x sector range and forward P/E is P24. The biggest risks are the governance gap from too few independent directors, which left the Audit Committee non-functional from 5 April 2026 in the latest filing, and the 12 November results, which will test whether Q1's growth and margins hold.

fundamental.thesis: Torrent Pharma is a branded-formulations business led by India, with Brazil, the US and Germany abroad, and the JB Pharma merger has added to its India chronic franchise; base India grew 20% against 12% for the market, and FDA status was last noted as clean in Q1 FY27. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 50.8% YoY to Rs 4,979 cr (slightly slower than +55.0% in Q1, and only about +18% on the base business excluding JB), while PAT fell 9.6% to Rs 534 cr, PAT margin dropped from 17.9% to 10.7%, and EBITDA margin held at 33.5% with gross margin at 75.4%, so the acquisition is lifting revenue and EBITDA but not yet profit, and new shares issued for JB dilute per-share earnings further. Valuation is expensive on P/E and EV/EBITDA with peer rank as the yardstick: trailing P/E of 69.1x is well above the 28-40x pharma range and the 36.4x peer median (P92), and EV/EBITDA of 37.5x compares with a 21.4x median (P85), though the snapshot's market cap and price data look inconsistent and may not fully reflect the new shares. The biggest risk is that FY EPS estimates have been cut 7.0% over 90 days while 23 of 28 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that can precede a lower multiple if JB synergies and deleveraging from net debt of Rs 12,961 cr (1.95x EBITDA) arrive slowly.

Zydus Lifesciences is a large Indian generics maker with a US-heavy pharma business (80.7% of H1 revenue), a growing consumer wellness arm and a new loss-making MedTech segment built through acquisitions (Comfort Click, Amplitude). H1 FY27 revenue grew 25.4% YoY to ₹15,927 cr, and the implied Q2 figure is about ₹7,910 cr, up roughly 29%. But much of that growth came from acquisitions: H1 EBITDA fell 5.8% to ₹3,872 cr, EBITDA margin dropped from 31.2% to 24.3%, and PAT fell 30.9% to ₹1,886 cr (11.8% margin). Even after stripping out the one-off items (₹1,091 cr Assertio settlement, ₹849 cr labour-code charge, ₹1,468 cr Teva receipt; net about -₹472 cr), the underlying margin is still shrinking, and US revenue already fell 5.7% in Q4 FY26 as gRevlimid-type windfall sales faded. On P/E, the sector yardstick, the trailing 21.7x looks cheap against the 28-40x sector band and sits at P8 among peers. The forward P/E of 23.3x is higher than trailing (P38, about 9% below the peer median), EV/EBITDA is 16.1x (P31), and the stock trades at 90% of its 52-week range, so overall it is fair rather than clearly cheap. The biggest risk is that the US generics business keeps shrinking or faces a tariff, at the same time as MedTech integration losses (-29% segment margin) keep weighing on earnings.

fundamental.thesis: IDFC First Bank is a mid-sized private bank with a retail-heavy loan book and a strong deposit franchise (CASA 48.4%), now scaling fast after years of rebuilding profitability. The main risk is that rapid growth is outpacing the bank's profitability engine: CASA slipped from 50.8% to 48.4% and NIM was diluted by FCNR(B) funding, Q2 ROA fell to 0.93% from 1.06%, and capital adequacy (CAR) dropped to 15.05% from 15.6% while the loan book grows about 30%.

fundamental.thesis: Punjab National Bank is India's second-largest public-sector lender, with ₹13.4 lakh crore of advances that grew 14.7% YoY, led by MSME (+19.8%) and overseas loans (+62.7%). In Q2 FY27, total income rose 5.4% YoY to ₹38,185 cr and net profit rose 12.8% to ₹5,532 cr; asset quality keeps improving, with Gross NPA down from 3.19% to 2.95% to 2.55%, Net NPA at 0.25%, slippage at 0.77% and provision coverage at 97%, though the revenue trend is noisy because one period row looks inconsistent. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, the stock trades at 0.83x book against a 13% TTM ROE (17.3% in the latest quarter), which is about 44% below the regional-bank median P/B of 1.5x and in the bottom 15% of peers, so it grades as cheap; the trailing P/E of 6.75x is consistent with that but is not the main yardstick. The main concern is funding: cost of deposits rose from 2.50% to 2.74% YoY, CASA slipped from 37.0% to 36.6%, domestic deposits grew only 9.5% against 12.5% domestic loan growth, and treasury income fell 57%, all of which could cap the 2.6–2.7% margin guidance.

GAIL is India's largest gas transmission and marketing company. Gas marketing produced about 56% of segment profit in H1 (₹7,131 cr), regulated pipelines added ₹3,964 cr at a 58% margin, and petrochemicals lost ₹168 cr. Growth was very strong in H1 FY27: revenue rose 24.7% to ₹88,651 cr and PAT rose 115% to ₹9,395 cr. Q2 looks even faster, with implied revenue of about ₹47,300 cr (roughly +33% YoY, against +16.7% in Q1). By the press-release figures, Q2 revenue was ₹45,924 cr and PAT ₹4,650 cr, a margin of about 10.1%, down from 11.3% in Q1. The pre-computed trend signals mix half-year and quarter periods, so I did not rely on them. Using enterprise value to operating profit (EV/EBITDA) plus dividend yield, as the sector card advises for a volume and tariff business, valuation is fair. EV/EBITDA is 11.6x, exactly the peer median, and trailing P/E is 14.65x, at the peer median and just above the 8–14x energy range. P/B is 1.26x against an annualised H1 ROE of about 19%, which looks attractive. The forward P/E of 9.5x depends on FY27 estimates that analysts raised 28% in 30 days while trimming next-year estimates by 3.5%. The biggest risk is that the doubling of profit comes mostly from gas-marketing spreads, which swing with LNG prices and are not structural. That makes FY27 look like a peak year. The newly started Mangalore PTA plant (purified terephthalic acid, a petrochemical) also adds exposure to a segment that is currently losing money.

fundamental.thesis: Muthoot Finance is India's largest gold-loan NBFC. It benefits from lower interest rates, which cut its borrowing costs, and from high gold prices, which let it lend more against the same gold. In Q1 FY27 total income was ₹8,695 cr, up 34.5% year on year, and profit (PAT) was ₹2,825 cr, up 43.1%. Q2, worked out from the H1 totals, was about ₹9,788 cr income and ₹3,221 cr PAT, a 32.9% margin. Growth is still very strong but slowing: income growth has eased from +58% (9M FY26) to +34.5% (Q1 FY27), loan book growth from about 51% to 43%, and PAT margin from 36.2% to roughly 33%. For a lender the right valuation test is price-to-book against return on equity. A P/B of 3.04x looks fair for a 30% ROE and sits right at the peer median, so we grade it fair, not cheap. The P/E of 11.2x (8.6x forward) is 44% below the peer median, so a cheap case is possible if the 30% ROE holds after gold prices stop rising. The main risks are that gold, now falling from its highs, could slow loan growth and squeeze loan-to-value headroom, and the open GST search under Section 67 of the CGST Act, disclosed on 2026-11-02.

fundamental.thesis: Aurobindo Pharma is a large Indian generics maker that earns 92% of its revenue abroad, including 44% from the US and 31% from Europe; 89% of revenue comes from finished medicines and 11% from APIs (the active drug ingredients). Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹10,263 cr, up 23.9% YoY, and profit after tax (PAT) was ₹1,124 cr, up 32.5%, a sharp pickup from +6–8% growth in Q3–Q4 FY26. PAT margin edged up to about 11.0% from 10.5%, but part of this jump comes from buying Lannett, a US generics company consolidated from June 29, 2026, so the underlying organic growth is unclear, especially after US revenue fell 13% in Q4 FY26. On valuation I relied mainly on EV/EBITDA and checked it against peers: EV/EBITDA is 12.0x against a peer median of 21.4x, P/E is 24.0x against the 28–40x sector range and P15 among peers, and forward P/E of 16.4x is the cheapest in its peer group (P0), so the stock is cheap, though part of that discount reflects a lower ROE of 9.9% and heavy US generics exposure. Some snapshot figures look wrong: a 27% dividend yield, debt/equity of 21x when the company reports net cash of $189M, and a consensus target that does not match the 52-week range. The biggest risk is the US: if the review of generics in US tariff policy goes against Indian makers, or Lannett's integration slips, earnings could fall, and the stock is already near the top of its 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics company that sells mainly chronic-therapy medicines. Its revenue comes from branded generics in India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%) plus US generics (29%), and it ranks #1 in India in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 Indian pharma companies (IQVIA, MAT Sep-26). Growth is speeding up: quarterly revenue growth went from +14% in Q2FY26 to +20% in Q3FY26, +24.8% in Q1FY27 and about +33% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr). Q2 profit after tax rose 49% to ₹388 cr (a 21.6% margin), and H1FY27 revenue of ₹3,420 cr (+28.8%) and PAT of ₹722 cr (+39.9%) show margins widening from 19.0% to 21.1% over the period. Using pharma P/E plus peer rank as the yardstick, the trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28–40x sector range and right at the peer median (46th percentile), and the forward P/E of 26.3x builds in more growth, so the stock is fair rather than cheap; it is above the peer median on P/B (77th percentile) and EV/EBITDA (69th percentile), and it trades at 68% of its 52-week range. The biggest risks are the 29% of revenue from US generics, which faces the pending US Commerce review of generics, and the fact that margins are quoted 'adjusted' for forex losses while cash conversion is only about 0.85x profit, so earnings quality needs watching.

In Q2 FY27, PAT rose 27% YoY to ₹416 cr, net interest income rose 31% to ₹873 cr, advances rose 26% and deposits rose 21%, while gross NPA improved from 2.17% (9M FY26) to 1.91% (FY26) to 1.44% (H1 FY27); however, the table's accelerating and margin-expansion signals are unreliable because the FY26 revenue row (₹2,830 cr) looks wrong and Q2 revenue has no YoY figure, so the firmer evidence is the implied sequential rise in PAT from about ₹382 cr to ₹416 cr. fundamental.thesis: Redington is one of India's largest IT and mobility distributors, with a large Middle East/Africa (ROW) arm. It earns about 2% EBITDA margins on very high volumes, so it is really a working-capital and distribution business, not the order-book Industrials or IT-services model its sector tags suggest. In Q1FY27, the latest extracted quarter, revenue was ₹34,922 cr, up 34.6% YoY. Growth has picked up from +22.1% in Q1FY26 and +15.7% in Q3FY26. PAT rose 94.6% to ₹453 cr and PAT margin widened from about 1.1% to 1.3%, though the SISA segment (+62.5%) drove much of this while ROW grew only 6.5%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E against low-margin distribution peers, not the Industrials or IT-services medians. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 14.3x, forward P/E 10.1x, EV/EBITDA 9.4x and P/B 2.1x with ROE of 13.1%, all in the bottom 10–20% of the broad market. All 6 analysts rate it a buy and have raised FY EPS estimates by 16% over 90 days. The biggest risk is cash conversion: FY26 operating cash flow was only 0.16x PAT, so faster growth may be soaking up working capital. Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-04 but have not been extracted yet, so this view is one quarter old.

fundamental.thesis: Gland Pharma makes injectable generics and does contract manufacturing (CDMO) for global pharma companies, with the US now its biggest market. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 23.3% YoY to ₹1,834 cr and PAT grew 58.3% to ₹291 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from +6.0% in Q2FY26 to around +20–23% over the last three quarters, helped by 42% US growth and 31% CDMO growth, and PAT margin rose from 12.0% to 15.9% YoY. Momentum did ease from the previous quarter, though: revenue rose only 2% QoQ, PAT fell from ₹317 cr to ₹291 cr, and EBITDA margin slipped from 27.0% to 26.2%. On valuation I used P/E and EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E of 35.3× sits inside the 28–40× pharma range and at the broad-market median (P50). Forward P/E of 24.1× and EV/EBITDA of 20.1× (P42) build in growth without looking stretched, so I grade it fair, with ROE of only 10.5% capping any re-rating. The biggest risk is concentration: the US is now 64% of revenue, so any US tariff review of generics or any outcome from the recently concluded USFDA inspection at Dundigal hits a business whose India, Canada/Australia/NZ and Rest of World revenues are all falling.

LG Electronics India is a leading consumer-durables maker in India. Home appliances (ACs, refrigerators, washing machines) bring in about 88% of revenue at a thin 9.4% segment margin, and home entertainment brings in about 12% at a much richer 38.9% margin. The business is speeding up: H1 FY27 revenue rose 17.4% YoY to ₹14,613 cr and PAT rose 26.5% to ₹1,142 cr. The implied Q2 (H1 minus Q1) shows revenue of about ₹7,380 cr (+19% YoY) and PAT of about ₹489 cr (+26% YoY), continuing a recovery in revenue growth from -6.4% to +8.1%, then +15.5%, then about +19% over the last four quarters. Earnings are backed by cash (CFO/PAT 1.43x) and the company holds ₹4,569 cr of net cash. The reported 5.99 debt/equity looks like a units error, since the only debt is ₹482 cr of lease liabilities. On valuation, the stock trades at 64.8x trailing P/E, 41.2x forward P/E and 42.5x EV/EBITDA. That puts it in the top quintile of the broad market (P81–P92; no tight durables peers were available), but inside the 60–100x premium band the sector card treats as normal for consumer discretionary. With earnings growing about 25% and a forward P/E of 41x, I grade it fair, not cheap, and the stock sits at 68% of its 52-week range. The main risk is the board-approved move into automotive electronics: it consumed ₹1,163 cr of capex in H1 and the company has given no financial targets for it. Together with price competition in appliances and rising crude feeding into input costs, this could dilute returns on equity (ROE, currently 24.7%) and squeeze margins.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a PSU mid-cap refinery (ONGC subsidiary) processing ~4.4 MMT/quarter of crude at Mangalore, operating in a policy-administered margin environment where GRMs, not crude price alone, drive earnings. H1FY27 revenue surged +67.6% YoY to ₹77,199 cr and PAT exploded +697.6% YoY to ₹2,846 cr (PAT margin 3.7%), a dramatic recovery from the near-zero-profit FY26 base (PAT margin 1.8%), with EBITDA margin expanding to 6.6% on strong throughput and higher product realisations — though a fire incident at the CHT unit on 30-Sep-2026 provisionally cost ₹118 cr and creates near-term operational uncertainty. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive refinery (per sector card guidance for PSU OMCs/refiners), MRPL trades at 5.97× EV/EBITDA versus a broad-market median of 23.3× — placing it at P3 in its peer universe — making it structurally cheap, though the sector card explicitly cautions this discount is 'policy-priced' (permanent policy risk, not a valuation error); trailing P/E of 14.5× sits at the upper end of the PSU OMC range (6–10× + yield), but the forward P/E collapses to 3.4×, implying the street is pricing in a very strong FY27 full-year earnings recovery. The key risk is that elevated crude at $97.97/bbl directly compresses refining marketing margins for OMC-adjacent refiners, estimate revisions are sharply negative (-9.6% 30d, -21.2% next-FY 90d) signalling analyst concern about GRM sustainability, and the CHT fire adds operational/insurance settlement uncertainty over the next 1–2 quarters.

fundamental.thesis: Oil India is India's second-largest government-owned upstream E&P company, producing crude oil and natural gas primarily from Assam and Rajasthan, now expanding offshore under the 'Samudra Manthan' initiative. Q1FY27 marks a sharp acceleration: consolidated revenue surged +47.3% YoY to ₹12,886 cr and PAT nearly doubled (+96.9% YoY) to ₹4,027 cr, with PAT margin expanding from 11.4% in Q2FY26 to 31.2% — pure operating leverage on elevated crude and gas realizations rather than structural improvement. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive PSU upstream business (sector card guidance), OIL trades at 8.31× EV/EBITDA and a trailing P/E of 10.33× — marginally above the sector card's PSU upstream range of 6–10× but forward P/E collapses to 6.86×; ranked P7 percentile (bottom cohort) across 473 peers on all metrics, making it clearly cheap in relative terms. The primary risk is the combined ~₹7,527 cr contingent tax and Assam land liabilities with imminent Supreme Court rulings, compounded by disclosed corporate governance non-compliance (missing independent/woman directors) and endemic PSU windfall-tax policy risk as crude prices rise.

ACME Solar is a mid-sized renewable power producer (IPP) with 2,990 MW running and about 5,080 MW under construction, and its 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs) are mostly with central-government buyers like NTPC. Such a company grows through new capacity and the spread between its returns and its cost of debt, and the new BESS (battery storage) and FDRE (round-the-clock renewable) projects are its growth engine. H1 FY27 revenue rose 78.2% YoY to ₹1,745 cr and PAT rose 105% to ₹504 cr. YoY growth has sped up from +59% (FY26) to +63% (Q1) to +78% (H1), and PAT margin rose from 19.9% to 24.7% to 28.9%. Within H1, the September quarter works out to roughly ₹791 cr revenue (below Q1, which fits the monsoon dip in solar output) but higher PAT of about ₹269 cr. Operating capacity barely moved in Q1 (+3.5% YoY), so near-term growth now depends on commissioning, which has started: 66.68 MW of solar plus BESS units went live in early November, and a 400 MW FDRE PPA was signed with NTPC. Valuation is fair: I graded it on EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for capital-heavy businesses. At 15.2x it is about 35% below the market median (P26), and the forward P/E of 13.7x is far below the trailing 40.7x, which suggests earnings growth is expected. But P/B of 4.0x against a 10.4% ROE is not cheap, and the stock sits at 80% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt/equity is about 3.9x, interest coverage is only 2.47x, finance costs take about 40% of EBITDA, and H1 free cash flow was -₹5,263 cr on ₹6,329 cr of capex. Grid connection delays (substations delivered on time only 60% of the time, about 6 months late on average) or higher interest rates could hold back the earnings ramp.

The valuation looks fair, not cheap, and the balance sheet is stretched: net debt is about 4.4 times yearly operating profit (EBITDA), and income from regulated tariffs is falling. News sentiment is neutral and out of date, and the results from the 5 November board meeting are not reflected yet. The chart is still in a long-term downtrend (death-cross, about 15% below the 200-day average). The recent short-term bounce is not a confirmed pullback to support, and in today's mean-reverting market that kind of setup cannot support a buy on its own. On top of that, the macro desk has Utilities on underweight and this is a midcap, so we don't hold it and won't start a position. We should look again once the November results are in and the price either holds support near 124 or climbs back above 137.

fundamental.thesis: CESC is a West Bengal-regulated power utility with a coal mine and other power operations, and its earnings depend heavily on tariff orders and regulatory income. In FY26, revenue rose 9.2% to Rs 18,570 cr and PAT rose 12.6% to Rs 1,542 cr, but no reliable filing data is available after FY26, and the trend signals mix annual and part-year periods, so I cannot confirm whether growth is speeding up or slowing down. Valuation is fair on EV/EBITDA of 10.92x, supported by a trailing P/E of 14.68x inside the 10-18x utilities range and P/B of 1.81x for 12.5% ROE; I gave little weight to the cheap broad-market peer rank because it does not compare utilities, and I ignored the 348% dividend yield, the +59.7% target upside (which does not fit the roughly Rs 170 price implied by the market cap and EPS) and the -100% estimate revisions as likely data errors. The biggest risk is that net debt of Rs 15,747 cr (4.44x EBITDA) and a 0.9 current ratio leave little cushion if regulatory income, already down from Rs 1,249 cr to Rs 903 cr, keeps falling or pending tariff appeals go against the company, and the results due from the 5 November board meeting could quickly change this view.

Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, Chennai-based vehicle-finance NBFC. Its group also includes housing finance, an asset manager and a general-insurance joint venture, and it is known for some of the best asset quality in its peer set. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 show standalone quarterly PAT of ₹475 cr (+21% YoY), H1FY27 consolidated PAT of ₹1,153 cr (+20%), disbursements up 28% YoY in Q2 (H1 +25%) and core lending AUM up 19% to ₹65,992 cr. Gross Stage 3 improved to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rose to 51% from 45%. One caution is that Q2 profit from operations grew only 11%, so part of the profit growth is coming from lower credit costs rather than core earnings; the pre-computed 'margin contracting' signal comes from mixed revenue bases and is not meaningful. On the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE), P/B of 3.5x against ROE of 16.75% (up from 15.9%) is fair to slightly rich: the stock is at P67 on P/B and P100 on forward P/E within its credit-services peer group, though the cheapest peers are the state-owned power lenders PFC and REC, a lower-quality comparison set. The biggest near-term risk is the chairman's resignation announced alongside results, alongside a capital adequacy ratio that slipped to 18.5% from 19.3% and a ₹66 cr Motor TP claims provision at Royal Sundaram after the Supreme Court judgment.

drivers: Management tone constructive but no formal guidance: 'steady sustainable growth' and 'outlook optimistic on domestic auto and financial services'. Results backed it up: consolidated PAT +20% to Rs. 1,153 cr, Q2 disbursements +28% YoY, AUM +19%
Market liked the H1FY27 results: stock rose 4.1% the day after filing (₹4,057 → ₹4,222)
Concerns: capital adequacy fell from 19.3% to 18.5%, and Royal Sundaram's PAT more than halved after a Rs. 66 cr motor third-party claims provision following the Supreme Court ruling
News gap: 2 headlines but no FinBERT score. Sector flow neutral (Financials +0.64% vs benchmark), so it adds nothing either way

technical.setup: Bounce inside a long-term downtrend: price has recovered above SMA20 (4,080) with MACD turning bullish, but it is still below a falling SMA50 (4,375) and SMA200 (4,640) in a death-cross structure, it lags both Nifty and its peers, and in the current mean-reverting market this looks like a relief rally into resistance rather than a confirmed pullback-to-support entry.

trader.reasoning: We are not buying today because the three analysts disagree. Q2FY27 results were solid (profit up 21%, loan disbursements up 28%, bad loans down) and the market liked them. But the valuation looks only fair, at 3.5x book value against a 16.75% return on equity. Underlying operating profit grew just 11%, so part of the profit jump came from setting aside less for bad loans. The chairman's sudden resignation alongside the results also adds governance and succession risk, which matters more for a midcap. On the charts, the stock is still in a downtrend below its falling 50-day and 200-day averages, and right now rallies like this have been fading rather than continuing. So we wait with no position. We would look again if the stock pulls back and holds near ₹4,080 (its 20-day average) or clearly breaks above ₹4,375 once there is more clarity on leadership.

drivers: Q2FY27 management tone: 'Margins at bottom in Q2; trajectory will be upward from Q3 onwards', helped by the October rate hike repricing about 70% of floating-rate loans by December. Deposits grew 18.8% YoY and retail disbursements rose to ₹90,000 cr from ₹76,000 cr.

Main risks: NIM is at a cycle low of 3.32%, and LCR is 113%, near the bottom of its 110–120% target range. The reported Q2 PAT of ₹1,950 cr looks inconsistent with the bank's size and should be checked against the results filing.
The market's results-day reaction was IN-LINE but slightly negative (-2.3% over 1–2 days), so it does not confirm management's optimism.

News since then is positive: 'shares witness strong buying, rise 7% in 1 month' and 'new CEO, improving fundamentals', though some reports also note 'challenges'. FinBERT data is missing and sector flow is neutral.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

Q2FY27 was a record quarter, with revenue up 27.8% and profit up 34%, and the stock jumped 11.6% the day after the results. But much of that growth came from refining margins inflated by Middle East supply disruption, which management itself calls temporary, while retail and media profits fell. That is why valuation is graded only fair, not cheap. On the charts, the stock has already rallied straight up to its falling 200-day average near 1,320 at the top of its recent range. With no position and only about ₹58.7k in cash, it makes more sense to wait for a pullback towards support near 1,232, or for a confirmed break above the 200-day average, than to buy after the post-results jump.

fundamental.thesis: SBIN is India's largest bank, with a ₹78.9 trillion balance sheet, and its loan book is still growing fast: advances rose 17.8% YoY in Q2FY27, with SME up 22% and agri up 22.6%. Q2FY27 total income was ₹1,51,084 cr (+8.2% YoY), slightly faster than Q1's +7.8%. PAT was ₹23,038 cr (+14.3%), but one-off gains flatter that figure: ₹6,879 cr from selling part of SBI Funds Management in the consolidated results, plus NSE/ARCIL stake-sale gains booked to reserves. Core quality is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 1.49% to 1.39% and credit cost fell to 0.22%, but whole-bank margin (NIM) slipped from 3.03% to 2.94% and the share of low-cost deposits (CASA) fell from 39.5% to 38.3%. Valuation is judged on price-to-book against return on equity, as the sector card says to for banks: at 1.53x book with 15.5% trailing ROE (18.7% annualised this quarter), the stock is fair, close to cheap, sits at the 57th percentile of its peers on P/B, and is mid-range at 45% of its 52-week band.

trader.reasoning: The fundamental (fair valuation at 1.53x book with about 15.5% ROE, 17.8% loan growth) and sentiment (bullish on record Q2 profit and better asset quality) views both lean positive, but only moderately, at 0.55 conviction each. Both carry clear caveats. Margin (NIM) has slipped to 2.94%, the share of low-cost deposits is falling, deposits are growing slower than loans, and this quarter's profit is helped by one-off stake-sale gains. fundamental.thesis: ITC is a conglomerate whose profits still come mainly from cigarettes, with FMCG, paper, agri and hotels-adjacent businesses around it; the sector card notes it trades on its own conglomerate multiple backed by dividends, so it should not be read as a pure FMCG name. Q2FY27 is the second quarter of a sharp profit decline after an unprecedented cigarette tax increase: consolidated revenue grew only +5% YoY, while implied Q2 PAT of about ₹4,229 cr (H1 ₹8,738 cr minus Q1 ₹4,509 cr) fell roughly -16% YoY, after -15.6% in Q1, against PAT growth of +1% to +3% through FY26. Cigarette net revenue fell -21% and segment results fell -27%, which drove consolidated EBITDA down -16%; non-cigarette businesses offset part of this, with EBITDA up +22%, FMCG Others revenue up +19% (a 14-quarter high) with margins up 50 bps, and paper PBIT up +48%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus peer rank because ITC is a conglomerate: at 12.1x EV/EBITDA and 16.9x trailing P/E it is the cheapest of 13 FMCG peers on every multiple (around 60-67% below the sector median of 51.5x P/E), near its 52-week low, and cash conversion has improved (CFO/PAT 0.96x vs 0.59x a year ago), so it is cheap. The cheapness looks like a tax-driven structural de-rating rather than a mispricing, and analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (FY EPS -4.8% over 90 days), so the multiple may stay low until cigarette volumes stabilise.

drivers: Market reaction beat the numbers: ITC rose 3.1% in the day after its 2 Nov results and 5.4% over two days, so investors looked past the weak profit print
Management results are mixed and give no outlook: H1 revenue grew 35.5%, but much of that comes from the 1 Feb 2026 cigarette excise hike, while PAT fell 17% and EBITDA fell 16%

But that low price looks like a lasting de-rating caused by the cigarette tax hike: profit has now fallen about 16% two quarters in a row and analysts keep cutting estimates, so the valuation alone does not make it a buy. The market's positive reaction to results is a mildly good sign, but it is not strong. The chart shows price stretched above its upper band, still just below the 200-day average and with no confirmed trend, and in this market recent jumps have tended to fade rather than continue. No analyst gives a clear buy, so we hold at zero shares for now. We would look again on a pullback toward ₹264 support, or once cigarette volumes show signs of steadying.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Unilever is India's largest FMCG company, with leading brands across home care, personal care and foods. Revenue growth sped up from +10.1% YoY in Q1FY27 to +14.5% in Q2FY27 (₹18,226 cr). Profit did not follow: PAT was flat at ₹2,790 cr (+0.3% YoY, after -3.2% in Q1), so PAT margin shrank from 17.5% a year ago to 15.3%. We also have no volume-growth figure for Q2; the last reported figure was 6% for Q4FY26, so we can't tell how much of the 14.5% is real demand and how much is price or mix. On P/E, the standard yardstick for FMCG, the stock trades at 46.6x trailing and 39.4x forward, inside the 40-60x sector range and only slightly above the peer median of 43.8x (P60 in its sector; P80 on forward P/E and EV/EBITDA), so we grade it fair. Being near its 52-week low gives some comfort on entry price, but it is not a bargain. The biggest risk is that sales keep growing while profit stays flat, which suggests input costs or extra spending are eating the gains.

fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

fundamental.thesis: UltraTech is India's largest cement maker with 210.1 mtpa of global grey capacity, and together with Adani it controls about 45% of industry capacity, which supports pricing discipline. Q2FY27 revenue rose 18.9% YoY to ₹23,024 cr and PAT rose 21.3% to ₹1,501 cr, with revenue growth accelerating from +15.8% in Q1, on 12.9% volume growth and EBITDA per tonne of ₹974 (+₹60 YoY, inside the ₹900–1,100 healthy band). The weak 6.5% PAT margin and the drop in EBITDA per tonne from ₹1,214 in Q1 mostly reflect the monsoon quarter, though fuel (+14%) and packing-bag (+30%) costs are rising with crude. The preferred cement yardstick, EV/EBITDA, was unavailable, so I graded on peers: a trailing P/E of 39.6x sits near the Materials peer median of 37.3x (P53) and the forward P/E is 25.1x, which makes it fair, but a P/B of 4.5x against a 10.6% ROE is rich, and the biggest risk is sell-side FY EPS estimates being cut 11–13% over 90 days while 33 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a classic pre-derating pattern.

ONGC is India's largest upstream oil and gas producer, so its earnings move with crude and gas prices, under a government-set policy framework (Energy sector card). The latest trend table stops at FY26, when revenue fell 3.9% to ₹132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to ₹32,894 cr. However, the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 show a sharp turn: standalone Q2 PAT of ₹15,489 cr is about +57% versus roughly ₹9,848 cr in Q2 FY26, and H1 PAT of ₹32,522 cr is about +82% versus ₹17,872 cr, mainly because crude is higher. Quarterly revenue was not available from the filings, and the yfinance Q1 row (₹1.64L cr revenue) is consolidated and includes the refining subsidiaries, so it is not comparable. On valuation, I used P/E and dividend yield as the sector card advises for state-owned upstream companies: trailing P/E of 8.0x (forward 6.1x) and EV/EBITDA of 4.6x sit inside the card's 6–10x policy-priced band and slightly below the peer median of 9.2x (P33 on P/E, P17 on P/B at 0.9x). That makes it fair rather than cheap, because the discount reflects lasting policy risk. The yfinance dividend yield of 699% is clearly a data error and I ignored it. The biggest risk is that the government takes back the crude windfall through a windfall tax, subsidy sharing or a gas-price cap. Analysts have cut next-year EPS estimates by 3.6% over 90 days, which suggests they expect profits to fall back.

drivers: Q2FY27 results send mixed signals: 'Net profit up 57% YoY to ₹15,489 crore' but 'Q2 misses estimates; profit falls 9% QoQ'

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finserv is a financial-services holding company. Its value comes mainly from its 51.3% stake in Bajaj Finance (AUM ₹5,84,624 cr, up 26%), plus its life insurance, general insurance, housing finance and AMC businesses. In H1 FY27, consolidated revenue grew 17.9% YoY to ₹85,453 cr and PAT grew 21.6% to ₹12,249 cr. That is a pickup from +11.8% revenue growth in H1 FY26, though the half-year figures imply Q2 alone grew a slower ~15-16% after Q1's +19.2%. Lending quality keeps improving: Bajaj Finance's gross NPA fell from 1.24% to 1.06% YoY, net NPA from 0.60% to 0.42%, and life insurance VNB rose 53% to ₹783 cr. The PAT margin jumped from about 6.5% in FY26 to 14.3%, which looks like a change in how PAT is defined rather than a real improvement, so we do not count it as margin expansion. For a lender-heavy holding company we graded valuation on P/B against ROE, not P/E. At 3.5x book for a 14.6% ROE, ranking P73 in its sector on both P/B and trailing P/E (28.2x vs a 17.5x median), the stock looks fair, leaning full. Two things argue against calling it expensive: the forward P/E of 18.7x implies earnings growth, and the stock sits low in its 52-week range (21%). No sum-of-the-parts holding-company discount data was provided. The main risks are general insurance underwriting, now loss-making (combined ratio 104.7%, PAT down 24%), and possible dilution from Bajaj Finance's ₹11,700 cr QIP plus ₹5,800 cr of promoter warrants.

The EBITDA margin trend is down, from 37–38% to about 30.5% for FY26. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA and P/B plus ROE, as the sector card suggests for capital-intensive regulated utilities. EV/EBITDA is 9.9x, P/B is 2.1x against a 16% ROE, and trailing P/E is 12.75x, which sits inside the 10–18x utilities range. So I grade it fair, not cheap. fundamental.thesis: Avenue Supermarts (DMART) is India's dominant value-format grocery retailer (~500 stores, FY26) built on an everyday-low-price model with best-in-class inventory turnover (4.93× for H1FY27), giving it durable structural advantages in organised grocery. H1FY27 revenue grew +16.4% YoY to ₹38,439 cr (steady within a consistent +13–16% band over six periods), but PAT grew only +10.0% to ₹1,603 cr as PAT margin contracted to 4.17% from 4.4% — finance costs surged 84% to fund aggressive expansion, the Avenue E-commerce subsidiary dragged ₹166.62 cr in losses, and CFO/PAT collapsed from 0.96× (H1FY26) to 0.34× (H1FY27), signalling a meaningful deterioration in earnings quality. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary valuation yardstick (capital-intensive retail with PAT margins distorted by lease and e-commerce costs), DMART trades at 52.4× EV/EBITDA — P100 (most expensive) among 13 Consumer Discr. peers and +51% above the sector median — while trailing P/E of 89.1× is also P100 and +73% above sector median; sell-side EPS estimates have been revised down -3.1% over 90 days, a textbook pre-derating signal. The biggest risk is that the quick-commerce threat from Blinkit erodes SSSG momentum just as e-commerce losses widen and leverage builds, triggering the 25–40% multiple reset the sector card explicitly flags for any guidance disappointment at these premium valuations.

fundamental.thesis: ICICIPRULI (now ICICI Life Insurance) is one of India's largest private life insurers, with ₹3.29 lakh cr of assets under management, a 229.9% solvency ratio and a 99.3% claim-settlement ratio. New business has picked up after a flat FY26: in H1FY27, annualised premium equivalent (APE) grew +15.1% YoY to ₹4,935 cr (FY26 was only +2.2%), retail APE recovered from -0.1% to +9.9%, VNB grew +22.3% to ₹1,283 cr, and VNB margin widened to 26.0% from 24.7% in FY26. Gross premium grew +15.3% to ₹24,505 cr and PAT +26.5% to ₹760 cr, but PAT is not the right yardstick for a life insurer. On the life-insurer yardstick, price to embedded value (P/EV), the stock trades at about 1.24x (₹70,497 cr market cap vs ₹56,669 cr EV, which grew +12.2% YoY; FY26 return on EV was 11.9%), which looks cheap. Peer ranks agree: P25 on P/B and forward P/E, at a 22–25% discount to the peer median. The biggest risk is growth fading: management has guided that protection growth will cool from the 40–50% pace of the last four quarters, and Prudential's pending reclassification from promoter to investor could mean an overhang of stake sales, while the market is in a RISK_OFF regime.

fundamental.thesis: Godrej Consumer Products is India's largest home and personal care company, commanding leadership in household insecticides (Goodknight), hair colour (Godrej Expert), and liquid detergents, with material EM exposure across Africa, Indonesia, and Latin America that amplifies both growth and FX risk. Q4FY26 (latest official quarter) showed revenue of ₹3,885 cr (+11.0% YoY, recovering sharply from +4.0% in Q2FY26) with PAT of ₹452 cr (+10.0% YoY), and volume growth accelerating to 8% from 3% two quarters prior — a genuine demand signal — though full-year FY26 PAT was up just +0.5% on +8.5% revenue growth, reflecting margin headwinds that only partially normalised by year-end. At trailing P/E of 54.9× the stock sits within the 40–65× FMCG sector card range but at P80 vs household-and-personal-care peers (+25% premium to sector median), making it expensive on peer-relative terms; however, forward P/E of 36.3× (vs trailing) signals meaningful earnings recovery is priced in, and the stock trading near its 52-week low (7.8% of range) provides modestly better entry optics than the headline multiple suggests. The biggest risk is the combination of elevated reported debt/equity (34.9) with active Argentina-hyperinflation drag (₹13.5 cr profit headwind cited in Q1FY27 exceptional items) and consistent downward EPS estimate revisions (-1.6% over 90 days), which could cap re-rating even if the domestic volume recovery continues.

Bajaj Holdings is a near debt-free holding company. Its earnings come mainly from its stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv, through dividends and its share of their profits. Its investment portfolio is worth about ₹2.40L cr at market value against a cost of ₹21,371 cr. In H1FY27, reported revenue fell 20.1% YoY to ₹576 cr and consolidated PAT fell 6.7% to ₹4,845 cr, and the trend table shows revenue growth slowing from triple digits to negative. That headline is distorted: last year included a one-off ₹1,522 cr gain from selling Bajaj Finserv shares. Without it, PAT grew about 37% YoY, and the share of associate profits rose about 32% to ₹4,626 cr, helped by Bajaj Auto (+62% PAT in Q2) and Bajaj Finserv (+23%). For a holding company the right yardstick is the discount to NAV, not P/E or EV/EBITDA. The EV/EBITDA of 128x and the 157% dividend yield in the snapshot are artefacts of this structure, and the yield figure looks like a data error. The share price is about ₹10,300, about 28% of the way up its 52-week range, against a reported NAV of ₹21,578 per share. That is roughly a 52% discount, inside the 40–60% norm for Indian holding companies, so I grade it fair. That fits the P/B of 1.5x with a 12.6% ROE and the trailing P/E of 11.4x, which is in the bottom third of its sector. The biggest risk is concentration: value and earnings depend almost entirely on two Bajaj Group stocks. Reported results are also lumpy, with one-off stake sales, lower dividends from Bajaj Auto after its buyback, weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.40x, mostly because associate profits are not cash) and a pending RBI decision on CIC status.

fundamental.thesis: Ambuja Cements is the Adani group's cement arm and, together with UltraTech, part of a roughly 45%-share duopoly forming at the top of Indian cement. It is part-way through absorbing ACC, Orient, Penna and Sanghi, and plans to add about 30 MTPA of capacity, funded from its own cash. The fundamentals are weakening: Q2FY27 revenue was ₹9,197 cr, about +1% YoY (estimated from H1 revenue of ₹18,640 cr, down 3.8%, and Q1 revenue of ₹9,500 cr, down 7.6%). Q2 profit fell to ₹236 cr, a 2.6% profit margin, down from 6.1% in Q1 and about 14% in FY26. EBITDA per tonne dropped to ₹770, below the ₹900–1,100 healthy band and down from ₹887 in FY26, because imported fuel costs rose (₹1.87 per 1,000 kcal vs ₹1.60 a year ago) and volumes were flat. Strong growth in trade sales (+8.6%) and ready-mix concrete (+19%) only partly made up for this. Measured on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, the stock trades at 18.5×, close to the sector median of 17.9× (P53), so valuation is fair rather than cheap. The low trailing P/E of 22× and P/B of 1.7× look attractive, but ROE is only 8.3%, forward P/E (26.9×) is above trailing P/E, and analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by 49% in 30 days and 68% in 90 days. The biggest risk is that fuel costs stay high (spot imported fuel is ₹2.80–2.85 per 1,000 kcal) while the Penna and Sanghi plants run at only about 50% utilisation, which would keep margins compressed and estimates falling, even though management guides for 2H volume growth ahead of the industry.

fundamental.thesis: PFC is India's largest government-owned infrastructure finance NBFC, the apex lender to the power sector (generation, transmission, distribution) and parent of REC Limited, with a combined consolidated AUM of ~₹10L+ cr — a proposed merger (PFC absorbs REC at 88:100, effective April 2027) would make it one of Asia's largest infrastructure lenders. Q1FY27 revenue was essentially flat at −0.04% YoY (₹28,527 cr) with PAT barely moving at +0.18% YoY (₹8,998 cr, 31.5% margin), loan book growth of only 7% YoY, and rising forex losses (₹837 cr vs ₹706 cr prior year) — a sharp deceleration from Q4/FY26's 16% PAT growth and a clear single-quarter slowdown, though CFO/PAT of 1.81x confirms earnings quality remains cash-backed. Using P/B + ROE — the correct yardstick per sector card for lenders — PFC at 1.08x P/B with 20.5% ROE is unambiguously cheap (threshold: P/B < 1.5 + ROE > 12% = cheap), and is ranked P0 (cheapest in peer group) on both P/B (1.1x vs sector median 3.0x) and trailing P/E (5.6x vs sector median 20.1x); asset quality is exceptional with GNPA 0.66% and net NPA 0.13%. The primary risk is that forward P/E (6.7x) exceeds trailing P/E (5.6x) — a market signal that earnings are expected to decline — compounded by PFC-REC merger integration complexity and EPS dilution risk from the 88:100 exchange ratio, all set against a RISK_OFF macro regime with sustained FII outflows (−₹41,850 cr 30-day net) that create a structural re-rating headwind for PSU financials.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Steel & Power is a large integrated domestic steelmaker in the middle of a big capacity ramp (15.6 MT, up from 12.6 MT a year ago), with 92% of sales in India and a rising share of flat products (61%). Q2FY27 revenue was ₹16,679 cr, up 42.7% YoY, the fourth straight quarter of faster growth (from +3.7% to +10.7% to +23.0% to +42.7%), driven by 27% higher sales volume (2.38 MT); EBITDA rose 34% to ₹2,504 cr (about ₹10,500 per tonne), but PAT grew only 21.4% to ₹771 cr (4.6% margin) because finance costs jumped 53% and EBITDA margin slipped from 16.0% to 15.0% YoY. On the sector card's yardstick for steel (EV/EBITDA, 5–8x at mid-cycle), 14.2x is expensive; it only looks fair against the 16-peer median (P33) because that median includes paint and adhesive companies, and the cheap forward P/E of 12.2x relies on earnings roughly tripling just as FY estimates have been cut 13.3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that higher interest costs on expansion debt, plus the weak Mauritius subsidiary (₹3,113 cr accumulated losses, ₹4,769 cr parent loan), keep absorbing volume gains while crude, a strong dollar and the risk-off market squeeze steel spreads.

fundamental.thesis: Alkem Laboratories is India's #3 pharmaceutical company by prescriptions and #1 in trade generics, operating a ~68% domestic branded-generic franchise supplemented by fast-growing international arms (US +20.3%, ROW +26.7% in FY26). FY26 revenue grew +13.5% YoY to ₹14,712 cr with EBITDA expanding +19.6% to ₹3,052 cr (20.4% margin), but PAT growth lagged at only +6.3% (₹2,302 cr, 15.6% margin) due to a revised upward tax rate and ~₹1,350 cr in Q4FY26 exceptional charges (gratuity liability reclassification + real estate impairment); PAT margin has structurally contracted from 19.4% in H1FY26 to 15.6% for FY26, and cash conversion is weak at 0.59× CFO/PAT. At 27.4× trailing P/E — fractionally below the 28-40× sector benchmark and at P31 among 14 pharma peers against a sector median of 36.4× — Alkem is fairly valued with a moderate discount; forward P/E of 23.1× signals earnings growth is priced in, and EV/EBITDA of 20.2× is modestly below the 21.4× peer median, leaving limited re-rating upside without a catalyst. The dominant risk to the thesis is the simultaneous departure of the CEO and CFO (both transitions flagged in FY27 filings), creating a senior management vacuum precisely when the Occlutech MedTech acquisition is pending integration, trade-generic growth is stalling at +4.3% YoY, and the US tariff framework for generics remains under an active one-year Commerce review.

fundamental.thesis: Mankind Pharma is a mainly India-focused branded drug maker, ranked #1 by prescriptions for nine straight years with a 15.2% share and limited direct exposure to US tariffs. Q2 FY27 is not reported separately in the data, but H1 less Q1 implies revenue of about Rs 4,337 cr (about +17% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 716 cr (about +38%), with quarterly revenue growth accelerating from +11.5% in Q3 FY26 to +11.8%, +12.9% and about +17%, and H1 PAT margin up 210 bps to 15.4%, backed by cash generation of 1.41x CFO/PAT. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, the stock is expensive: the listed 50.5x P/E appears to use FY26 EPS and is about 43x on my trailing-12-month estimate, still above the 28-40x sector range, while EV/EBITDA of 28.0x is 31% above the peer median (P77); I ignored the implausible 8.0% dividend yield and used net debt of 1.1x EBITDA (FY26) rather than the 38.11 debt/equity flag, which looks like a percentage. The biggest risk is that this premium assumes the Q2 jump will last, yet the source of the step-up is not visible in this data, Consumer Healthcare grew only 2.6% in H1, and FY26 volume growth was just 2.3%.

fundamental.thesis: Ashok Leyland is India's second-largest commercial vehicle manufacturer (MHCV + LCV), with a dominant domestic franchise and Hinduja Group backing — a cyclical play on infrastructure-linked freight demand and government fleet renewal (Parivartan). At a trailing P/E of 23.86× the stock sits within the Auto sector benchmark range of 18–28×, grading as fair; EV/EBITDA at 10.89× and a forward P/E of 17.25× (well below trailing) suggest modest earnings growth is priced in, and the peer ranking of P0 on both P/E and EV/EBITDA vs the Industrials peer group offers relative cheapness, though that comparison set is diluted by high-multiple capital goods and defence names. fundamental.thesis: Supreme Industries is India's largest plastics processor, selling plastic pipes (including CPVC), industrial, packaging and consumer products through about 50,000 distributors. Dixon Technologies is India's largest contract electronics maker (EMS). It assembles smartphones, TVs, lighting, IT hardware and telecom gear, and is building camera-module and display capacity under the PLI scheme and the China+1 shift. The filed H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹37,938 cr and PAT of ₹1,129 cr, with PAT up 51% YoY. That leaves an implied Q2 of about ₹21,900–22,400 cr revenue and ₹411–466 cr PAT, which is only about a 2% PAT margin against 4.3–4.5% in Q1 FY27. Q1 revenue grew +21% to +25% (the two extracted Q1 rows disagree). The reported +147% H1 revenue growth and the ₹4,959 cr FY26 row do not reconcile with the quarterly figures, so the growth rate cannot be trusted. Margins are being diluted as volume grows faster than profit. Because this is an assembly-heavy, low-margin business, I graded on EV/EBITDA plus trailing P/E. EV/EBITDA is 32.3x, and trailing P/E of 42.9x sits at the top of the 28–45x Industrials range, so I grade it fair-to-full rather than cheap even though the stock is only 22% up its 52-week range. The peer-rank block compares Dixon with IT-services companies (WIPRO, INFY, PERSISTENT), which are not real peers, so I gave its 'P100 expensive' verdict little weight. The forward P/E is above the trailing P/E, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7% over 30 days and 10% over 90 days while ratings stay 22 buy. That pattern often comes before a de-rating. FY26 cash conversion was also weak: cash from operations was only 0.22x PAT and free cash flow was -₹271 cr.

The backlog of Rs 14,250 cr (+16%) covers only about 1.3x trailing revenue, well below the 3x level that gives multi-year visibility. Using EV/EBITDA, the right measure for an order-book capital-goods business, the stock trades at 53.5x versus a peer median of 34.0x (P82). Trailing P/E of 76x and forward P/E of 50x (P82) are both above the 28-45x sector band, and the stock sits at 91% of its 52-week range, so it is expensive. fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. That makes it a high-beta bet on market activity, not a lender. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. For a fee-based broker I graded on P/E cross-checked with P/B against ROE: trailing P/E of 35.8x is above the 18–28x NBFC/capital-markets band and in line with the broad market (P52), while forward P/E of 20.3x prices in a further earnings recovery. P/B of 5.25x against only 15.5% ROE is rich, so overall this is fair at best, with the stock at 97% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 3.5% in 30 days and 4.8% in 90 days. The biggest risk is regulatory: further SEBI tightening of retail F&O, or a drop in market activity in this risk-off tape, would hit volumes directly. Cash flow from operations was also deeply negative in FY26 (-4.5x PAT) because the borrowed-money margin-funding book grew about 39%, which adds leverage (debt/equity about 1.0–1.3x).

In H1 FY27, revenue grew 21.4% YoY to ₹3,566 cr: plumbing rose 18.2% at a 12.9% segment margin and paints & adhesives rose 29.0%, but that segment's margin is only about 3.1%. PAT grew more slowly, up 15.7% to ₹248 cr (6.9% margin), and operating cash flow swung to -₹68 cr from +₹389 cr a year ago because of a large tax outflow, inventory build-up and 29% higher capex. The prior-period rows in the trend table are clearly wrong (for example, Q4FY26 revenue of ₹17,347 cr), so there is no reliable multi-quarter trend to rely on. On the sector card's preferred yardstick, EV/EBITDA is 35.7×, about 5% above the peer median of 34.0× (P59). Trailing P/E is 68.2× against a peer median of 53.8× (P62), and forward P/E is 43.3×, which already prices in earnings growth. That makes the stock fairly valued: there is no clear mispricing, though it sits at 32% of its 52-week range, which is a reasonable but not compelling entry point. The biggest risk is quality of growth. Profit is lagging revenue, cash conversion turned negative, paints is a low-margin segment, and the ₹95 mn goodwill impairment on Seal It (US) shows past acquisitions have not all paid off.

fundamental.thesis: GIC Re is India's dominant state-owned reinsurer. It takes on risk from domestic insurers across fire, motor, health, agriculture and other lines, and AM Best rates it A- (Excellent) with a stable outlook. In H1 FY27, gross written premium grew 11.7% year on year to ₹24,713 cr, faster than the +5.8% to +6.4% of FY26 and H1 FY26. Profit fell the other way: consolidated PAT dropped 12.8% to ₹4,709 cr, PAT margin shrank from 26.8% to 19.1%, and the combined ratio worsened slightly from 106.36% to 106.79%. That means the company loses money on underwriting and relies on ₹5,015 cr of investment income. Q2 alone (about ₹2,966 cr of PAT, implied by H1 minus Q1) was much better than Q1, whose PAT fell 31%. For an insurer I grade value on price-to-book against ROE, not P/E. At 0.62x book, the cheapest in the peer set and near the bottom of its 52-week range, the stock is cheap even for a below-par 9.1% ROE, and the 4.18x solvency ratio gives a large capital buffer. The trailing P/E of 6.8x supports this but is not my yardstick. The ROE gap is the main reason the market keeps this PSU at a discount to book. The biggest risk is that underwriting losses stay above 100% of premium while estimates keep being cut (FY EPS down 10% over 90 days), so earnings would depend on volatile investment gains.

fundamental.thesis: Choice International is a mid-sized diversified financial services group. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for lenders and brokers rather than P/E: a P/B of 8.4x for a 16.2% ROE is expensive (P74 vs the broad market), and the trailing P/E of 63x (P80) is well above the 18-28x NBFC range. A forward P/E of 47x shows the market already expects strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that much of this business rises and falls with market activity, so a slowdown in broking volumes or IPO deals would hit growth that is already fully priced in, while the bonus issue and two fresh acquisitions add integration and accounting noise.

Authum Investment & Infrastructure is a mid-cap NBFC and investment holding company. Its earnings come mainly from gains on its investment portfolio and from buying distressed assets through the insolvency (NCLT) process, so profits swing a lot from quarter to quarter. It does not run a steady lending book. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 12.6% YoY to ₹685 cr, but PAT fell 45.5% YoY to ₹418 cr and PAT margin dropped to 61.0% from 74.6% in Q1. Revenue growth has also slowed, from +21.4% in Q1 to +12.6%. H1FY27 cash flow from operations was negative at -0.49x PAT, which means reported profits are not turning into cash. For a lender or holding company, P/B against ROE is the right yardstick, not P/E. On that basis the stock is fair rather than cheap: P/B is 2.91x for an ROE of 13.1%, well above the 'cheap' bar of P/B under 1.5 with ROE over 12%. The headline trailing P/E of 8.95x, in the bottom 5% of the market, overstates how cheap it is because it rests on large investment gains that may not repeat. The biggest risk is that earnings depend on market-linked investment gains and lumpy distressed-asset deals, and profits are not backed by cash. Leverage is also unclear: the live snapshot shows debt/equity of 24.59, which is unverified and could be a percentage misread.

fundamental.thesis: GPIL is an integrated steel and power producer (iron ore pellets → sponge iron → billets/wire rods with captive power) headquartered in Chhattisgarh, recently allotting industrial land at AURIC Bidkin, Maharashtra, signalling a next-phase capacity push. Revenue has deteriorated from near-flat +0.8% YoY in H1FY26 to -11.4% YoY in Q3FY26 (₹1,166 cr), while PAT margin compressed steadily from 16.3% in Q1FY26 to 12.3% in Q3FY26 — both revenue growth and margins are moving in the wrong direction over four consecutive periods. Assessed on EV/EBITDA of 13.5× (the appropriate yardstick for a capital-intensive steel business; P/E is secondary), GPIL trades at a 42% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× and sits at P22 of 473 peers — genuinely cheap, but the discount reflects real fundamental headwinds rather than neglected quality; a forward P/E of 10.9× versus trailing 19.5× implies the market is pricing in an earnings recovery that the current revenue trajectory has not yet validated. The primary threat to any recovery thesis is extreme financial leverage (D/E 7.58) paired with sustained sell-side EPS cuts (-19.1% over 90 days from only one covering analyst), which compresses the margin of safety materially if the steel-price downcycle extends into FY27.

Escorts Kubota is one of India's major tractor makers and also sells construction equipment. Agri machinery brings in about 87% of revenue, so it trades more like a farm-equipment and auto-cyclical stock than a capital-goods order-book business. In H1 FY27 revenue rose 21.9% to ₹6,451 cr, but the implied Q2 numbers are weak: revenue of about ₹3,243 cr is up only about 16% YoY, slower than Q1's +28.3%, and PAT of about ₹250 cr is down about 21% YoY, so PAT margin fell to about 7.7% from 12.0% in Q1. Agri EBIT margin fell 340 bps to 9.3% on higher commodity costs and a weaker product mix, operating cash flow turned negative (-₹107 cr) as inventory and receivables built up, and management now expects margins to return to normal only in FY28. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against farm-equipment and auto peers, because the Industrials order-book yardstick does not fit this business. A trailing P/E of 22.6x is mid-range for auto (18-28x) and well below the Industrials band, EV/EBITDA is 16.3x and P/B is 2.5x against a 12% ROE, so it is fair, not cheap. Analysts have cut this year's EPS estimate by 11.6% in 30 days, which explains the discount and the stock sitting near its 52-week low. Some inputs conflict: the dividend yield, the price implied by the 52-week range versus the analyst target, debt/equity of 1.31 against a reported net-cash position, and a Q2 EBITDA margin that works out to an implausible ~2.6%. So I am trusting the reported revenue and PAT more than the derived ratios.
