fundamental.thesis: GE Vernova T&D India is India's leading power transmission and distribution equipment maker (transformers, switchgear, grid substations), directly leveraged to the government's ₹9 lakh cr grid build-out through 2032 and a structural T&D order-book upcycle. Q1FY27 revenue grew +38% YoY to ₹1,836 cr with PAT up +24.6% to ₹363 cr, sustaining a consistent multi-quarter ~38% execution run-rate — but EBITDA margin contracted 300 bps YoY from 30.4% to 27.4%, operating profit grew only 25% against 38% revenue, and PAT margin fell 210 bps to 19.8%, signalling negative operating leverage as costs scale faster than revenue. Using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials per sector card), the stock trades at 73.2× versus the sector median of 28–45×, sits at the P95–P97 of the broad peer universe with a 214% premium to the median, and is at 99.5% of its 52-week high — unambiguously expensive by every lens. fundamental.thesis: Jupiter Wagons (JWL) is a leading Indian freight wagon and rolling-stock manufacturer exposed primarily to Indian Railways' capital procurement cycle, a segment that has sharply underperformed the broader capex upcycle; the company reported a -26% YoY revenue decline for full FY26 (₹2,961 cr vs ₹3,963 cr in FY25), with PAT collapsing -56% to ₹166 cr as PAT margin contracted from 9.6% to 5.7% — a consistent deterioration across every sub-period (Q1FY26: -47.8% revenue, -64.4% PAT) and the order book-to-revenue cover has fallen from 2.36x (9MFY26) to just 1.58x (FY26), well below the 3x threshold for meaningful revenue visibility. Valuation is unambiguously expensive: trailing P/E of 69.7x sits nearly 100% above the broad-market median of 35.2x (P83 peer rank), EV/EBITDA of 30.04x is 29% above peers (P66), and the P/B of 4.04x against a TTM ROE of only 5.8% is egregious — paying 4x book for sub-cost-of-capital returns — with the forward P/E of 28.45x implying an aggressive earnings recovery that analyst downward revisions (-24.6% EPS cut in 90 days) directly contradict. The biggest risk is further order book depletion without new inflows (H1FY26 inflows of only ₹570 cr against a ₹1,480 cr annualised revenue run-rate), compounded by high balance-sheet leverage (D/E 33.37), persistently weak cash conversion (FY25 CFO/PAT 0.43x, FCF -₹344 cr), and recurring exceptional charges from Stone India's court-mandated lease-rent dues — all in a RISK_OFF macro with rising crude raising input costs.

Jyoti CNC Automation is an Indian maker of CNC machine tools that also owns the Huron group of subsidiaries in France, Germany, Canada, Turkey and China, so its results depend on demand from manufacturing and defence capex. Sales are growing well but profits are shrinking. H1 FY27 revenue rose 21.0% YoY to ₹1,110 cr, and the implied Q2 FY27 (H1 minus Q1) was about ₹602 cr, up roughly 18.5%. Consolidated PAT, however, fell 17.4% to ₹130 cr in H1, and implied Q2 PAT fell about 15% to roughly ₹73 cr. PAT margin dropped from 16.8% to about 12.1% and EBITDA margin from 26.3% to 21.6%, mostly because overseas subsidiaries lost ₹73 cr in H1. Valuation is fair but rich: I used EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive name, and at 31.6× it sits at P67 against the broad market. Trailing P/E of 47.4× is just above the 28–45× Industrials band, and P/B of 8.0× is high for an 18% ROE. The forward P/E of 28.3× and rising estimates (+15% over 90 days) assume a profit recovery the filings do not show yet. The filings give no order-book or order-inflow figures, which are the sector's key metrics, so I cannot check revenue visibility. The biggest open risk is the French judicial investigation of Huron Graffenstaden for alleged dual-use export violations. It sits on top of rising subsidiary losses and negative free cash flow.

fundamental.thesis: IRB Infrastructure is India's largest private toll-road operator and developer. It runs 27 highway projects with about 1.5 million vehicles crossing its plazas each day, a share of about 10% of India's toll revenue, and an asset base of about ₹94,000 cr. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,945 cr, up 8.1% YoY, recovering from +0.4% in Q1FY27 and -20.1% for FY26. PAT was ₹260 cr, up 84.4% YoY, for a 13.4% margin, and EBITDA was ₹1,102 cr at a 56.7% margin, up 13%. Toll revenue grew 15% YoY, faster than the 11% a year earlier. Two cautions on these numbers: much of the PAT jump comes from InvIT distributions and asset transfers rather than from tolls, and the earlier trend rows look like a mix of standalone and consolidated figures, so the YoY bases are not fully comparable. This is a capital-heavy toll business, so I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, which is 16.2× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P29). Trailing P/E is 30.6×, inside the 28–45× Industrials range, and forward P/E is 16.0×. P/B looks cheap at 1.2× (P6), but ROE is only 4.2%, which explains the low book multiple. Overall I grade it fair, not cheap. The main risk is debt: net debt is ₹10,283 cr, about 2.3× annualised EBITDA, and earnings depend on InvIT monetisation. Meanwhile analysts have cut their FY EPS estimates by 4.2% (current year) and 6.8% (next year) over the last 30 days, even though all 5 still rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

Jain Resource Recycling is a non-ferrous metal recycler that makes copper, lead and aluminium from scrap. It is a commodity-spread business, recently listed, and copper is now about two-thirds of its revenue. Revenue is growing fast, but much of that comes from copper prices and profit is not keeping up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 65.5% YoY to ₹6,061 cr while PAT rose only 3.1% to ₹160 cr. Taking Q1 out of H1 suggests Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,337 cr (around +58% YoY, slower than Q1's +75.9%) and PAT of about ₹91 cr, which is roughly 8% lower than a year ago. EBITDA margin has fallen from 7.0% (9M FY26) to 5.7% (Q1) to 4.5% (H1), and PAT margin from 4.4% to about 2.7%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because the sector card says to judge cyclical, commodity-spread businesses that way. On that measure the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 25.1×, against roughly 5–8× for cyclicals at mid-cycle, and trailing P/E is 35.8×, against a 12–22× Materials benchmark. The 19.9× forward P/E depends on earnings growth, but analysts have cut those estimates by about 19% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while net debt is high (about 3.3× EBITDA, debt/equity about 82%). If copper prices or recycling spreads reverse, earnings could fall sharply.

fundamental.thesis: Chambal Fertilizers is one of India's largest private urea makers. It also sells traded and complex fertilisers and crop-protection products, and it has just started a new Technical Ammonium Nitrate (TAN) plant at Gadepan from August 20, 2026. Its earnings depend heavily on the government subsidy rules (New Urea Policy 2015 and NBS). Growth is going the wrong way: Q1FY27 revenue was ₹5,027 cr, down 11.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹524 cr, down 4.6%, after FY26 grew 25% on traded complex fertilisers. Q2FY27 PAT margin slipped to about 9.0% from 10.4% in Q1, but the Q2 revenue figure was not extracted from the filing and the yfinance quarterly rows (Q2 revenue ₹4,367 cr) do not match the PDF figures, so the latest-quarter picture is only partly confirmed. I graded this as a capital-intensive commodity business on EV/EBITDA, which at 7.3x sits at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals. Trailing P/E of 9.9x is below the 12–22x Materials benchmark, ROE is 20.5%, net debt is slightly negative (the 10.27 'debt/equity' looks like a percentage, given 48x interest coverage), and the stock is in the bottom decile of the broad market on every multiple, so the verdict is cheap. Cash conversion is the biggest worry: FY26 operating cash flow covered only 0.07x of PAT and receivables jumped from ₹368 cr to ₹2,075 cr, which looks like delayed subsidy payments and makes the reported earnings less solid than they appear.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Ingrevia is a mid-cap Indian chemicals maker with three segments: Specialty Chemicals, Nutrition (vitamin B3 and feed premixes) and Chemical Intermediates (acetyls). It is now adding CDMO capacity and has bought a 40% stake in ZettaOne, an electronics-materials business. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,394 cr, up 24% YoY and an all-time high, compared with low-single-digit growth through FY26 (+1.3% in Q1FY26, +5.0% for FY26). PAT rose 61% to ₹111 cr, and both PAT margin (8.0% vs 6.1–7.2% across FY26) and EBITDA margin (16.0% vs 13.6–14.8%) widened, but Q1FY27 is missing from the filings data, so the speed-up rests mainly on one quarter. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to for chemicals: at 18.1x it is far above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for commodity chemicals, though that range doesn't fully fit a specialty/CDMO mix; it is 22% below the broad-market median (P35), with trailing P/E of 34.6x at P48 and forward P/E of 22.3x, so I call it fair overall, not cheap. The main risks are muddy cash flow and earnings quality: finance costs jumped 85% YoY on acquisition-related borrowing, H1 FY26 earnings were weakly backed by cash (0.67x CFO/PAT, negative free cash flow), and analysts have trimmed next-year EPS estimates (−2.4% over 30 days, −3.7% over 90 days) even as they raised this year's.

fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. Gases bring in about 71% of segment revenue at a 26.4% segment margin, while project engineering earns only 9.8%. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹694 cr, up 21.6% YoY, but PAT fell 2.4% YoY to ₹105 cr. PAT margin has slipped to 15.1% from the low-to-mid 20s in earlier periods, and the H1 EBITDA margin dropped 850 bps to 31.8%. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. EV/EBITDA was not available, so I fell back on peer multiples: trailing P/E of 99.6x, forward P/E of 73.8x and P/B of 12.7x put it at P93/P98/P89 against the broad market, roughly 180-220% above the median, which is clearly expensive. Sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut about 14% over the last 30-90 days. The Q2FY27 results (filed 3 Nov) have not been extracted yet, so this view rests on Q1 and H1 data.

fundamental.thesis: Concord Biotech is a midcap maker of fermentation-based pharma ingredients and formulations, with low debt (debt/equity 0.12), though this pack does not contain enough data to judge its market position. Revenue growth has swung from -20.3% in Q2 FY26 to +26.2% in Q1 FY27 and about +25% in Q2 FY27 (derived as H1 Rs 567 cr less Q1 Rs 257 cr, or about Rs 310 cr), but this is an easy-base recovery: Q2 revenue is only back to roughly its Q2 FY25 level, implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 68 cr is up only about 7% YoY, and implied EBITDA margin has fallen to about 29% from 36.7%, while H1 cash conversion stayed healthy at 1.32x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, cross-checked with P/E because no tight listed peers were available, the stock looks expensive at 37.0x EV/EBITDA (P78 and 59% above the broad-market median) and 50.8x trailing P/E against a 28-40x pharma range; the 34.4x forward P/E already prices in a strong profit recovery, and the +23.8% sell-side upside looks unreliable because the Rs 1,520 mean target is only about 5% above the roughly Rs 1,450 price implied by market cap and EPS. The biggest risk is that profit does not catch up with revenue, since FY27 EPS estimates were cut 2.8% in the last 30 days and the valuation leaves little room for further margin slippage; confidence is also limited because the FY26 revenue and PAT rows appear overstated tenfold, the 51% dividend yield is clearly wrong, and no sector KPIs or management guidance were available.

Anthem Biosciences is a contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) company with a smaller specialty-ingredients arm; CRDMO made up 84% of H1 FY27 revenue. It has a clean record with regulators (USFDA, TGA, ANVISA), net cash of ₹1,538 cr, and FY26 cash flow of 1.48x PAT. Revenue has gone from +15.0% growth in FY26 to a -7.2% fall in H1 FY27 (₹1,012 cr). Q1 fell 22.6% to ₹418 cr. Q2 recovered to about ₹594 cr, roughly +8% YoY, a figure we worked out from the H1 and Q1 numbers. H1 PAT rose 7.2% to ₹331 cr, a 30.2% margin, but part of that margin comes from other income booked inside EBITDA (₹84 cr, about 17% of EBITDA). We graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the measure the sector card favours for capital-heavy CDMO businesses. At 50.8x EV/EBITDA and 76x trailing P/E, the stock is far above the 28–40x pharma P/E range and sits around P86–P93 against peers on every multiple, so it is expensive even allowing a China+1 CDMO premium. The analyst mean target is only 0.7% above the current price, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 3.6% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Pharmova is a diversified Indian pharma company spanning CDMO Sterile Injectables, Allergy Immunotherapy, Radiopharma, and Generics — a complex, multi-segment business with meaningful US and Canada exposure. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue accelerated to +17.3% YoY (₹2,229 cr), continuing a multi-quarter re-acceleration from +9.8% in Q1FY26, but PAT collapsed 45% YoY to ₹56 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from 15.9% (Q1FY26) to 12.0%, with CDMO Sterile Injectables margins imploding from 11% to 1.4% and the Generics segment swinging to a ₹10 cr operating loss — a dangerous divergence between topline and bottom-line trajectories. Trailing P/E of 38.8× sits near the top of the pharma sector benchmark range (28–40×) on deeply-depressed earnings; EV/EBITDA of 14.17× (P23 percentile vs broad peers) looks more attractive but still reflects deteriorating EBITDA; forward P/E of 19.16× embeds a steep earnings recovery that consensus has already cut by ~25% in the last 30 days, making the 'cheap-on-forward' narrative fragile. The biggest risk is a dual FDA compliance overhang — OAI at Montreal (remediation expenses of ₹535 mn already booked, manufacturing suspended) plus a live USFDA Spokane update — alongside a GST show-cause notice and a high debt/equity ratio (50.94×), any one of which could derail the assumed margin recovery.

Lloyds Metals and Energy is a fast-growing midcap that mines iron ore and makes pellets and sponge iron (DRI). It is in the middle of a heavy capacity build-out, so its earnings swing with iron-ore and steel spreads. Subtracting Q1FY27 from H1FY27 (₹13,009 cr revenue, ₹2,791 cr PAT) gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹5,655 cr (+52.5% YoY vs ₹3,707 cr) and PAT of about ₹1,057 cr (+86% YoY vs ₹567 cr). But revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +204.5% in Q3FY26 and +208.6% in Q1FY27 to +52.5%. Revenue fell about 23% and PAT about 39% from Q1, partly due to the monsoon season, and PAT margin dropped from 23.6% to about 18.7%. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cyclical, the stock trades at 19.1×, far above the 5–8× mid-cycle norm for steel and mining names. Trailing P/E of 26.3× is also above the 12–22× Materials range, so I grade it expensive. The 12.1× forward P/E and analysts' +38% upgrades to FY earnings estimates only hold up if the new capacity delivers on time, and the stock is already at 84% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt/equity of about 1.45×, FY26 free cash flow of -₹1,853 cr and fresh NCD (bond) raises mean any delay in commissioning or a fall in iron-ore prices would hurt both earnings and the leverage story.

fundamental.thesis: Max Healthcare is one of India's largest listed hospital chains, with about 6,100 network beds running at more than 75% occupancy. It is growing by adding beds at existing hospitals and buying new ones (Kalinga in Bhubaneswar, a land parcel in Pune, 85 more beds at its Noida hospital). Taking H1 FY27 minus Q1, Q2 FY27 revenue comes to about ₹2,569 cr, up about 20% YoY, and EBITDA margin has widened from 26.8% to 28.2% over the trend window. But revenue growth has slowed from above 30% to about 17–20%, and H1 PAT fell 7.7% YoY to ₹737 cr. Most of that fall comes from the tax rate going back to normal: it rose from an unusually low 5.6% to 24.5% because of a one-off merger-related tax reversal last year. Cash generation is solid, with operating cash flow at 1.35x PAT and ₹406 cr of free cash flow in H1. Because hospitals are capital-heavy, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, which is 45.6x, about 96% above the broad-market median (P86). Trailing P/E is 73.9x against a 35.2x median (P85), and P/B is 9.9x for only a 14.3% ROE, so the stock is expensive even with forward P/E falling to 44.9x. fundamental.thesis: Lemon Tree Hotels owns and manages hotels and is expanding through brand-licence and franchise signings, including an MoU with Omaxe for about 4,000 keys, while a pending demerger would separate hotel ownership from the management and brand businesses. Revenue growth has slowed from +17.8% in Q1 FY26 to +9.1% in Q1 FY27 (Rs 345 cr), and from +20.1% in FY25 to +12.3% in FY26; PAT rose 19.2% to about Rs 57 cr, but EBITDA margin slipped from 45.0% to 44.1%, and the trend table's PAT margin jump from 12.1% to 16.6% looks overstated because the Rs 38 cr base does not match the reported growth (Rs 57 cr at +19.2% implies a base near Rs 48 cr, or a margin of about 15.2%). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 16.07x is 31% below the broad-market median (P29) and the stock is near its 52-week low at 15.1% of the range, but with no hotel peer set or card-specific norm and a 39x trailing P/E (P56), I grade it fair rather than cheap. The 22x forward P/E assumes about 77% EPS growth over the trailing base, which looks demanding against 19-21% recent profit growth and FY estimates cut 5.8% over 90 days despite 21 of 22 analysts rating it a buy, and Q2 FY27 results on 2026-11-05 will test this with no RevPAR or management guidance data available here.

fundamental.thesis: PVR INOX is a leading Indian multiplex operator whose results depend on film releases and cinema footfall, and it sold its Zea Maize food business in January 2026. H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

TBO Tek runs a B2B travel-distribution platform that connects travel agents worldwide to hotel and airline inventory, and since the Classic Vacations acquisition it also has a North American leisure arm. In Q2FY27 reported revenue of ₹866 cr grew 52.5% YoY, slower than Q1's +81%, and most of that headline growth comes from the acquisition: organic GTV grew 22% and organic gross profit 21%, while organic adjusted EBITDA grew 36%. Consolidated EBITDA margin has contracted from 22.5% to 17.6% over the trend window, and the last PAT margin we have is 9.0% in Q1FY27, down from about 14% a year earlier, because the lower-margin Classic Vacations business now makes up more of the mix. Q2 PAT was not available from the filings, and the revenue scale in the trend table does not match the yfinance rows, so treat the absolute figures with some caution. On valuation, the sector card says platform names should be judged on EV/EBITDA and growth delivery, not P/E alone: at 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81 vs the broad market) and 68.4x trailing P/E (P83), with the stock at 88.8% of its 52-week range, the shares look expensive even though the forward P/E of 33.5x assumes strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes perfection while FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days and governance issues are piling up: an unprovisioned ED/FEMA penalty of about ₹22 cr, an ₹8.1 cr employee fraud at an overseas subsidiary, and ₹8.9 cr of FX losses.

fundamental.thesis: Endurance Technologies makes auto parts, mainly for two-wheelers in India, including suspension, braking, transmission and aluminium castings. About 76% of its H1 revenue came from India and 24% from its plants in Italy and Germany. In H1FY27, revenue grew +31.6% YoY to ₹9,159 cr and PAT grew +14.4% to ₹519 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives an implied Q2 revenue of about ₹4,811 cr (+33.5% YoY, up from +29.6% in Q1) and PAT of about ₹274 cr (+21% YoY, up from +8% in Q1). Profits are growing much more slowly than sales, though. EBITDA margin fell from 13.1% in Q1 to about 12.1% in Q2, PAT margin is stuck near 5.6–5.7%, and analysts cut their FY earnings estimates by 4% over the last 90 days. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 39.4x is above the 18–30x auto range and the 18–28x auto-ancillary range. But the forward P/E of 26.4x sits inside that range, and EV/EBITDA of 18.7x is below the broad-market median of 23.3x, so overall the stock is fair, with no margin of safety. The biggest risk is that the very strong sales growth keeps failing to lift profit margins while estimates keep getting cut, which would squeeze the premium the stock trades at.

fundamental.thesis: ABFRL is a midcap fashion retailer that owns Pantaloons (value retail, 399 stores), an ethnic-wear portfolio including TCNS and Jaypore, the TMRW digital brands and a small luxury arm, with about 1,286 stores in total. Revenue growth has slowed from about +11% YoY in Q1 FY27 (₹2,026 cr) to +6.4% for H1 FY27 (₹4,056 cr), so Q2 grew only about 2% YoY (Q2 revenue ≈ ₹2,030 cr, worked out from H1 minus Q1). Losses got worse: Q2 PAT was about ₹-376 cr, a margin of about -18.5%, against -12.3% in Q1. H1 EBITDA fell 28% YoY to ₹130 cr, and free cash flow was ₹-288 cr. The business is loss-making, so P/E means nothing here; I graded on EV/EBITDA and P/B. EV/EBITDA is 18.2x, against 23.3x for the broad-market median (P36). P/B is 1.28x (P7), which looks cheap, but return on equity is -12.7%, so we call valuation fair, not cheap, even though the stock sits near its 52-week low (19% of range). The biggest risk is that the turnaround keeps failing: no segment makes money at the profit line, the ethnic segment's margin is -23%, and net debt of ₹1,334 cr is about 10x EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: Motherson Sumi Wiring India makes wiring harnesses for Indian carmakers and two-wheeler makers, and its sales depend mostly on Indian volumes, which makes it a direct play on India's premium-vehicle and EV mix. In the latest quarter extracted from filings (Q1 FY27), revenue grew +36.6% YoY to Rs 3,407 cr, up from +14.2% in Q1 FY26, but profit barely moved (+1.6% to Rs 145 cr). The profit margin fell from 6.0% to 4.3% and the operating margin from 10.2% to 7.7%. There are early signs of a recovery: the half-year filing implies Q2 profit of about Rs 224 cr (+35% YoY, which matches yfinance's Rs 223 cr), FY EPS estimates were raised +7.3% in the last 30 days, and the half-year revenue figure is labelled H1FY26 in the table but is probably H1 FY27. However, the 30 Oct Q2 FY27 results have not been extracted yet and the Q2 revenue figures conflict, so this recovery is unconfirmed. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA and forward P/E, as the Auto card suggests for ancillaries: EV/EBITDA of 23.9x is at the peer median (P52), forward P/E of 25.1x sits inside the 18-30x Auto band, and trailing P/E of 40.2x is inflated by the margin dip. That makes the stock fair, not cheap, even though it trades near its 52-week low (11.5% of range) and has a 32.4% ROE. The 293% dividend yield and 10.79 debt/equity readings look like data-unit errors; the filings show net debt of only Rs 58 cr. The biggest risk is that margins stay squeezed by copper and commodity costs, rising crude and a new-plant ramp-up, so revenue keeps growing without profit following it.

fundamental.thesis: Ola Electric is India's largest EV two-wheeler OEM with vertically integrated battery ambitions (Ola Cell Technologies), but it remains deeply pre-profit and is facing a severe revenue downturn — Q1FY27 revenue fell 45% YoY to ₹455cr (from ₹828cr in Q1FY26), with PAT margin contracting sharply from -51.7% in Q1FY26 to -73.8% in Q1FY27, suggesting unit economics are deteriorating, not improving, as scale has shrunk. Using the appropriate yardstick for pre-profit/platform businesses (EV/Sales + growth-delivery + unit-economics trajectory), P/Sales of 8.29× for a company with deeply negative and declining revenues is expensive — there is zero growth delivery to justify a platform premium, and the EBITDA margin trend (-20.4% → -29.9%) is moving in the wrong direction. The single biggest risk is the auditor-qualified going concern assessment: management itself flagged negative operating cash flow of ₹215cr in Q1FY27, and a fresh rights issue announced September 28, 2026 confirms that the company requires continuous external capital — dilution and solvency risk are both live.

fundamental.thesis: Schaeffler India is a precision components manufacturer (bearings, transmission systems, clutch parts) for automotive and industrial customers, leveraging its German parent's technology IP and commanding ~79% of revenue from the Mobility segment with a quality premium over domestic-only ancillaries. H1 2026 showed revenue growth of +18.1% YoY to ₹5,346 cr and PAT growth of +19.1% to ₹642 cr, with EBITDA margin expanding from 19.6% to 20.1% across the tracked periods — an accelerating trajectory, though CFO/PAT of 0.61× is borderline weak and the ₹547 cr dividend paid against only ₹389 cr CFO raises a capital-allocation flag. Trailing P/E of 53.77× is nearly 2× the auto ancillary sector median of 18–28× and sits at P72 in the broad market; EV/EBITDA of 34.46× likewise approaches the upper end of even the capital-goods range (28–45×), making the stock expensive on both primary metrics — the forward P/E of 41.53× confirms growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is the premium valuation built on an uninterrupted growth story, which offers no margin of safety if growth decelerates due to auto-sector cyclicality, rising crude input costs, ongoing subsidiary losses (KRSV PAT −₹32 cr H1), or EV disruption of traditional drivetrain demand.

JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India, bought by the JSW Group in Dec 2025) is a mid-sized decorative and industrial paints maker. It has been gaining volume, but its profit margins are under heavy pressure. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,927 cr, up 5.8% YoY as reported and up 20% on a like-for-like basis that excludes the divested Powder Coatings and IRC divisions, with volume up 23%. Reported revenue growth has improved from -4.0% (Q1FY26) to -2.8% (Q1FY27) to +5.8% (H1FY27). Over the same window PAT margin has fallen from 9.2% to 8.3% to 7.8%, and gross margin fell 1,180bp YoY to 35.4% as raw-material inflation outran price increases. Implied Q2 PAT of about ₹71 cr is below Q1's ₹80 cr. I used forward P/E rather than trailing P/E. The 7.45× trailing P/E and the P4 'cheap vs peers' rank are not real: they are inflated by the ₹1,874 cr one-off gain from the divestiture in H1 FY26, and the reported -91.5% H1 PAT drop is distorted by that same gain. On forward P/E of 31.3× (P67 vs the broad market) and P/B of 6.0×, the stock is fair: below listed paint leaders but not cheap for a business whose margins are falling. Sell-side FY-EPS estimates have been cut 8.8% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that crude is near $91 and rising, which pushes up paint raw-material costs and could cut margins further while the new JSW owners push for market share.

fundamental.thesis: Allied Blenders and Distillers is a midcap Indian spirits maker, with a Rs 17,700 cr market value and thin margins on reported revenue that includes excise duty. Revenue growth has improved from -6.2% in FY26 to +1.9% in Q1 FY27 and +4.3% to Rs 3,903 cr in H1 FY27 (about +7% to Rs 2,094 cr in Q2, derived from the H1 and Q1 figures), but H1 PAT fell 3.6% to Rs 114 cr, the 2.9% PAT margin is slightly below H1 FY26's 3.2%, and the data shows neither volume growth nor a reliable gross margin trend. Using the sector card's FMCG P/E norm, cross-checked with broad-market EV/EBITDA and P/B ranks because there are no tight peers, the stock is expensive at 77.3x trailing P/E against 40-65x, with EV/EBITDA of 34.5x and P/B of 10.7x against 13.6% ROE; the 39.9x forward P/E implies EPS nearly doubling while near-term estimates are slipping about 1%. The biggest risk is a valuation de-rating if profit does not catch up with those expectations, and conviction is limited by data conflicts: implied Q2 PAT of Rs 65 cr vs Rs 71.5 cr on yfinance, a likely misstated 86% dividend yield, debt/equity of 68.25 that probably means 0.68x rather than 68x, and a price implied by the consensus upside (about Rs 694) that does not match the one implied by the 52-week position (about Rs 633).

fundamental.thesis: Radico Khaitan is a premium-led Indian spirits maker whose Magic Moments brand holds about 60% of the Indian vodka market. Q2FY27 net revenue rose 16.8% YoY to Rs 1,745 cr and PAT rose 66.1% to Rs 231 cr; the table's 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are unreliable because it mixes revenue before and after excise duty, but on a net basis revenue growth did slow from +24.7% in FY26 while EBITDA margin improved from 16.8% to 20.4%, with Prestige & Above volumes up 35.8%, Regular & Others down 9.7%, and total volume growth (+7.2%) trailing price/mix (+9.6%). Using P/E as the main yardstick with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the valuation is expensive: the 81.8x trailing P/E appears to use FY26 PAT and falls to about 62x on my estimate of trailing-12-month PAT (about Rs 796 cr), near the top of the sector card's 40-65x range, while forward P/E is 51.1x, EV/EBITDA is 40.3x, broad-market ranks are P82-P93 and the stock sits at 96% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that this price needs the premium growth and roughly 20% margin guidance to hold while grain costs, state policy and higher inventory (H1 CFO/PAT 0.82x) create pressure; three snapshot fields also look unreliable, as the 15% dividend yield and 20.94 debt/equity look like unit errors and the +16.1% consensus upside does not match the roughly Rs 3,690 price implied by market cap, and the October 28 earnings call transcript is not reflected here.

BLS International runs outsourced visa and consular processing for foreign governments, where it earns high margins (H1FY27 segment margin 39.7%). It also has a fast-growing but low-margin Digital Services and e-governance arm (H1FY27 revenue ₹793 cr, up 50% YoY, at only a 6.2% margin). Revenue growth picked up from +25.3% YoY in Q1FY27 to +32.0% in Q2FY27 (₹973 cr), but profit is not keeping pace. Q2 PAT rose only 8.6% to ₹202 cr, PAT margin fell from 25.2% to 20.8% YoY, and EBITDA margin dropped from about 30% in FY26 to 25.5%. The causes are the shift toward the low-margin digital business and costs from the Atyati and Trefeddian Hotel acquisitions. On valuation we used EV/EBITDA and P/E rather than the sector card's 60-100x consumer-discretionary multiples, because this is a services contractor, not a premium consumer franchise. At 10.2x EV/EBITDA and 13.8x trailing P/E (11.0x forward), the stock sits around the cheapest 11% of the broad market and well below the market median of 35x P/E, and net cash of ₹1,665 cr (about 17% of market cap) supports that. So we grade it cheap, though the stock near its 52-week low shows the market is already pricing in the falling margins. The main risk is that margins keep sliding as the digital business grows and acquired businesses are integrated, which would leave earnings flat even while revenue grows.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Consumer Products is India's second-largest branded foods-and-beverages company, with leading positions in tea (Tata Tea, Tetley) and salt (Tata Salt), supplemented by an inorganic expansion into nutrition and adjacent FMCG via Capital Foods, Soulfull, and Organic India acquisitions. Q1FY27 revenue grew +11.9% YoY to ₹5,349 cr — a meaningful deceleration from +15.0% in Q3FY26 — though PAT surged +28.8% YoY to ₹427 cr (margin 8.0% vs 7.0% a year ago), powered by lower tea input costs and gross-margin expansion from 40.1% to 42.7%; volume growth in the India business was ~13%, solid but to be weighed against the sector card's caution on >10% volume claims. At a trailing P/E of 60.51× — at the upper bound of the FMCG benchmark range of 40–60× and ranked P78 among broad-market peers — the stock screens as expensive even near its 52-week low; however, a forward P/E of 41.78× (31% below trailing) signals the market is pricing in a meaningful earnings step-up from acquisition integration and tea-cost tailwinds. The principal risk is sustained revenue growth deceleration toward sub-10% alongside a reported Debt/Equity of 12.16 (reflecting heavy acquisition financing), which leaves the stock highly exposed to multiple compression if earnings delivery disappoints or high-rate conditions pressure interest coverage.

UNO Minda is a domestic auto-component supplier that sells lighting, switches, alloy wheels, sunroofs and EV parts to Indian two-wheeler and car makers, so it benefits from premiumisation and the rising share of EVs. Growth is accelerating: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹12,212 cr (+31.3% YoY) and PAT was ₹756 cr (+19.7%), up from Q1 FY27's +23.8% revenue and +2.1% PAT. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives a Q2 of about ₹6,655 cr revenue and ₹440 cr PAT, in line with the company's own press release reporting 38% YoY growth in both. Profitability is not keeping pace, though: EBITDA margin fell from 11.76% to 10.69% YoY and H1 free cash flow was negative (₹-96 cr) after ₹806 cr of capex. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA for an auto ancillary, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 53× and forward P/E of 35.5× are both well above the 18–28× auto range, EV/EBITDA is 29×, P/B is 10×, and it sits at P71–P82 versus the broad market. The stock is near the low end of its 52-week range (27%) and the average analyst target is about 1% below the current price. The main risk is that the high multiple is priced for growth while margins and cash conversion keep slipping.

fundamental.thesis: Affle 3i is a mobile ad-tech platform that sells cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) advertising, mainly in India and emerging markets; it is a platform business, not a headcount-based IT services firm. Growth is steady but not speeding up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 20.8% YoY to ₹1,531 cr and PAT rose 19.5% to ₹258 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹784 cr (around +21% YoY) and PAT of about ₹130 cr (about 16.6% margin), so YoY growth has held in a tight 19–21% band for six periods with PAT margin flat at 16.6–17.2%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA (31.6x) plus forward P/E (29.7x), not the static IT-services P/E table, because Affle is a platform business. Trailing P/E of 46x is above the 22–30x IT range and about 31% above the broad-market median (P66). Forward P/E is at the top of that range, and the stock sits at 25.5% of its 52-week range. For a business growing about 20% with a ₹1,752 cr net cash cushion, I grade it fair, not cheap. Several things just added risk. The company agreed to acquire Israel-listed Perion Network, cancelled its earnings call citing a 'material development', and still has a ₹1,358 cr Bobble investment caught in insolvency, with a Supreme Court hearing on 25 Nov 2026. Cash conversion has also weakened to 0.65x CFO/PAT in H1.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Energy is a large private power producer with 15.1 GW of installed capacity, about 61% of it renewable, and a stated path to 30 GW by 2030 built on long-term power contracts. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 24.2% YoY to Rs 6,658 cr and PAT rose 38.5% to Rs 1,141 cr (17.1% margin, EBITDA margin 58.7%), but revenue growth has slowed from +78.6% in Q1FY26 and +59.8% in Q2FY26 as acquisitions enter the base, and Q1FY27 is missing from the trend table while the signals mix annual and quarterly rows. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation grades expensive at 17.0x, backed by a trailing P/E of 45.1x against the 10-18x Utilities benchmark and a P/B of 3.29x against ROE of only 8.8%; the 'fair' broad-market peer read carries little weight because it has no tight industry peers. The biggest risk is that net leverage of 4.94x operational and 5.55x total, above the 4.5x target, must fund Rs 20,000 cr of FY27 capex while finance costs are up 14% and FY EPS estimates have been cut 3.1% over 90 days.

Latent View Analytics is a mid-cap data-analytics and AI consulting firm with about 1,800 employees and 40 Fortune 500 clients; it is still growing much faster than tier-1 Indian IT, which is close to flat. Growth is slowing quarter by quarter, though. Revenue growth fell from +27.3% YoY in H1FY26 and +24.3% in FY26 to +14.2% in Q2FY27 (₹294 cr). Q2 PAT was ₹48 cr (+6.1% YoY), and H1FY27 PAT was flat at -0.8% even though revenue grew 17.7%. Margins are shrinking because employee costs rose 21.8% YoY and now take 68.8% of revenue, and outside Industrials (+21.4%) the segments are barely growing (Financial Services +3.5%, CPG/Retail +2.7%). On valuation I used the IT sector P/E range plus EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 32.3x, a little above the 22–30x IT range. Forward P/E is 22.1x and EV/EBITDA is 24.2x, close to the broad-market median (about P50). That makes it fair overall, not cheap, since estimates are being cut. The biggest worry is earnings quality: in H1 only about 26% of profit turned into operating cash (CFO/PAT 0.26x, down from 0.60x), and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 6% over 90 days. Both suggest the growth premium could shrink further.

fundamental.thesis: Physicswallah is a fast-growing Indian test-prep company that sells low-priced online courses and is expanding offline coaching centres, and it is still only around breakeven. The latest numbers we have are for Q1 FY27: revenue of ₹1,054 cr, up 24.4% YoY, against 35.0% growth for full-year FY26 (₹3,900 cr), so growth looks to be slowing. EBITDA margin was only 4.9% in Q1 FY27 versus 14.1% for FY26, and FY26 ended with a net loss of ₹24 cr (-0.6% PAT margin), though part of that margin gap is likely seasonal since Q1 is usually weak for coaching businesses. The Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-04 have not been extracted yet, so this view is stale by one quarter. Because the business is barely profitable, I graded valuation on EV/sales and EV/EBITDA rather than P/E: price-to-sales of 8.43x and EV/EBITDA of 72.1x (P96 vs the broad market, about 3x the 23.3x median) are expensive for a business with slowing growth, unproven offline unit economics and -0.8% ROE. The biggest risk is that growth keeps slowing while the offline build-out and the Utkarsh Classes acquisition squeeze margins, which would knock the rich multiple down sharply.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Power is India's largest integrated power utility — spanning thermal generation (Mundra), renewables (4+ GW operational, TP Solar manufacturing), and T&D distribution in Mumbai/Delhi — and is structurally positioned at the intersection of India's energy-transition and electrification themes. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹19,051 cr with PAT up 11.0% YoY to ₹1,401 cr (7.4% PAT margin), representing a meaningful acceleration from the -1.8% revenue trough of 9MFY26 — EBITDA margin expanded to 23.6% from 21.2% YoY driven by a high-margin renewables segment (32.1% EBITDA margin) and T&D revenue surging 13.5% YoY; TP Solar's 2GW H1FY27 output milestone further validates the manufacturing flywheel. Using EV/EBITDA of 15.23× as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive hybrid (the sector card explicitly calls for EV/EBITDA over P/E), Tata Power sits at the 26th percentile vs broad-market peers and 34.7% below the median — fairly valued to modestly cheap — though the trailing P/E of 34.41× far exceeds the 10–18× utilities sector benchmark, an artefact of high financial leverage (D/E 168×) and a renewable-growth premium embedded in the equity. The single biggest risk is a USD 490 million (≈₹4,100 cr) contingent SIAC arbitration liability (Kleros Capital NDA breach) with no provision recorded — an adverse ruling would effectively erase roughly three full quarters of PAT and could necessitate dilutive equity issuance against an already stretched balance sheet.

Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

fundamental.thesis: Vodafone Idea is the third and weakest player in India's telecom market, which has roughly 2.5 players. It runs on a large government-linked debt and dues structure and is trying a capex-led turnaround while Jio and Airtel hold most of the industry's revenue. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 6.0% YoY to ₹11,689 cr, up from +1.9% in Q3FY26, and EBITDA margin rose to 43.1% from 42.5%; ARPU climbed 10.2% YoY to ₹195 and subscribers grew for the first time since the merger (193.1 mn), but the PAT loss was still ₹3,754 cr, a -32.1% margin, after ₹5,120 cr of finance costs and ₹5,467 cr of D&A. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive telecom. On that basis the stock is expensive: 28.6x versus the card's 9–12x norm for Indian mobile operators, 63rd percentile against the broad market, and the price sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The 4.3x trailing P/E is meaningless because a one-off FY26 gain distorts it, book value is negative, and the forward P/E is also negative. The biggest risk is solvency: negative net worth of ₹38,327 cr, deferred spectrum and AGR dues of about ₹1.56L cr with ₹9,259 cr due by June 2027, and a turnaround that depends on lender support and ₹45,000 cr of capex. The Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov are a near-term event risk.

fundamental.thesis: Indus Towers rents mobile tower space to telecom operators, with about 2.7 lakh towers and 1.63 tenants per tower in the latest KPI data. Revenue growth slowed from +7.9% in Q3 FY26 to +4.6% in Q1 FY27 and +4.0% (₹8,516 cr) in Q2 FY27, while PAT growth went from +0.5% to -2.5% (₹1,793 cr), leaving H1 PAT down 1.6% at ₹3,519 cr; I treated the row labelled Q2FY26 as Q2 FY27 because H1 less Q1 revenue is exactly ₹8,516 cr, but the same subtraction gives PAT of ₹1,773 cr and the 55.3% H1 EBITDA margin sits above both quarters (53.6% and 54.4%), so the margin figures are only approximate. On EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, 8.12× is below its 9-12× range, which is written for mobile operators rather than tower companies, so I grade the stock cheap, helped by a 15.29× trailing P/E and H1 free cash flow of ₹4,332 cr, though the bottom-quartile peer ranks are against the broad market rather than true peers and slowing growth justifies part of the discount. The biggest risk is a major customer under AGR-related stress that is paying only monthly billings, which has already kept ₹198 cr of revenue unrecognised in H1, while the 13.31× forward P/E assumes roughly 15% EPS growth even as PAT falls and estimates are being cut (FY EPS -1.4% over 90 days); leverage is also unclear, because the reported 2.33× net debt/EBITDA does not reconcile with debt of about ₹21,000 cr implied by the 53% debt/equity, or roughly 1.1× annualised EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: ITI Limited is a Government of India-owned telecom equipment manufacturer (PSU under Department of Telecommunications) engaged in defence communication, broadband gear, and telecom network products — a structurally impaired business currently in a BIFR-supervised revival plan, NOT a telecom service operator and therefore the Telecom sector card (ARPU/EBITDA framework) does not apply here. fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue grew +12.8% YoY to ₹1,075 cr — a clear acceleration from +5.4% in Q1FY26 — with PAT rising faster at +22.9% to ₹395 cr and PAT margin expanding to 36.7% from 25.3%; the EBITDA margin, however, contracted to 54.7% from 62.5% quarter-on-quarter, the residential segment effectively shut down at -92% YoY, and FY26 full-year CFO/PAT of 0.34× signals that a large portion of reported earnings is not yet converting to operating cash. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

Mahanagar Gas is the dominant city gas distributor in Mumbai, Thane and Raigad, supplying CNG to vehicles and piped gas to homes and businesses, so its earnings depend on the gap between what it pays for gas and what it can charge customers. Sales are growing but profit is shrinking. H1FY27 revenue rose 18.5% YoY to Rs 5,377 cr, while PAT fell 35.7% to Rs 328 cr. By our calculation, Q2FY27 revenue was about Rs 2,778 cr (+23% YoY) and PAT about Rs 135 cr (about -29% YoY), the third straight period of shrinking margins: EBITDA margin fell from 20.6% in 9MFY26 to 14.3% in Q1 and 12.7% in H1. Because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-style utility, we graded valuation on EV/EBITDA (7.4x) and P/E (14.2x trailing, 12.9x forward), both inside the 10-18x Utilities / Energy range, so we call it fair. The low multiple reflects the margin squeeze and should not be read as a bargain; the broad-market peer rank is a fallback with no true gas-distribution peers and carries little weight. The biggest risk is that gas costs keep rising faster than prices, given cuts to cheaper domestic gas allocation, more costly gas in the mix and crude near $91.

fundamental.thesis: Brigade Enterprises is a Bengaluru-focused developer with residential projects plus a steady leasing and hospitality annuity business; its leasing segment earns a 67.5% margin and grew 1.3% YoY. fundamental.thesis: NHPC is India's largest hydropower generator, a government-owned company that earns a regulated return on the power plants it has commissioned, so its profits grow with commissioned capacity rather than with power prices; the Subansiri Lower project (1,250 MW of a planned 2,000 MW now running) is its main growth driver. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 26.0% YoY to ₹8,291 cr and PAT grew 20.6% to ₹2,836 cr (PAT margin 34.2%), faster than the +14.5% revenue growth a year earlier; however, ₹918 cr of that revenue is provisional Parbati-II income still awaiting CERC tariff approval, finance costs more than doubled (+115%), and EBITDA margin fell from 65.7% to 63.0%. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive utilities, NHPC trades at 25.5x, slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3x; its trailing P/E of 27.4x is well above the 10–18x utilities range, and a P/B of 1.85x against an ROE of only 9% is not cheap, so I grade it expensive on current earnings. The low forward P/E of 11.9x (estimates raised 3.9% over 90 days) and the stock sitting near the bottom of its 52-week range are the main counterpoints. The biggest risk is that heavy borrowing (net debt about ₹56,700 cr, debt/equity 1.36, negative free cash flow) keeps pushing up interest costs faster than new capacity adds earnings, especially if the remaining Subansiri units are delayed or the Parbati-II provisional revenue is cut when CERC sets the tariff.

Grasim is an Aditya Birla holding company with cement (through UltraTech), cellulose fibre (VSF), chemicals, the Birla Opus paints entry, renewables and financial services (Aditya Birla Capital) all reported in one set of accounts, so I judged it as a conglomerate rather than a pure materials stock. Consolidated revenue in Q1 FY27 was ₹48,716 cr, up 21.4% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,846 cr, up 38.8%, continuing five quarters of 17-25% revenue growth. The PAT margin jumped from about 1.4-3% to 7.9%, but the trend table has a mislabelled 'FY26' row and mixes consolidated and attributable profit, so I'm treating that margin jump as unconfirmed rather than a clean improvement. In cement, the main earnings driver, volume rose 15% and profit per tonne (EBITDA) held at a healthy ₹1,051-1,253 through FY26. Because this is a capital-heavy group, I used EV/EBITDA to grade valuation: at 13.2x it is 26% below the sector median (P27), and P/B of 2.1x is cheap against peers (P19). That cheapness is largely explained by a weak 6.3% ROE, the lending book inside the group and the usual holding-company discount. Trailing P/E of 42x (P73) is above the 12-22x materials range, but forward P/E of 21x is in line with peers, so overall valuation is fair. The stock sits at 87% of its 52-week range, which limits upside. Biggest risk: Q2 FY27 results are due on 13-Nov, and analysts have cut FY-EPS estimates 4-7% over 90 days even though all 10 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating.

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card mandate for capital-intensive industrials, SIEMENS at 52.75× trades at a 55% premium to the sector median of 34× and sits at P76 in its peer set; even granting the electricals sub-group premium band of 50–80× cited in the sector card, declining EBITDA and a -4.5% 30-day sell-side EPS revision trend make the upper-range multiple difficult to sustain, grading the stock expensive. The key risk is accelerating margin erosion — commodity and FX headwinds compressing EBITDA even as the order book grows, which combined with continued downward estimate revisions historically precedes the 30–50% de-rating the sector card explicitly flags for capex-cycle industrials.

Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, as the sector card advises for commodity names, the stock is cheap: 5.71x is the lowest of 16 Materials peers (sector median 17.9x) and at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. Prestige Estates is a Bangalore-anchored, multi-city branded developer with residential, office, retail and hospitality arms, and it is one of the larger listed players in the consolidating RERA-era sector. H1 FY27 reported revenue was flat at about ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY), down from +72.7% growth in FY26. PAT fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr (11.2% margin), the owners' share fell 36.4%, and EBITDA was down 5.7% as land, contractor and finance costs rose. One caveat: reported P&L here trails bookings by 2-4 years, and the Q2 pre-sales and collections figures from the Oct-13 operational update were not in the extracted data, so I cannot assess the metric that matters most for a developer. Using EV/EBITDA and P/B+ROE rather than P/E (55x trailing is not meaningful for developers), the stock looks roughly fair. EV/EBITDA of 21.6x sits about 7% below the broad-market median, but a 4.0x P/B for an 8% ROE is rich, and with the stock at 60% of its 52-week range the margin of safety is limited. The CPPIB hospitality deal (₹15,000 cr first tranche closed Oct 2026, up to ₹30,000 cr committed) and strong H1 operating cash flow (₹1,311 cr, CFO/PAT 2.5x) are real positives. Against them, debt/equity is about 1.05x and consensus EPS has been cut 7-11% over 90 days even though 19 of 21 analysts rate it a buy, which is a classic pre-derating pattern.

Indian Oil is India's largest state-run refiner and fuel marketer, so its earnings depend on government fuel-pricing policy as much as on crude prices: falling crude helps it, rising crude hurts. H1FY27 revenue rose 28.4% YoY to ₹549,972 cr and PAT rose 35.2% to ₹21,362 cr, but the half was very uneven: Q1 was a loss (₹-1,141 cr; EBITDA margin 1.9%), then Q2 PAT jumped to about ₹21,630 cr as refining margin (GRM) rose from $15.59 to $18.52/bbl. Revenue growth looks driven mostly by price rather than volume, since marketing sales fell from 26.2 to 25.2 MMT quarter-on-quarter and diesel sales from 10.9 to 9.0 MMT. On the yardstick the sector card names for oil marketing companies (P/E plus dividend yield, EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock looks low on trailing numbers: P/E 4.4x against a peer median of 9.2x, EV/EBITDA 4.1x against 6.1x, and P/B 0.85x with 21% ROE. Those trailing numbers are inflated by an unusually strong Q2, though. Forward P/E is 7.7x, close to the 8.1x peer median and higher than trailing, which means analysts expect earnings to fall, so I grade it fair: priced for policy risk rather than mispriced. The biggest risk is crude at about $91 and rising while retail fuel prices stay frozen, which could push marketing margins back toward Q1-style losses; earnings are also turning into cash poorly (H1 CFO/PAT 0.48x, free cash flow ₹-1,450 cr).

Gross NPA improved from 2.26% (Q3FY26) to 1.98% (FY26), and provision coverage rose to 94.45% in H1FY27. Profit growth is therefore coming from lower credit costs and other income, not from lending spreads, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-23 have not been extracted yet, so the latest-quarter trend is unconfirmed. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book plus ROE), the stock trades at 0.74x book against a 12-15% ROE, the cheapest in its 15-bank peer set on P/B (P0) and about 50% below the 1.5x median, which grades as cheap. The main risk is margin squeeze: loans are growing faster than deposits, NII growth is flat, and the rate-cut cycle is repricing loan yields down faster than deposit costs, which could stall earnings once the boost from lower provisioning fades.

Sun Pharma is India's largest pharma company by revenue. Its earnings come from leadership in Indian branded formulations, where market share rose 0.3pp to 8.6% and formulations sales grew 16.6% in H1, and from a growing global innovative-medicines (specialty) business that is now about 21.5% of sales. H1FY27 revenue grew 11.0% YoY to ₹31,499 cr, and Q2 (₹16,315 cr, worked out as H1 minus Q1) grew 11.8%, a little faster than Q1's 10.1%. The bigger trend is slowing: growth was +15.1% in 9MFY26, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 31.9% to about 29%. Implied Q2 reported PAT of about ₹1,988 cr gives only a 12.2% margin after large Organon-acquisition and US pricing-settlement charges, and US formulations fell 8.2% in Q2 as Lenalidomide sales eroded. On the yardstick that suits a branded/specialty pharma, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E is 37.4x, inside the 28–40x sector band and at P54 among peers. Forward P/E of 27.7x (P62) and EV/EBITDA of 24.2x (13% above the peer median) leave no room for a re-rating. The biggest risk is integrating the USD 14bn Organon deal. It is several times Sun's ~₹17.7k cr net cash, so the clean balance sheet will likely take on debt, and more deal costs are flagged for coming quarters. Meanwhile sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 2.9–3.4% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Auto makes two- and three-wheelers and is a leading Indian exporter, with about 48% of India's two-wheeler exports and 63% of its three-wheeler exports in H1, plus a 23% Q2 market share for its Chetak electric scooter. Q2FY27 consolidated revenue rose 60% YoY to Rs 25,126 cr and PAT rose 60% to Rs 3,400 cr, but the 'accelerating' revenue signal (+19% to +32% to +60%) looks inflated by full consolidation of KTM, so unit volumes are the better guide, and their growth slowed from +29% in Q1 to +20% in Q2 while PAT margin fell from 17.1% in Q4FY26 to 14.9% and then 13.5%. Valuation is fair on the auto card's P/E yardstick, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA because the Rs 25,126 cr revenue includes low-margin consolidation effects: trailing P/E of 26.6x is inside the 18-30x OEM range and 1.9% below the 27.1x peer median (P40), while EV/EBITDA of 19.8x is 8.1% above the peer median (P67) and the stock sits at 85% of its 52-week range, which limits upside despite FY EPS estimates rising 10.3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that input-cost inflation of about 8% of revenue in H1, only about 60% recovered through pricing, continues into Q3 just as rupee support fades and rural demand weakens; some data also conflicts, including a stale-filing flag, a yfinance revenue mismatch and an implausible 145% dividend yield, so those items were not relied on.

Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). The quality of that growth is mixed: offtake rose +7.6% to 384.2 MT while production fell -2% to 321 MT, so part of the growth came from selling down inventory, which fell 49% to 130.3 MT. Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: IndusInd Bank is a mid-sized private lender, heavy on vehicle finance (28% of loans, 58% retail), that is still rebuilding after the FY26 accounting-discrepancy year in which full-year PAT fell 65% to ₹891 cr and ROA dropped to 0.17%. Per the H1FY27 filing, total income rose 26.8% YoY to ₹23,873 cr and PAT rose 36.4% to ₹2,279 cr, but this flatters the core business: the comparison base includes a Q2FY26 loss, Q1FY27 includes a one-off ₹868 cr IFR transfer, and operating profit actually fell 7.9% YoY to ₹10,323 cr. Loan growth has recovered from -8.5% (FY26) to +11% YoY, but NIM has slipped to 3.23% from 3.39–3.48%, credit cost is elevated at 1.4%, cost-to-income is high at 57.9%, and annualised Q2 ROE is only 7.4%. On P/EV, the stock trades at about 2.1x (₹1.8L cr / ₹87,350 cr), which I grade fair on a provisional basis because no peer or historical P/EV is provided; the 71.7x trailing P/E (peer median 53.7x) is not the right yardstick, and the 15% of 52-week range position offers a better entry only if growth holds, while the 15.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and is ignored. Pidilite Industries is India's leading adhesives and sealants company (Fevicol, Dr. Fixit), a consumer franchise with strong pricing power, not a commodity chemicals business. The latest quarter extracted is Q1FY27, where revenue was ₹4,552 cr (+21.3% YoY) and PAT was ₹884 cr (+29.8% YoY), with EBITDA margin up to 28.6% from 23.4% in Q4FY26 and PAT margin up to 19.4% from 16.8% in FY26. Revenue growth has picked up from +11.1% for FY26 and +15.3% in Q4FY26. However, the Q2FY27 numbers filed on 2026-10-28 were not extracted, and the Q3FY26 revenue of ₹996 cr looks like a partial or bad row, so the trend is incomplete. I graded valuation on the sector card's consumer-franchise yardstick of 30–60× P/E for paints and adhesives, not the cyclical Materials median. On that basis it is fair but near the top of the band: trailing P/E is 57.1× and forward P/E is 46.8×, which assumes earnings keep growing. The stock sits at P93–P100 among Materials peers, but most of those peers are steel and metals cyclicals, so that ranking overstates how expensive it is. The stock is mid-range in its 52-week band (49.9%), and the average analyst target is only +6.8% above the price. The biggest risk is that a premium multiple leaves no room for a growth slowdown, and the slight 30-day EPS estimate cuts (-1.7%) are an early warning to watch. The snapshot's 77% dividend yield and 3.78 debt/equity look like data errors for a business that is close to debt-free, so I ignored them.

fundamental.thesis: Cholamandalam Investment is a large, diversified non-bank lender focused on vehicle, MSME/property-backed and consumer loans, with AUM growth accelerating from +21% in Q4 FY26 to +23% in Q1 and +24.7% in H1 FY27. H1 FY27 revenue rose 22.6% YoY to about Rs 18,351 cr and PAT rose 43.3% to Rs 3,284 cr, but Q2 figures derived by subtracting Q1 from H1 show revenue growth of about +23% and PAT growth slowing from +45.5% to about +41%, with PAT slipping sequentially from Rs 1,654 cr to about Rs 1,630 cr and PAT margin falling from about 18.5% to about 17.3%; NIM was flat at 8.0% against Q4 FY26, while credit cost eased from 1.5% to 1.4%. On the P/B-versus-ROE yardstick for lenders, the stock looks expensive at 4.62x book with ROE of 19-20%, which is at P89 of peers and 51.5% above the 3.0x median, although strong growth and low-priced state-owned peers such as PFC and RECLTD explain part of the premium; the 26.77x trailing P/E (P78) appears to use FY26 EPS, and is closer to 23x on my estimate of trailing-twelve-month PAT. The biggest risk is that this premium leaves little room for credit slippage, as gross NPA of 4.44% is better than 4.57% a year ago but above 4.36% in March 2026, Ind AS provision cover has fallen from 47.29% to 45.32% since March, and consumer-loan losses are elevated at 2.2%.

LIC is India's dominant life insurer, with a 58.8% share of first-year premium income (37.5% in individual policies, 70.5% in group) and ₹59.6L cr of assets under management. In H1FY27, gross premium income grew 11.6% YoY to ₹2,75,423 cr, up from +4.8% growth in H1FY26. PAT rose 22.0% to ₹25,699 cr, though PAT margin slipped from 9.8% to 9.3%. The better quality signal is that Value of New Business (VNB, the profit expected from new policies) grew 34% to ₹6,846 cr, and VNB margin widened 470 bps to 22.3%. Weaker spots: policy count fell 2.25%, individual non-participating APE fell 6%, and Indian Embedded Value (EV) slipped 1.95% to ₹7,97,378 cr. For valuation I used P/EV, the right yardstick for life insurers, and ignored P/E. A market cap of about ₹5.0L cr against EV of ₹7.97L cr gives P/EV of roughly 0.63×, well below book embedded value. LIC is also the cheapest of its 4 listed life-insurance peers on every multiple (P/B 2.05× vs a 6.8× peer median), so I grade it cheap, even after allowing a discount for state ownership and a lower-margin product mix. The main risk to this view is that EV and individual-policy volumes are both falling while VNB margin rises, which may mean growth relies on a mix shift and could be squeezed by IRDAI's proposed commission rule changes.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Power is India's largest private thermal generator (18.3 GW operating, 23.7 GW under construction), with about 88-95% of capacity tied to long-term PPAs and the rest sold on the merchant market, which makes it a power-cycle business rather than a regulated annuity like NTPC or POWERGRID. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 28.5% YoY to Rs 17,528 cr, recovering from -3.5% in FY26 to +10.0% in Q4 FY26 and +33.9% in Q1 FY27, though growth eased slightly in Q2; reported PAT of Rs 7,019 cr (+141.5%, 40.0% margin) includes a one-time Rs 2,422 cr recovery of past dues, so underlying PAT is closer to Rs 4,600 cr (about 26% margin), and EBITDA margin fell from 44.3% to 36.1% as fuel costs jumped 41.8%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive generator: at 25.2x it is 118% above the Utilities peer median of 11.6x, and trailing P/E of 35.4x sits far above the 10-18x sector band, with the stock at 86% of its 52-week range, so it is expensive despite a strong 27% ROE and improving leverage (net debt/EBITDA 1.91x). The biggest risk is that the market is paying a premium for headline profit inflated by one-offs, while margins are compressing, next-year earnings estimates are being trimmed (-1.7% over 90 days), and a Rs 2 trillion capex programme must be executed across 13 projects.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Green Energy is India's largest renewable power producer. It runs 20,763 MW of operating capacity, up 24% YoY, with the 30 GW Khavda park at its core, and it sells power under 25-year fixed-tariff contracts. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 27.6% YoY to ₹8,689 cr and PAT rose 17.8% to ₹1,730 cr, a 19.9% margin. H1 minus Q1 implies Q2 revenue of about ₹4,258 cr, faster than Q1's +16.6%, but Q2 PAT margin of about 17.5% is below Q1's 22.2%. The 'expanding margin' signal compares half-year, full-year and nine-month figures, so it is not like-for-like and overstates the improvement. This is a capital-intensive business, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, and on that basis it is expensive. EV/EBITDA is 31.8x against a utilities peer median of 11.6x, the highest in the group. Price-to-book is 12.7x while ROE is only 7.6%, and the stock sits at 93.6% of its 52-week range. Sell-side earnings estimates have been cut 14.5% over 90 days even though 9 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower. The main risk is the balance sheet: net debt is 5.6x run-rate EBITDA, gross debt is ₹1.12 lakh cr and H1 free cash flow was -₹7,141 cr, so the equity depends on capacity coming online on time and on cheap refinancing. That is happening while US yields are at 5% and the rupee is weakening.

Lodha (Macrotech) is one of India's largest residential developers, mainly in Mumbai (MMR) and Pune, and is expanding into Bangalore and rental income (annuity assets and data centres). Its reported numbers look strong: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹9,464 cr (+29.8% YoY) and PAT was ₹2,387 cr (+62.9%), with PAT margin up to about 25% from 20% in FY26. But revenue growth slowed from +43% in Q1 to roughly +30% for the half, and in this sector reported profit reflects sales booked 2–4 years ago. The forward-looking numbers are weaker: pre-sales were ₹96.7bn, up only 7% YoY, and collections fell 7%. Hitting the ₹240bn FY27 pre-sales guidance means H2 must deliver about ₹143bn, roughly 1.5x H1, which depends heavily on launching a ₹190.7bn H2 pipeline on time. On valuation I used the sector yardstick, EV/pre-sales, rather than P/E: an enterprise value of about ₹95k cr is roughly 4x guided FY27 pre-sales, or about 4.9x H1 annualised. P/B of 3.9x with ROE of 15.7% and a trailing P/E of 26.5x (inside the 20–35x real estate range and P34 vs the broad market) support a 'fair' grade. The stock sits at 29% of its 52-week range and earnings estimates are being raised, so the entry point is reasonable but not a bargain. The biggest risk is that slow pre-sales and falling collections signal the plateau typical of a late upcycle, and a shortfall against the back-ended guidance would hit the stock.

fundamental.thesis: Canara Bank is a large public sector bank (62.93% GoI ownership) and one of India's top-5 lenders by advances (₹13.6L cr), with a franchise spanning retail, wholesale, and treasury segments; the key yardstick here is P/B vs ROE, per the sector card, not P/E. H1FY27 shows a notable bifurcation: PAT grew strongly +31.3% YoY to ₹10,562 cr on dramatically improved asset quality (Gross NPA 1.33%, Net NPA 0.30%, PCR 95.34%), but total income contracted -3.38% YoY — revenue trajectory has decelerated from +7.7% (FY26) to -3.4% (H1FY27), driven by treasury revenue declining -18% YoY and NIM compression (2.06% FY26 vs 2.51% in Q4FY26), while PAT margin has expanded from 11.7% (FY26) to 13.1% (H1FY27) on sharply lower credit costs. At P/B of 1.02× against ROE of 15.9%, the stock is unambiguously cheap by the sector card's prescribed lender yardstick — sector card benchmark is P/B < 1.5 with ROE > 12% = cheap — and sits at P0 (cheapest) in its 14-peer regional bank cohort on both trailing P/E (6.1×, -64% vs median 16.8×) and forward P/E (5.7×), though much of this structural discount is explained by PSU overhang and below-median CASA (29.86% vs private sector ~40%+). The single biggest risk is NIM pressure persisting through the deposit repricing cycle — NIM at 2.06% for FY26 is already thin for a PSU bank and any further compression from EBLR-linked loan repricing faster than deposit cost decline would erode the PAT margin expansion thesis and keep revenue growth negative.

Britannia is one of India's leading packaged-foods companies, a market leader in biscuits with a growing presence in dairy, cakes and rusk. Q2 FY27, worked out as H1 FY27 minus Q1, had revenue of about ₹5,598 cr, up roughly 15.6% YoY (the press release says consolidated sales grew 16.6%). That is faster than the +7–8% of the prior three quarters. But PAT growth has slowed from +21.1% in Q4 FY26 to +14.1% in Q1 and about +10.8% in Q2 (≈₹726 cr), and gross margin fell from about 46% in FY26 to 41.5% in Q1. Revenue is speeding up while profits are not keeping pace, which suggests input costs or price cuts are eating into margins. The filings do not give volume growth, so we cannot confirm how much of the sales jump is real demand. On the FMCG yardstick of P/E against the 40–65× sector norm, the trailing P/E of 48.4× (forward 39.1×) sits inside the band and at only the P42 percentile among 12 peers, with EV/EBITDA of 34.6× in line with the peer median. That makes it fairly valued, and the stock is near its 52-week low (4.8% of its range). The balance sheet has weakened in H1: inventory rose by about ₹975 cr, short-term borrowings more than doubled to ₹2,440 cr, net debt is about ₹2,175 cr (≈1.1× EBITDA), and only 0.71× of PAT came through as operating cash.

fundamental.thesis: Marico is a leading Indian FMCG company built on Parachute coconut oil, Saffola and value-added hair oils, with growing Foods and digital-first brands and about a quarter of revenue from international markets (Bangladesh, Vietnam, MENA). Q1 FY27 was strong: India volumes grew 11%, India revenue grew about 21%, Parachute gained 400 bps of volume share, and EBITDA margin rose 40 bps to 20.7%. The extracted Q2 FY27 numbers do not hold together, though. Revenue of ₹2,722 cr (+8.4% YoY) sits below Q1's ₹3,957 cr, and PAT of ₹683 cr (+71.6%) is a 25.1% margin that includes ₹133 cr of minority interest and unitemised exceptional items, so the apparent slowdown in growth and jump in margin cannot be trusted until the full results PDF is checked. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers: trailing P/E is 59.4x, at the top of the 40–65x FMCG norm, but it is the most expensive in its peer group (P100) at +35.5% above the 43.8x median, EV/EBITDA is 44.1x (+42% vs peers), and the stock is at 80% of its 52-week range, so valuation is expensive even though forward P/E of 42.9x implies earnings growth. The biggest risk is a de-rating: if Q2 shows real slowing in volume or value growth, a stock priced at a premium to every peer has little room for error, and rising crude (an input-cost risk for packaging and some raw materials) adds pressure on margins.

fundamental.thesis: Berger Paints is India's number-two decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemical and international businesses, and it says its market share stayed stable through Q2 even as Birla Opus pushes into the market. Revenue growth has sped up from +0.4% YoY in Q3FY26 to +6.7% in Q4FY26, +12.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.2% in Q2FY27. H1FY27 revenue was ₹6,784 cr (+12.5%) and PAT ₹622 cr (+19.3%). Margins are moving the other way: subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 revenue of about ₹3,200 cr and PAT of about ₹217 cr, a PAT margin near 6.8% against 11.3% in Q1. Q2 operating profit grew only 5.2% and standalone EBITDA margin fell 4.4pp because of sharp raw-material inflation and higher ad spend. Because paints are a consumer franchise, I graded valuation on P/E against the sector card's 30–60× band rather than against steel and metals stocks: a trailing P/E of 50.9× (38.7× forward) is fair, though top quartile within Materials (P87), and it sits below the priciest peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND. The 52-week position is mid-range at 48%. The biggest risk is that management sees no easing in input costs and is relying on further price increases from November, while a new entrant makes it harder to pass costs on. Cash conversion is also very weak, with H1 CFO/PAT at 0.23x and free cash flow of -₹82 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Lupin is a large Indian generics maker. It ranks 3rd in the US by prescriptions with about 5% share of generic prescriptions, and its India business is 66% chronic therapies, where it is growing faster than the market (anti-diabetes +28.6% vs +18.8%, chronic +19.5% vs +17.2%). Growth is slowing and profit is shrinking: Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹7,827 cr (an estimated +11% YoY, down from +32.1% in Q1 and partly helped by the VISUfarma acquisition), Q2 PAT fell 24.6% YoY to about ₹1,186 cr, and H1 PAT fell 10.9% even though revenue grew 20.9%. fundamental.thesis: MMTC is a Navratna PSU and India's historically largest international trading company dealing in metals, minerals, and agricultural commodities, but its core trading operations have been effectively dormant for several years, leaving it structurally as an investment-income vehicle. Available revenue data (₹3 cr in Q3FY26; near-zero or zero in every other period) contrasted with PAT of ₹104–261 cr across recent quarters confirms that reported earnings derive entirely from investment/non-operational income rather than business execution — this PAT-over-revenue anomaly makes multi-quarter trajectory analysis meaningless and precludes any growth narrative. Trailing P/E of 29× sits at the lower bound of the Industrials sector median (28–45×) and at P39 vs broad-market peers, which appears superficially fair, but a Price/Sales ratio of 3,297× and negative EV/EBITDA of –52.71× expose that this multiple is being applied to non-operational earnings — a fundamentally unreliable valuation basis, and the stock trading at 88% of its 52-week high prices in near-perfection with no operational story to anchor it. The dominant risk is a de-rating if investment/one-time income normalises, compounded by an auditor tenure transition and no management guidance on any forward business model.

Eicher Motors owns Royal Enfield, which holds about 87% of India's premium motorcycle segment, and also has a commercial-vehicle joint venture (VECV), so it sits right on the sector's premiumisation trend. In Q1 FY27 revenue rose 31.6% YoY to Rs 6,632 cr and PAT rose 21.4% to Rs 1,463 cr. Revenue growth is strong but uneven (+14.8%, +45.0%, +23.0%, then +31.6% over the last four quarters), and the PAT margin has slipped from 23.9% to 22.0% over the same span, so profit is growing more slowly than sales. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA, the auto sector card's yardstick: a trailing P/E of 37.9x is above the 18-30x OEM range and 40% above the peer median of 27.1x (P80), and EV/EBITDA of 33.7x and P/B of 8.3x are the highest among peers (P100), so the stock is expensive even after allowing a premium for quality and a forward P/E of 28.8x. fundamental.thesis: Fortis Healthcare runs a large hospital network of about 6,300 operational beds plus a diagnostics arm of about 400 labs, and it grows through occupancy, revenue per patient and adding beds.
