Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock is expensive at 35.6x vs a sector median of 23.3x (P81), and a trailing P/E of 69.3x vs a forward P/E of 40.9x implies about 69% EPS growth, although the mostly pharma peer set makes the comparison imperfect and the 34% consensus upside looks overstated because the 52-week position implies a price near Rs 957, or about 15% upside to the Rs 1,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit while FY EPS estimates, already cut 5.8% over 90 days, fall further against a valuation that needs a sharp earnings rebound.

Glenmark is a mid-cap generic and specialty pharma company that sells in India, the US, Europe and emerging markets, with a growing branded respiratory and dermatology business (Ryaltris is commercialised in 55 markets with 50% secondary-sales growth) and an innovation arm whose ISB 2001 deal with AbbVie is worth up to USD 1.9bn, including USD 700m upfront. The latest reliably extracted quarter is Q4FY26: revenue of Rs 3,771 cr (+15.8% YoY) and PAT of Rs 301 cr, an ~8% margin. Several trend-table rows look mislabelled or standalone-only, the yfinance quarterly revenue (~Rs 1,250 cr) is far below the consolidated scale, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet, so the current trajectory cannot be confirmed. In the India business, secondary sales grew only 1.5% in Q4FY26, which is soft for a chronic-heavy franchise. On valuation (P/E against the sector band, cross-checked with peer EV/EBITDA), the trailing P/E of 37.9x sits inside the 28-40x pharma band and near the peer median of 36.4x (P62). Forward P/E of 24.7x (P46) and EV/EBITDA of 14.0x (P15, 35% below the peer median) look cheaper, but the stock is at 83.5% of its 52-week range, the consensus target of Rs 2,513 is below the current price, and EPS estimates have been cut by 1.5-2.8% over 30-90 days, so overall the stock is fairly valued. fundamental.thesis: SRF is a diversified Indian chemicals and packaging-films maker; most of its profit comes from refrigerant gases and specialty chemicals for agrochemical and pharma clients. fundamental.thesis: Deepak Nitrite is an integrated Indian chemicals maker with a leading position in phenol and acetone (Phenolics), plus an Advanced Intermediates (AI) business serving agrochemical and other customers. Quarterly revenue growth has accelerated from +3.0% in Q3 FY26 and -3.0% in Q4 to +36.4% in Q1 FY27 and about +62% in Q2, while H1 FY27 revenue was Rs 5,654 cr (+49.0%) and PAT Rs 743 cr (+222%); Q2 is derived as H1 minus Q1 (revenue about Rs 3,076 cr, PAT about Rs 398 cr, margin about 12.9% vs 13.4% in Q1), and the gain leans on Phenolics, with H1 EBIT of Rs 933 cr, while AI margin fell to 7% from 10%. Using EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for chemical cyclicals, I grade valuation fair: the 24.6x headline (+37% vs the 17.9x peer median, P67) and 41.6x trailing P/E appear to use FY26 earnings, and my rough trailing-12-month estimates are about 14x EV/EBITDA and 22x P/E, which is below the headline but still above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle range on what may be peak earnings, while the 27.6x forward P/E implies PAT of only about Rs 830 cr, so either that figure is stale or earnings are expected to fall despite upward EPS revisions (the snapshot's dividend yield and implied price also look unreliable). The biggest risk is that Phenolics spreads normalise, as management itself signals with its 'new normal' language, just as the long-dated polycarbonate project (FY27 capex plan Rs 2,500 cr vs FY26 FCF of Rs 348 cr, commercialisation targeted by end FY2030) adds debt without near-term earnings.

PI Industries is a specialty agrochemical maker: it manufactures molecules under contract for global innovator companies (CSM exports), sells its own crop-protection brands in India, and is building a pharma/CDMO arm. Its core agchem business is still under pressure from the China price war that the sector card describes. Results have weakened: H1FY27 revenue fell 9.8% YoY to ₹3,404 cr (from ₹3,773 cr), and Q1FY27 revenue was down 11.1% with PAT down 39% to ₹244 cr (13.8% margin). Consolidated H1 PBT fell 51% to ₹505.8 cr, which implies Q2 PBT of only about ₹186 cr. The pharma segment lost ₹147.7 cr in H1, and EBITDA margin has slid from 25-27% in FY26 prints to 20.9% in Q1. Following the sector card, which says chemicals should be valued on EV/EBITDA, the stock looks expensive: 22.1x EV/EBITDA against 5-8x for mid-cycle chemicals and 23% above the Materials peer median of 17.9x. The 29.4x trailing P/E sits only at P33 among peers because paint companies inflate the median, and the 21.3x forward P/E assumes an earnings recovery that the filings do not yet show. The biggest risk is that the CSM export slowdown and pharma losses continue, so earnings keep falling while the multiple stays high. Even near the 52-week low, the stock could be a falling knife rather than a value buy.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Housing Finance is a large housing-finance NBFC in the Bajaj group, lending to home buyers, property owners and developers, with AUM up 25% YoY to ₹1,58,205 cr and asset quality that remains very clean (GNPA 0.29%, NNPA 0.12%). Credit quality is also slipping, with gross NPA rising from 1.19% in Q3FY26 to 1.42% in Q1FY27 and 1.52% in H1FY27. On the lender yardstick of price-to-book versus sustainable ROE, a P/B of 2.69x for a 20% ROE is fair, toward the cheaper end (trailing P/E 14.5x, forward P/E 10.5x, 52-week position 47%). The biggest risk to the thesis is that rising NPAs, with only about 25% provision coverage, push credit costs up and squeeze its high returns just as loan growth slows.

fundamental.thesis: CreditAccess Grameen is India's largest pure-play microfinance lender, with a gross loan book of about ₹29,294 cr that grew 21.5% YoY as of H1 FY27 and 2,276 branches lending mostly to rural women borrowers. That is roughly 7-8x the year-ago quarter, but off a provisioning-hit base, so the +691% H1 PAT and +144% revenue figures overstate the underlying growth, and the revenue figure also mixes NII with total income across periods. Asset quality is the real story: GNPA improved from 4.04% (9M FY26) to 3.17% (FY26) to 2.18% (Q1 FY27), with collection efficiency at 97.4% and provision coverage holding around 65%. Using the sector card's P/B-vs-ROE yardstick for lenders, a P/B of 2.91x against a TTM ROE of 16.4% (annualised H1 ROE about 24%) looks fair rather than cheap. The low forward P/E of 11x simply reflects the earnings normalisation, and analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by 9.8% in the last 30 days. The main risks are a fresh stress cycle in unsecured rural lending, a borrower count that is shrinking (-2.4% YoY) even as loan size grows, and a risk-off macro backdrop for a leveraged midcap lender.

HUDCO is a government-owned (75% promoter, now under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs) lender that funds housing and urban infrastructure, mostly for state-government agencies, and the RBI moved it into the NBFC Upper Layer in August 2026. In H1 FY27, total income rose 25.7% YoY to ₹7,789 cr and PAT rose 31.5% YoY to ₹1,762 cr, giving a 22.6% PAT margin against 21.6% a year earlier. The loan book grew about 29% to ₹1.87 lakh cr. Income growth has eased slightly from about +28.8% in FY26, but asset quality is very clean: gross credit-impaired assets are 0.71%, net are 0.04%, and provision coverage is 93.8%. Lenders are valued on price-to-book against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. At 2.35x book with an annualised H1 ROE of 15.7% (20.2% on a trailing basis), the stock looks fair rather than cheap. The 10.5x P/E and the cheap ranking against peers come from a broad-market comparison, not true lender peers, so they say little. The main watch-point is that capital is being used up fast: the capital adequacy ratio (CRAR) fell from 38.3% at 9M FY26 to 32.6%, and with debt at 7.2x equity, wholesale borrowing costs and spreads matter a lot.

fundamental.thesis: IFCI is a government-owned Development Financial Institution effectively in run-off mode — its active lending business has collapsed, with the loan book shrinking -23.56% YoY to ₹1,194cr, and the company now derives income primarily from residual assets and investments rather than fresh origination. Using P/B + ROE, the appropriate yardstick for lenders per the Sector Card: at P/B 1.36× the stock is optically below the cheap threshold, but ROE of 4.43% is mechanically depressed by an outsized CAR of 30.1% (2× typical regulatory minimums), making fair the more honest grade — the market has partially re-rated the name (stock at 96.2% of 52-week range) and at P33 on trailing P/E the consensus-peer view corroborates a fair assessment rather than a screaming-cheap one. The biggest risk is the sustained CASA ratio decline from 32.5% (Q1FY26) to 27.2% (Q2FY27), signalling a weakening liability franchise and rising cost of funds that could cap NIM improvement as the excess capital gets progressively deployed into the loan book.

PB Fintech runs Policybazaar and Paisabazaar, India's largest online marketplaces for insurance and credit. It earns commissions and does not lend, so the lender yardsticks in the Financials sector card (P/B plus ROE) do not fit, and the debt/equity figure of 4.92 is probably a data artefact, not real leverage. The latest quarter we can verify, Q1FY27, had revenue of ₹1,888 cr, up 40.0% year on year, faster than +37.0% in Q3FY26 and +36.5% for FY26 as a whole. PAT was ₹163 cr, up 92%, but PAT margin has slipped from 10.7% to 9.9% to 8.6% and EBITDA margin from 11.2% to 7.4%, so growth is costing more margin than before. Q2FY27 numbers have not been extracted from the filed results; the yfinance figure of ₹773 cr revenue does not match a ₹1,888 cr Q1 run-rate, so it was ignored. Judged as a high-growth platform on price-to-sales and growth, the stock looks expensive: P/S is 11.0x, EV/EBITDA is 140.6x (99th percentile of the broad market), trailing P/E is 111x and forward P/E is 47.8x (91st percentile). That is a full price even for ~40% growth, while next-year earnings estimates have been cut 15.1% over 90 days and 7.9% over 30 days. The biggest risk is that the premium multiple shrinks if margins keep falling while analysts keep cutting estimates.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Investment Corporation is a Tata Group listed investment holding company (middle-layer NBFC by RBI classification), whose income is overwhelmingly driven by dividends from investee companies (75% of Q1 FY27 revenue) and realized/fair value gains on its equity portfolio — making it a market-beta proxy, not a lending or operating business. Q1 FY27 revenue grew modestly +4.3% YoY to ₹152 cr, while PAT declined marginally by -1.9% YoY to ₹143.51 cr (PAT margin 94.6%), with the drag coming from a 51.6% collapse in net fair value gains (₹21.96 cr vs ₹45.44 cr in Q1 FY26), a structurally volatile income line; the full-year FY26 picture was stronger (+38.9% PAT growth, +30.2% revenue), but that was driven by buoyant equity markets and realized gains, not earnings quality improvement. Using the appropriate holding-company yardstick (P/B vs NAV discount, per Sector Card) rather than P/E: at P/B of 1.07×, the stock trades at essentially zero NAV discount — yet historically listed holding companies command 40–60% NAV discounts, making this expensive by sector norms, despite appearing cheap at P4 on the broad-market P/B peer rank (which is misleading given operating companies dominate that peer set). The biggest risk is that 75% of income depends on Tata investee dividend decisions plus equity portfolio performance, with OCI swings of ±₹4,000–5,000 cr per quarter confirming that NAV — and thus the fundamental floor — is highly sensitive to a RISK_OFF equity drawdown, which the current macro regime directly exacerbates.

fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized, government-owned lender with gross advances of ₹2,87,690 cr. Its loan book is growing faster each quarter (+16.6% YoY in Q2FY26, +21.2% in Q1FY27, +24.7% in Q2FY27). Q2FY27 net profit rose 26.8% YoY to ₹786 cr, up from +8.1% growth in Q1FY27, and asset quality kept improving: gross NPA fell from 2.56% to 1.96% and net NPA from 0.43% to 0.18% over four quarters, with provision coverage at 98.4%. Net interest income (NII) of ₹2,886 cr is about 13.9% above the year-ago revenue line of ₹2,533 cr, but that row may not be strictly NII, so treat the growth figure as approximate. For a bank we judge value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. That pressures margins as the bank pays more for deposits, and it comes in a risk-off market where foreign investors are selling financials.

The main caution is that profits are rising much faster than income, which leans on low provisions and margin gains that may not last as rates reset, and 164 fraud cases (₹1,206 cr, nearly all already provided for) are a reminder of PSU governance and underwriting risk.

fundamental.thesis: BEML is a Schedule-'A' defence PSU under India's Ministry of Defence, manufacturing heavy equipment across mining, construction, defence platforms, and metro/rail segments, with revenue heavily dependent on government order execution. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹820 cr (+29.3% YoY from ₹634 cr) and the operating loss narrowed substantially (EBITDA swung from -₹41 cr to +₹3.6 cr YoY), yet PAT remained negative at -₹27 cr (-3.3% margin); more critically, FY26 full-year PAT collapsed 49.7% and order inflows landed at only ₹1,286 cr vs a ₹6,800 cr target — an 81% miss that is the single most important leading indicator for an order-book business. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial (Sector Card guidance), the stock trades at 48.4× (P88 among peers, 107% premium to sector median 23.3×) and trailing P/E of 94× versus the sector benchmark range of 28–45×, placing it firmly in expensive territory despite a more palatable forward P/E of 28× that already discounts a sharp earnings recovery. The biggest risk is that FY27 order inflows remain structurally below target, eroding book-to-revenue cover and triggering a 30–50% de-rating (consistent with Industrials sector card cycle-risk warning) before the earnings recovery the valuation demands actually materialises.

Apar Industries is a leading Indian maker of power-transmission conductors, specialty oils and cables, and it benefits directly from the grid and transmission capex cycle; its conductor order book is the highest it has ever been at ₹12,025 cr (+67% YoY), with Q2 new orders up 123% to ₹4,775 cr. Growth has held steady rather than sped up: H1FY27 revenue rose 25.0% YoY to ₹13,522 cr (Q2 +21.3% to ₹6,931 cr, against +23.3% for FY26 and +21.9% for 9MFY26), while PAT jumped 77.7% to ₹915 cr and margins widened, with PAT margin moving from 4.3-4.8% to 6.8% and EBITDA margin from about 9% to 11.8%. This quality is offset by weaker underlying numbers: conductor volumes fell 8% and oil volumes fell 17%, so the gains came mainly from pricing and product mix; US revenue fell about 30% in Q2; and operating cash flow turned negative at -₹863 cr (CFO/PAT -0.94x) because of a ₹900+ cr inventory build and higher receivables. On valuation I used trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA together because this is a product and manufacturing business rather than an EPC order-book business: trailing P/E is 59.2x against the Industrials range of 28-45x, EV/EBITDA is 32.2x, the stock sits at P77-P90 on P/E and P/B versus the broad market and at 90% of its 52-week range, so the stock is expensive and the margin surge is already priced in, even though forward P/E of 46x and 21% upward EPS revisions show the growth is real. Data caveats: the yfinance Q2 revenue (₹5,387 cr), the 34% dividend yield and the 17.72 debt/equity look like data errors and were ignored in favour of the filing figures.

fundamental.thesis: Cochin Shipyard (COCHINSHIP) is India's largest PSU shipyard executing defence (Navy/Coast Guard) and commercial vessel contracts, backed by an order book of ₹21,100 cr (~5× annualised revenue) that provides multi-year execution visibility — structurally the most compelling asset on the balance sheet. Revenue growth has decelerated from +38.5% YoY in Q1 FY26 to +15.5% for 9M FY26, but more critically, PAT has swung sharply negative (-18.5% YoY in 9M FY26 vs +7.8% in Q1 FY26) as EBITDA margins compressed from 28.0% to 21.3% — a classic fixed-price-contract cost-creep pattern, likely driven by ISRF ramp-up overheads and higher input/subcontracting costs; cash conversion is deeply negative (CFO/PAT -2.40×, FCF -₹812 cr in H1 FY26), which is the most immediate red flag. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive model per the sector card, 45.51× sits at the upper bound of the 28–45× Industrials range and at P86 in the broad market (95% premium to median), grading expensive; the forward P/E discount (33.25× vs 54× trailing) signals the street is pricing in a sharp earnings recovery — but that recovery has not yet appeared in filed numbers and Q1 FY27 extraction is blank despite the August 2026 filing date. The single biggest risk is that margin compression deepens further on the ISRF ramp and rising crude-linked operating costs, in a RISK_OFF macro with D/E at 28.47 — any slippage in earnings recovery would unwind the current rich valuation quickly.

fundamental.thesis: Firstsource Solutions (FSL) is a mid-cap BPS/digital-services provider servicing Banking, CMT, and Healthcare verticals for global clients, with a growing $1m+ client roster (45 accounts), six consecutive quarters of 4+ large-deal wins, and 11 straight quarters of QoQ revenue growth — the deal pipeline signals reasonable near-term revenue visibility for its scale. Q1FY27 delivered 12.3% constant-currency revenue growth — a sharp deceleration from +24.5% a year ago — while adjusted PAT grew +31.2% YoY to ₹22cr (8.2% margin) and EBIT margin hit 12.4% for a seventh consecutive quarter of expansion; the company maintained FY27 guidance of 10-13% CC growth and 12.25-12.75% EBIT margin despite absorbing a 1-1.5% headwind from a healthcare BPaaS wind-down, a show of confidence in the deal ramp pipeline. On valuation, trailing P/E of 25.1× sits within the IT sector benchmark of 22-30×, but EV/EBITDA of 12.5× ranks at the P20 percentile of the broad market (-47% below the market median of 23.3×) and forward P/E of 15.25× trades at a -34% discount to the market median — with the stock at 18.8% of its 52-week range, the risk/reward skews cheap, though in a RISK_OFF, FII-selling environment the re-rating catalyst is absent near-term. The dominant risk is that CC revenue growth has halved over four quarters, the 27.5% voluntary attrition rate constrains margin expansion headroom, and a 66% concentration in cyclical Banking+CMT verticals leaves earnings vulnerable to any corporate IT/BPS budget tightening.

fundamental.thesis: Finolex Cables is a leading Indian cables manufacturer with electrical cables (~88% of revenue) and communication/OFC cables (~9%) as core segments, a direct beneficiary of the government-led T&D capex upcycle, 5G rollout, and data-centre-driven optical fiber demand. Q1FY27 revenue re-accelerated sharply to +44.2% YoY (₹2,013 cr) — recovering from a +5.0% trough in Q2FY26 — with PAT up 53.1% YoY to ₹249 cr and PAT margin expanding to 12.4% from 11.2% a year ago; however, the communication segment's exceptional 29.75% margin reflects legacy high-cost inventory drawdown, and management has explicitly guided normalization to low double-digits once that inventory is consumed. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for capital-intensive industrials (per sector card), FINCABLES at 22.76× sits at the broad-market median (P49 peer rank, -2.4% vs median), while trailing P/E of 24.84× is modestly below the Industrials sector benchmark lower bound of 28×; the stock is at 94.6% of its 52-week range with analyst consensus mean target implying -0.7% from current price, pointing to fair — not cheap — valuation. The central risk is communication cable margin normalization in H2FY27 compressing consolidated margins, compounded by the copper rod plant remaining operationally impaired due to Middle East LPG/PNG supply disruptions.

Niva Bupa is a standalone health insurer with about 11% of India's retail health market, covers about 27 million lives, and is growing its agent, branch and broker network quickly. Gross written premium rose 35.0% YoY to ₹2,484 cr in Q2FY27, up from +32.0% in Q1FY27, and retail health premium grew 47%. PAT rose 124% YoY to ₹136 cr (5.5% margin), helped by a weak base, and the combined ratio improved from 100.2% in Q1 to about 98.8% in Q2. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for financials, with growth as a second check, not on trailing P/E. Trailing P/E of 75x is inflated by the depressed FY26 base, which had an Ind-AS transition and a Q3FY26 loss. P/B of 3.84x on a 12.1% ROE is rich on the strict lender rule, but forward P/E of 23.5x sits at the median (P51) and P/B is below the broad-market median (P42), so I call it fair, not cheap or clearly expensive. The biggest risk is that underwriting profit is wafer-thin: with the combined ratio near 99-100%, a small rise in medical claims costs or a pricing push-back from IRDAI could wipe out the underwriting margin.

fundamental.thesis: Engineers India is a state-owned engineering consultancy and turnkey contractor for hydrocarbon, refinery and petrochemical projects, so its revenue comes from working through its order book. H1FY27 revenue fell 8.2% YoY to ₹1,644 cr, and the implied Q2 figure (about ₹824 cr, H1 minus Q1) is down roughly 10% YoY, after +36% to +45% growth in FY26. That makes revenue a clear deceleration story: Turnkey revenue collapsed 46.7%, while the higher-margin Consultancy segment grew 32.9%. That mix shift lifted H1 PAT 138% to ₹355 cr, PAT margin from 8.3% to 21.6% and EBITDA margin to 28.4%. Cash conversion was strong at 1.76x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA, the Industrials sector card's preferred measure for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 16.75x against a market median of 23.3x (P30), and trailing P/E is 20.6x against the 28–45x Industrials range, so it looks cheap. But it sits at 87% of its 52-week range, and next-FY earnings estimates were cut 8.1% over 90 days, which tempers the upside. The biggest risk is that the margin jump depends on mix (shrinking low-margin turnkey work) and possibly other income, and no order-inflow or order-book figure was given to show that revenue can grow again.

fundamental.thesis: Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation, now promoted by the Adani Group) is a mid-sized EPC contractor building marine, metro, tunnel and foundation projects, and it has a record order book of ₹32,715 cr, about 3.1 times its trailing revenue and up roughly 58% from ₹20,646 cr a year ago. Growth picked up sharply in Q2 FY27: revenue rose 25.2% YoY to ₹2,749 cr (from +5.6% in Q1) and PAT rose 21.3% to ₹131 cr, taking H1 revenue to ₹5,470 cr (+14.6%) and H1 PAT to ₹271 cr (+10.8%). Profits did not keep pace with revenue because Q2 EBITDA margin slipped to 10.2% from 11.1%, and operating cash flow was negative at about -₹78 cr as money got tied up in contract work (contract assets +₹474 cr). On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-intensive EPC business: 19.9x, about 15% below the broad-market median, with trailing P/E of 34.3x inside the 28–45x Industrials range and forward P/E of 20.1x. That makes the stock fair, not cheap, especially with the price at 91% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 7.9% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that profits are not turning into cash while the company dilutes equity through a ₹1,400 cr QIP. Note that the snapshot's 26% dividend yield is clearly a data error and was ignored.

fundamental.thesis: GMR Airports runs a portfolio of airports, led by Delhi (38.5 mn passengers in H1) and Hyderabad, plus Mopa, Medan and the newly opened Vizag and Nagpur sites. It earns from regulated aero tariffs and a growing non-aero business. H1FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹8,273 cr and PAT was ₹213 cr against a ₹102 cr loss a year ago, but growth is slowing quickly: by our calculation (H1 minus Q1), Q2FY27 revenue was about ₹4,188 cr, up roughly 11.6% YoY, after +48.6% in Q3FY26 and +23.0% in Q1FY27. EBITDA margin has also slipped from 43.8% to 37.9%, and passenger traffic grew only about 1%, with Hyderabad down 11.7% and Mopa down 14.4%, so most of the growth came from tariffs and non-aero (Delhi non-aero +20.3%). For a capital-intensive business we graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, not the meaningless 850x trailing P/E: at 25.1x it sits close to the market median (P56), so the grade is fair. However, the stock is at 98% of its 52-week range, forward P/E is 82.6x, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 19% in 30 days and 26% in 90 days, which leaves limited upside. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: book value is negative (P/B -46.5x) and H1 interest of ₹1,931 cr took up most of EBITDA, so pending tariff decisions (DIAL CP-4 implementation by AERA, Vizag's regular tariff) carry a lot of weight.

fundamental.thesis: Godrej Industries is the Godrej group's listed holding company, not a classic order-book industrial: its earnings come from its own chemicals business plus stakes in Godrej Properties (real estate), Godrej Agrovet (animal feed, veg oils, dairy, crop care) and a growing finance arm, so the Industrials order-book KPIs do not apply. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue rose 22.2% YoY to ₹5,448 cr, sharply faster than the roughly +5% of the prior quarters, helped by chemicals (+31.4%), veg oils (+42.8%) and finance (+43.5%). But PAT to owners fell 36.5% YoY to ₹239 cr, cutting the PAT margin to 4.4% from 7.8%, and real estate revenue dropped 17.5% to ₹1,335 cr, so faster sales are not turning into profit. On valuation (EV/EBITDA used as the main yardstick for a capital-heavy conglomerate), the stock trades at 23.8x, almost exactly the broad-market median of 23.3x (P51), with trailing P/E of 32.1x (P45, inside the 28–45x Industrials band) and P/B of 3.4x (P38), mid-way in its 52-week range, so it is fairly valued with no clear mispricing. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: gross debt-to-equity rose to 2.38x from 1.90x, FY26 free cash flow was about -₹9,883 cr with negative operating cash flow, and Q2FY27 results are due on 13-Nov-2026, a near-term event that could move the stock either way.

fundamental.thesis: Graphite India makes graphite electrodes for electric-arc-furnace steelmaking. It runs about 80,000 tpa of capacity at roughly 97% utilisation, so it trades more like a cyclical Materials stock than an order-book Industrials name, and it is driven by electrode prices and steel demand outside China. Q1 FY27 was strong: revenue of ₹842 cr was up 26.6% and PAT of ₹171 cr was up 28.6%, with a 28.6% EBITDA margin. H1 FY27 PAT of ₹265 cr implies Q2 PAT of only about ₹94 cr, so the profit margin fell from about 20% in Q1 to roughly 9–14% in Q2. The Q2 revenue figure itself is unclear, because H1 minus Q1 gives about ₹1,029 cr while yfinance shows ₹466 cr. Valuation is mixed, so I grade it fair: trailing P/E is 72.4x (sector band 28–45x, P84 vs peers) and EV/EBITDA is 51x (P89), both expensive because FY26 PAT collapsed 62% to ₹175 cr, while forward P/E is 12.4x (P16) and P/B is 2.2x. That cheap forward multiple depends on earnings recovering, and analysts cut current-year EPS estimates by 10% over 30 days and 13% over 90 days despite three Buy ratings. The snapshot's 6.27 debt/equity and 2.9% ROE look out of line for this historically low-debt company and need checking against the balance sheet. H1 FY26 free cash flow was negative (-₹98 cr, CFO/PAT -0.09x), so earnings are not yet clearly turning into cash.

fundamental.thesis: IRCON is a state-owned railway and highway EPC contractor; about 76% of its ₹21,296 cr order book is railways, so its revenue depends on how fast it executes that book. Revenue has turned around from -21.9% YoY in Q1FY26 to +9.5% in Q1FY27 and +14.9% in Q2FY27 (about ₹2,272 cr, implied as H1 minus Q1). Profit has not followed: PAT fell 36% YoY to ₹192 cr in H1FY27, with Q2 PAT of about ₹100 cr down roughly 27%. PAT margin fell from 9.2% to 4.4% and EBITDA margin from 17.1% to 13.6% over the six periods shown. Because this is a capital-intensive order-book business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus order cover rather than P/E. EV/EBITDA is 17.8x, and P/B is 2.0x for an ROE of only 9.1%. The order book is about 2.3x FY26 revenue and has shrunk about 11% YoY from ₹23,865 cr. Trailing P/E is 22x and forward P/E 16.5x, which looks cheap against the 28–45x industrials band. That discount is explained by thin margins, a shrinking order book and FY26 free cash flow of ₹-1,150 cr, so I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that a shrinking order book plus weak cash conversion caps the revenue recovery while margins keep falling.

fundamental.thesis: Suzlon is India's largest domestic wind turbine maker, with a 6.1 GW order book (84% from PSU and commercial/industrial buyers). Growth is slowing and margins are shrinking: Q1FY27 revenue grew +22.5% YoY to ₹3,819 cr, down from +54.7% a year earlier and +42% in Q3FY26. PAT fell -5.9% to ₹305 cr, PAT margin dropped from 10.4% to 8.0%, and EBITDA margin dropped 360 bps to 15.6%. Execution growth also slowed to +14%, and the order book covers only about 2x revenue, well short of the 3x+ that would give strong visibility. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is an order-book industrial. At 25.7x it is about 10% above the broad-market median (P58), so it is fair, not cheap. The 25.3x trailing P/E looks low against the 28–45x Industrials range, but FY26 PAT (19% margin, including a ₹1,114 cr Q4) looks inflated by one-off tax credits, which also distorts the 40.6% ROE and 10.2x P/B. The 5.87 debt/equity figure looks inconsistent with Suzlon's historically low-debt balance sheet and should be treated as suspect data. The biggest risk is that margins keep compressing while earnings fail to turn into cash (CFO/PAT 0.38x in FY26). Analysts cut FY EPS estimates 10.6% over 90 days, and Q2 results are due on 29 Oct.

Shipping Corporation of India is a state-owned shipping company that earns most of its money from tankers (₹2,878 cr of H1 FY27 revenue at a 44% segment margin), with smaller liner, bulk-carrier and offshore businesses. Its results depend on freight rates, which go up and down with the cycle. Growth picked up sharply: H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹2,290 cr (roughly +71% YoY) and PAT about ₹578 cr (25.2% margin), up from +40.3% revenue growth in Q1 and +3.1% for FY26. The cash backs this up, with cash from operations at 1.10x PAT in H1 against 0.82x in FY26. For valuation I used P/E and P/B, not order-book metrics, because this is a freight-rate business rather than a capital-goods order-book name. On trailing P/E of 10.65x (P7 among broad-market peers) and P/B of 1.69x the stock looks cheap, but I grade it fair: low P/Es are normal near the top of a freight cycle, and the forward P/E of 93.7x and EV/EBITDA of 35.2x do not fit with H1 EBITDA of about ₹1,975 cr, so I don't trust that part of the snapshot. The biggest risks are a fall in freight rates from today's strong Middle East-driven levels and stress at the LNG joint ventures, which led to a ₹240 cr provision and going-concern warnings from auditors. Board committees that still break SEBI listing rules and a government stake sale stuck since 2020 add to the governance risk.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Fertilisers is a mid-cap ammonia-chain business. On the official filings, FY26 revenue grew 12.0% to ₹11,506 cr, but PAT fell 21.8% to ₹739 cr. Profitability has been shrinking through the year: PAT margin slid from 8.1% (H1) to 7.0% (9M) to 6.4% (full year), and EBITDA margin from 17.3% to 14.6%. The filing-extracted trend table has no Q1 FY27 revenue or PAT, and the unverified yfinance figure (PAT ₹490 cr on ₹1,886 cr revenue) looks like it may include a one-off. Treating this as a cyclical chemicals business, we judge it on EV/EBITDA: 11.1× is about half the broad-market median (bottom 15% of the market), but it is above the 5–8× the sector card calls normal for chemical cyclicals at mid-cycle. Trailing P/E of 16.9× sits inside the 12–22× Materials range, so overall we grade it fair. The forward P/E of 10.6× and analysts raising this year's earnings estimates by 43% over 30 days already assume the new plants succeed. The biggest risks are a slow ramp-up at the new plants with debt high (debt/equity about 0.76) and free cash flow negative (−₹396 cr in H1 FY26), together with raw-material squeeze from the Middle East and a falling-margin trend.

Hindustan Copper is India's only vertically integrated copper miner, with mines at Malanjkhand, Khetri and Ghatsila, so its earnings move with global copper prices and its own ore output. In the latest reported quarter, Q1 FY27, revenue rose 81.4% YoY to ₹936 cr and PAT rose 162.5% to ₹352 cr. PAT margin widened to 37.6% from 26.0% and EBITDA margin reached 56%, a clear step up from +4.6% revenue growth a year earlier, though FY26 cash conversion was soft (CFO/PAT 0.76x, FCF -₹182 cr). Because this is a capital-intensive, commodity-linked business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA as the sector card says: at 33.4x it is far above the 5-8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals, and the trailing P/E of 53.5x is well above the 12-22x Materials median, so the stock is expensive and already prices in peak copper margins, even though forward P/E of 25.6x and rising analyst estimates (+10% over 90 days) show more earnings growth is expected. The biggest risk is that a fall in copper prices compresses margins against this rich multiple, and the Q2 FY27 results on 11 Nov 2026 are a near-term event that could move the stock sharply either way.

fundamental.thesis: GMDCLTD is a Gujarat state-owned miner whose main business is lignite. Mining brings in nearly all its revenue (FY26 mining revenue ₹2,508 cr out of ₹2,653 cr total), and the loss-making power segment adds the rest. In Q2FY27, revenue from the official filing rose 71.2% YoY to ₹903 cr, faster than +23.8% in Q1FY27. Reported PAT fell 63.3% to ₹171 cr, but that is because Q2FY26 included a one-time ₹474 cr GST credit; without it, PAT grew about 27%. The PAT margin is 18.9%, close to Q1's 18.0% and well below FY26's 36% (which was inflated by the one-off). The quarter was strongly cash-backed: operating cash flow was 3.9x PAT and free cash flow ₹376 cr. Because this is a capital-heavy commodity miner, the right measure is EV/EBITDA, and the reported 43.9x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for cyclicals. However, that figure, the 163% dividend yield and the 4.47 debt/equity do not fit with Q1 EBITDA of ₹267 cr and the low liabilities in the segment data, so I treat them as unreliable. On the more dependable cross-check, trailing P/E of 20.6x is at the top of the 12–22x Materials range and P/B of 2.78x with 14.2% ROE is not cheap. Forward P/E (22.0x) is above trailing, which means earnings are expected to fall, so the grade is fair, not cheap, even though the stock ranks low on P/E against the broad market. The biggest risk is that the 71% revenue jump does not match the yfinance figure (₹538 cr), and it brought only modest underlying profit growth while margins shrank.

fundamental.thesis: NALCO is a government-owned (PSU), integrated aluminium and alumina producer and one of the world's lowest-cost bauxite/alumina miners, so its profits move closely with global aluminium (LME) prices. H1 FY27 was a record: revenue ₹10,722 cr (+32% YoY) and PAT ₹3,838 cr (+55%), with cash flow backing the earnings (CFO/PAT 1.14x, net cash about ₹12,172 cr). The derived Q2 shows growth slowing: revenue about ₹5,420 cr (+26% YoY, down from +39% in Q1) and PAT about ₹1,835 cr (+28%, down from +88%), while PAT margin dropped from 37.8% to about 33.9% quarter on quarter. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for commodity cyclicals, the stock trades at 7.4x, inside the 5–8x mid-cycle band, with trailing P/E 11.0x and forward P/E 9.8x, about 68% below the broad-market median; I grade it fair rather than cheap because these multiples sit on record-cycle earnings and aluminium prices. The main risk is that LME aluminium prices fall back from cycle highs, which would quickly reverse the margin gains; the chemicals (alumina) segment is already shrinking (-5.8% YoY), and the 5th-stream refinery and the Anugola smelter add execution and capex risk.

fundamental.thesis: Navin Fluorine is an Indian fluorochemicals maker in refrigerant gases (HFC/R32), specialty chemicals and contract manufacturing (CDMO), and is adding 15,000 MTPA of R32-equivalent capacity on the back of the China+1 shift. Revenue growth has held at roughly +41% to +51% YoY for six periods: H1FY27 revenue was ₹2,236 cr (+50.7%) and PAT was ₹513 cr (+93%). The implied Q2FY27 is about ₹1,191 cr revenue (+57% YoY vs ₹758 cr) and ₹270 cr PAT (+82%), and EBITDA margin rose to 33.7% from 28.6% a year ago, though cash conversion slipped to 0.89x CFO/PAT as receivables grew. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive chemicals business, the stock trades at 34.6× against 5–8× for mid-cycle chemical cyclicals, alongside 56× trailing P/E, 38.8× forward P/E and around P75–P79 across all four peer metrics; with the price at 93% of its 52-week range, it is expensive even after strong upward EPS revisions (+22.6% over 90 days). The biggest risk is that refrigerant-gas prices come off their cycle high while ₹319 cr of half-year capex and ₹1,070 cr of net debt are still ramping, which would squeeze margins on a valuation that leaves no room for a miss.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC is India's largest iron-ore miner and a government-owned company, so its earnings follow ore prices and volumes rather than any brand strength. Growth has nearly stopped: Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹6,795 cr (+0.8% YoY) and PAT was ₹1,976 cr (+0.4% YoY), against +27% revenue growth in H1 FY26 and +33% in FY26. Margins look better: EBITDA margin was 46.9% and PAT margin 29.1%, and the iron-ore segment grew 9.7%. Two caveats apply. The trend table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so it is not a clean like-for-like series. Cash conversion is also only middling, with CFO/PAT of 0.66x in FY26. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive commodity business, the stock trades at 7.8x, at the top of the sector card's 5–8x mid-cycle range. Trailing P/E is 10.5x against a 12–22x sector benchmark, forward P/E is 8.8x, and it sits around P6–P7 among the broad-market peers on EV/EBITDA and P/E. That makes it cheap, but not deeply cheap, given that margins may be near a cyclical high. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: a ₹15,786 cr contingent liability from the Karnataka Mineral Tax Bill (about 20% of market cap, awaiting Presidential assent), plus about ₹11,000 cr owed by NMDC Steel and RINL. Q2 results on 12-Nov-2026 are a near-term event risk.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC Steel runs a single 3 MTPA integrated steel plant at Nagarnar, demerged from NMDC Ltd, and is still ramping up. The Government holds 50.79% and is looking for a strategic buyer. Revenue growth has slowed sharply from +129–179% during the ramp-up to +8.8% YoY in Q1FY27 (₹3,662 cr), but margins have turned around: EBITDA margin went from -37.9% (Q3FY25) to 7.9% (9MFY26) to 12.1% (₹442 cr), and PAT turned positive at ₹51 cr, up 97.6% YoY. Even so, the PAT margin is a thin 1.4%, the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is only 0.17, and finance costs of ₹126 cr took about 29% of EBITDA. We use EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for steel, because P/E means little on near-zero profit (235.6x). At 11.7x the stock looks expensive against the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for steel, even though it ranks cheap (P17) against the broad market. That broad-market comparison is a fallback, not a true steel peer set. P/B of 1.05x is not a bargain when ROE is only 0.4%. The main risk is that profit stays too thin to cover heavy SBI loan repayments (₹3,177 cr outstanding, 30 quarterly instalments to 2031), with Q2FY27 results due on 12 Nov 2026 as a near-term binary event. The reported debt/equity of 35.02 is most likely a percentage (about 0.35x), which fits the loan size, so it is not a sign of extreme leverage.

fundamental.thesis: PCBL is one of the world's top three carbon black makers, with 900,000 MTPA of capacity after the Mundra specialty line was commissioned. It also owns the Aquapharm water-treatment chemicals business. The latest quarter from the filings, Q1FY27, was strong: revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹2,474 cr and PAT jumped 65% YoY to ₹155 cr, with EBITDA per tonne around ₹22,900. However, about ₹70 cr of that came from cheap inventory, and management flagged that ₹40–50 cr of it would reverse in Q2. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2 Nov have not been extracted from the official PDF yet. Unverified yfinance figures show Q2 PAT of ₹74 cr, roughly half of Q1, which fits the expected reversal and softer demand. Analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 9.8% over the last 30 days. Since this is a capital-intensive, cyclical chemicals business, I graded it on EV/EBITDA: at 17.7× it sits far above the 5–8× mid-cycle norm for cyclical chemicals in the sector card. Trailing P/E of 50.8× is well above the 12–22× Materials range, and forward P/E of 21.2× is at the top of that range, so I rate it expensive even though it looks cheaper than the broad market. The biggest risk is rising crude (around $91) feeding into feedstock costs, combined with high leverage, while volumes are weak in the near term.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Infotech sells CCTV and video-surveillance equipment under the CP PLUS brand, makes it in India through its AIL Dixon joint venture, and is now adding AI video analytics through a ₹45.39 cr purchase of a 30% stake in KGraph AI. The latest official half-year is labelled H1FY26 in the trend table, but because it includes the September 2026 QIP and the Q2 fire it almost certainly covers the six months to 30 Sep 2026. In that period revenue was ₹3,148 cr, up 89.7% YoY, and PAT was ₹328 cr, up 218% YoY, at a 10.4% PAT margin and 16.4% EBITDA margin. That is a clear improvement on the earlier periods' 31–36% growth and 7–9% PAT margins. However, the table is mislabelled and its FY26 row (₹422 cr revenue) does not match yfinance's roughly ₹970 cr per quarter, so the trend should be treated as directional only. Judged mainly on EV/EBITDA, plus P/E and peer rank, the stock is expensive: 70.2x EV/EBITDA against a broad-market median of 23.3x (P95), and 109.5x trailing P/E against an industrials range of 28–45x. Forward P/E of 51.4x already prices in a doubling of earnings, the price sits at 92.6% of its 52-week range, and the mean analyst target is about 1.3% below the price even though all 6 analysts rate it a buy. The biggest risk is earnings quality: operating cash flow was negative (CFO/PAT -0.20x, FCF -₹180 cr) because inventory and receivables built up. On top of that there is a ₹308.6 cr customs penalty under CESTAT appeal, so any slowdown in growth could trigger a sharp de-rating from these peak multiples.

fundamental.thesis: Abbott India is the Indian listed arm of Abbott. It is a branded-formulations franchise focused on the domestic market (Thyronorm, Duphaston and other women's health, gastro and chronic-therapy brands), so it is in the sector card's 'safe template' group with no US-tariff exposure. The only reliable figures are full-year FY26: revenue of ₹6,929 cr (+8.1% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,552 cr (+9.7% YoY), with a 27.7% EBITDA margin and a stable 22.4% PAT margin. Cash conversion was good but not excellent (CFO/PAT 0.85x, FCF ₹1,278 cr). The Q1FY27 yfinance row does not add up (₹932 cr revenue against a ~₹1,730 cr quarterly run-rate, and a 46% PAT margin), so I ignored it. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet, which means I cannot read the current trend. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 35.8x sits inside the 28-40x pharma range and at P52 against peers, and EV/EBITDA is 28.1x (P62), so I grade it fair. The forward P/E of 28.8x points to expected earnings growth, and the stock trades at 8.4% of its 52-week range, a better entry point if the Q2 numbers hold up. The biggest risk is that the price slide reflects a weaker Q2 or growth slowing to mid-single digits, which this stale data cannot confirm or rule out. Two of the snapshot figures are almost certainly data errors and I ignored them: a dividend yield of 201% and debt/equity of 3.6 for a company that has historically had no debt (the second may be lease liabilities or a unit mismatch).

fundamental.thesis: Emcure Pharmaceuticals is a mid-sized pharma company. About 41% of revenue comes from branded medicines sold in India and 59% from exports, mainly Europe, Canada and the rest of the world; it has little US generics exposure, so the US tariff risk is limited. Growth has sped up: revenue growth rose from +13.4% YoY in Q2FY26 to +20.4% in Q3FY26, +22.8% in Q1FY27 and +24.3% in Q2FY27 (₹2,820.5 cr). Q2FY27 profit after tax rose 29.3% to ₹325.1 cr. Operating margin (EBITDA) improved 70 bps to 20.0% in H1, and cash from operations was 1.10x profit, so earnings are backed by cash. International sales grew 34.5%, but India formulations growth has slowed to about 10%. On valuation I used trailing P/E plus EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 37.1x, inside the 28–40x pharma range, and EV/EBITDA is 20.3x, about 13% below the broad-market median. Forward P/E is 25.5x and analysts raised EPS estimates by 10% over 90 days. Overall the stock is fair, not cheap: it sits at 91% of its 52-week range and the average analyst target is only 0.9% above the price. The main risks are higher net debt after the ₹2,077 cr Gennova minority buyout and gross margin falling from 61.3% to 59.0% in H1.

Subtracting Q1 (₹1,304 cr revenue, ₹157 cr PAT) gives an implied Q2 of about ₹1,469 cr revenue (roughly +33% YoY) and about ₹219 cr PAT (roughly +38% YoY, against a base that included about ₹36 cr of one-off gains). Revenue growth has sped up from the low teens to +27–33% over recent periods, but part of that is the Indore acquisition, and EBITDA margin has slipped from about 25% to 23.4%. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital business, the stock is expensive: 36.2x EV/EBITDA, 61x trailing P/E against the sector's 28–40x, 8.5x P/B, and about the 75th–80th percentile against the broad market on every multiple. The forward P/E of 39x already prices in strong growth, and analysts' estimate changes are flat to slightly down over the last 30 days. The main risk is that new beds (Noida, Indore, Ghaziabad) ramp up slower than expected while staff costs (+23%) and finance costs (+77%) keep squeezing margins, leaving no room at this valuation.

fundamental.thesis: IRCTC is the government-backed monopoly on Indian Railways' internet ticketing, catering, tourism, and packaged drinking water (Railneer), benefiting from structural exclusivity but exposed to policy risk and PSU governance constraints. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue accelerated to +18.1% YoY (₹1,370 cr), driven by a 420% surge in Tourism (₹768 cr) and 34% Catering growth (₹732 cr), but the highest-margin segment — Internet Ticketing (80% PBIT margin) — grew only 0.6% YoY, a saturation signal in the core earnings engine; annual PAT growth decelerated sharply from +17.5% (FY25) to +6.0% (FY26) alongside EBITDA margin contraction from 39.1% to 37.3%, confirming that volume-driven revenue is not translating to earnings quality. At 30.1× trailing P/E (P41 vs 473 broad-market peers, -14% discount to median 35.2×, and only 10.2% above its 52-week low), headline valuation looks fair-to-cheap on P/E and at the median on EV/EBITDA (23.4×), but the forward P/E of 23× being priced in is contradicted by 90-day sell-side EPS estimate cuts of -14%, suggesting the market has not fully absorbed the margin deterioration — graded 'fair' with downside skew. The primary risk is a convergence of core ticketing saturation, material GST litigation (₹397+ cr debited in FY26 alone, plus a ₹50 cr anti-profiteering case pending at GSTAT since 2022), and sustained downward EPS revisions that carry a pre-derating pattern in a RISK_OFF macro regime.

EIH runs the Oberoi and Trident luxury hotel chains, a top-tier franchise in India's premium travel market, and is adding 6 new properties (about 667 rooms) to its development pipeline. Revenue growth has picked up: Q3 FY26 revenue rose +9.1% YoY to ₹873 cr, and Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose +15.0% to ₹698 cr. Profit is not keeping pace. EBITDA grew only +6% to ₹208 cr, the EBITDA margin was 29.8% versus 32.3% on a standalone basis, and the headline +226% PAT jump to ₹120 cr came from one-off exceptional gains; underlying PAT grew only about 1%. Hotels need a lot of capital, so we valued EIH mainly on EV/EBITDA: 16.1x is about 31% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P29), and a trailing P/E of 25.2x is far below the 60–100x the sector usually commands. With the stock near its 52-week low (11% of the range), we grade it fair rather than cheap, because the trailing earnings are inflated by one-offs. The biggest risks are costs rising faster than room revenue while foreign tourist arrivals stay weak, and the Q2 results due on 12-Nov, which could swing the stock either way.

fundamental.thesis: Lenskart is India's largest omnichannel eyewear retailer. It makes and sells its own frames and lenses through a big company-run store network and online, and it is a premium-consumption franchise inside Consumer Discretionary. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 32.5% YoY (per the 4 Nov press release), and PAT more than doubled to about ₹232 cr. That puts Q2 revenue at roughly ₹2,845 cr (H1 ₹5,559 cr minus Q1 ₹2,714 cr) and the PAT margin at about 8.2%, close to Q1's 8.4% and up from 5.6% in FY26. H1 earnings are cash-backed, with CFO/PAT of 1.84x and FCF of ₹365 cr. But revenue growth has actually slowed from +43.3% in Q1 to about +32.5% in Q2. The 'accelerating' trajectory flag comes from mixed period ordering and should not be relied on, and the FY26 row (₹881 cr) is clearly corrupted. I graded valuation on the card's retailer yardstick: EV/sales, EV/EBITDA and growth delivery. At 90.6x EV/EBITDA, 12.3x sales, 181.8x trailing and 95.5x forward P/E, it sits at P97–P99 against the broad market, well above even the 60–100x premium band for consumer names. The stock is at 94% of its 52-week range, and the mean analyst target of ₹718 is slightly below the current price, so this is expensive. Upward estimate revisions (+12–13% over 90 days) support the growth story but look largely priced in. The biggest risk is a de-rating: with no explicit management guidance and growth already cooling, any further slowdown at this multiple could trigger the 25–40% single-reset drawdown the sector card warns about.

fundamental.thesis: FSN E-Commerce (Nykaa) is India's leading online-plus-offline beauty platform with 65 million customers and 338 stores, plus a smaller Fashion arm that is still scaling. Revenue growth has held steady at 27-29% for three quarters (+26.7%, +29%, +28%), and EBITDA margin has widened from 7.2% to 8.5% to 8.7%, against 6.8% a year ago. The key business metrics also look healthy: GMV is up 30%, Beauty EBITDA up 51% and House of Nykaa NSV up 36%, while Fashion's EBITDA margin is barely positive at 0.2%. For a platform business I judged valuation on EV/sales, EV/EBITDA and whether unit economics keep improving, not on trailing P/E. At about 8.5x sales and 106x EV/EBITDA (98th percentile of the market, forward P/E 112x at the 100th percentile), with the stock near the top of its 52-week range, the price already assumes years of margin gains, so I grade it expensive. The biggest risk is valuation, not execution: these names can drop 25-40% on a single growth or margin miss, and that risk is higher with no explicit FY27 guidance plus fresh spending on Nykaa NOW quick-commerce and the Simply Nam acquisition.

fundamental.thesis: PG Electroplast is a contract manufacturer of room air-conditioners, washing machines, TVs and plastic components for consumer-durable brands, so its earnings depend on brand outsourcing volumes and seasonal cooling demand rather than consumer pricing power. Revenue growth in the trend table has slowed from +118% to +9%, and PAT margin has narrowed from 27.6% to 24.1%. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 42.5x is above the 28–40x pharma band. EV/EBITDA of 35.8x ranks in the 75th percentile of the broad market, and P/B is 7.3x. The forward P/E of 29.5x does build in an earnings recovery, so I grade it expensive, mainly on EV/EBITDA and P/E against the pharma band. The biggest risk is that the unread Q2 results confirm the slowdown, which would leave a premium multiple without growth to support it. The ₹800 cr QIP at ₹506 per share also dilutes existing shareholders and will push ROE down until the money is put to work.

fundamental.thesis: Whirlpool of India is a leading single-segment home appliances manufacturer (refrigerators, washing machines, ACs) with a well-established urban franchise, though it faces intensifying competition from Haier, LG, and listed peers. The biggest risk is that margins continue to deteriorate under rising crude-driven input cost pressure while aggressive sell-side estimate cuts (-25.2% in 90 days) signal further earnings-led de-rating from an already distressed 7.1% of 52-week range.

Saregama is one of India's largest music-rights owners, with a big film and non-film catalogue that it earns from through streaming, licensing, and live events and video content. Q2 FY27 revenue from operations was ₹314.3 cr, up 37% YoY, adjusted EBITDA was ₹118 cr (up 39%) and PBT was ₹85.8 cr (up 43%). That is a sharp reversal from FY26, when revenue fell 15.9% and the 9M FY26 decline was 25.1%, and it comes off a soft base (H1 FY26 revenue was down 2.3%). Margins rose slightly to about 37.5% EBITDA, against 34-38% in recent periods. Because this is a content-IP business that spends heavily on catalogue, I graded it on EV/EBITDA plus P/E: 25.5x EV/EBITDA is P58 against the broad market and the 43.9x trailing P/E is P64 (about 25% above the 35.2x median), both well below the sector card's 60-100x range for consumer discretionary premium names. The 32.3x forward P/E and the 14-16% rise in earnings estimates over 90 days support earnings growth, but the stock sits at 74% of its 52-week range and the consensus target is only 2.4% above the price, so I call it fair, not cheap. The main weakness is cash conversion: FY26 free cash flow was ₹-114 cr and cash from operations was only 0.48x PAT, because content-acquisition spending is running ahead of the cash it earns back.

fundamental.thesis: Sai Life Sciences is a mid-sized Indian contract research and manufacturing (CDMO) partner to global pharma companies, benefiting from the China+1 shift in outsourcing, and it is moving clients toward broader discovery-to-manufacturing relationships. Growth has slowed: H1 FY27 revenue rose 17% YoY to Rs 1,213 cr and PAT rose 19% to Rs 172 cr, down from +29% revenue growth in FY26 and +27% in Q3 FY26. Q2 FY27 alone grew 23% to Rs 659 cr, which implies Q1 grew only about 10–11%, so the slowdown was mostly in Q1. Margins have also eased: EBITDA margin was 28% in H1 versus 30% for FY26 and 34% in Q3 FY26, though these periods are not strictly like-for-like. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 40.6x versus a 23.3x broad-market median (P83). Its trailing P/E of 73.5x is far above the 28–40x pharma range, and it sits at 93% of its 52-week range, so we grade it expensive. The main risk is that management's promised stronger second half (new capacity, pipeline progress) does not arrive while the business is spending heavily on capacity (Rs 621 cr capex in H1). That would hit a valuation priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: Asahi India Glass is India's leading maker of car glass (about two-thirds of revenue) and has a growing float-glass business, so it is tied both to passenger-vehicle demand and to building-glass pricing. Growth has picked up sharply over six periods, from -0.1% revenue growth in Q2 FY26 to +15% in Q1 FY27; Q2 FY27 revenue, worked out as H1 minus Q1, is about ₹1,586 cr (+36% YoY), and PAT is about ₹167 cr (+188% YoY). Over the same window EBITDA margin rose from 16.9% to 22.4% and PAT margin from 4.7% to 10.5%, helped by float-glass growth of +49.7% at a 22% PBIT margin and car-glass growth of +26.6%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for a capital-heavy glass maker: 24.96x is close to the broad-market median of 23.3x (P55), so the stock is fair. The trailing P/E of 55.7x is well above the 18–28x auto-ancillary range, but it is inflated by the weak FY26 earnings base, and the forward P/E of 41.8x shows that strong growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that the float-glass profit surge is cyclical or comes from new capacity, while the company carries ₹1,853 cr of net debt (2.76x EBITDA) and spends about 17% of revenue on power and fuel, which hurts when crude prices rise.

fundamental.thesis: Ather Energy is a pure-play premium electric two-wheeler maker with 15.1% market share, down from 17.2% a year ago, and 15% of revenue comes from non-vehicle sources. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 62.8% YoY to Rs 1,464 cr on 42% higher volumes and 14.6% higher revenue per unit, compared with +53% in Q3FY26 and +66% for FY26, while PAT improved from a Rs 154 cr loss to a Rs 1.26 cr profit and EBITDA margin moved from -3.0% in Q3FY26 to 5.0%, although the missing Q1FY27 row and mixed annual and quarterly periods make the 'accelerating' signal unreliable. Valuation is expensive using the pre-profit yardstick of EV/sales proxied by P/S, growth delivery and unit economics rather than trailing P/E: P/S is 15.5x (about 11x annualised Q2 revenue), forward P/E is 374x, and the stock is near its 52-week high with the mean target about level with the price, though EV/EBITDA is not meaningful, no tight peer set is available, and the price inputs and 25.82 debt/equity figure look inconsistent or unclear and were given little weight. The biggest risk is that aluminium, copper and memory-chip cost inflation interrupts margin gains while share is falling, a concern supported by next-FY EPS estimates being cut 49% in 30 days even as all 12 analysts stay at buy.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. Q2FY27 revenue grew a strong +26.2% YoY to ₹4,762 cr, but PAT collapsed -39.8% YoY to ₹112 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from ~13–14% (FY26/Q3FY26) to just 9.5% today — this is the defining trajectory: top-line accelerating while margins are structurally compressing, driven by commodity cost headwinds from the West Asia conflict and the Camso acquisition integration costs; the DSCR of 0.84× (below the 1.0× sustainability floor) and a current ratio of 0.67× flag tightening liquidity. Valuation looks outright cheap: EV/EBITDA at 7.4× sits at P5 vs the broad market (median 23.3×), trailing P/E of 20.2× is at P23 vs peers and -43% below market median — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock screens as cheap, but the multiple compression is warranted given the margin collapse, and forward P/E of 15.1× implies the market expects earnings recovery, which is far from assured. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

fundamental.thesis: Craftsman Automation makes engine and powertrain parts, aluminium products (61% of H1 revenue) and industrial and engineering products, and German operations contributed 17% of H1 revenue, so some of the growth may be acquired rather than organic. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 23.5x only matches the median of a broad-market peer set rather than close auto-parts peers, and it looks full next to a 60.98x trailing P/E (P79, above the 18-28x auto benchmark), a 32.98x forward P/E and 8.53x P/B, so the valuation is expensive. fundamental.thesis: JBM Auto combines a components business (Q2FY27 revenue about Rs 1,037 cr, +24.7% YoY) with a fast-growing electric bus business (about Rs 548 cr, +21.8% YoY, 24% reported market share and 578 buses delivered in the quarter). Reported revenue growth has accelerated from +8.6% in Q2FY26 to +16.2% in Q3FY26 and +21.1% to Rs 1,656 cr in Q2FY27, with PAT up 12.5% to Rs 59 cr, but PAT margin has slipped from 3.9% to 3.6% to 3.5%; Q1FY27 and FY26 data are missing, and the table's Q2FY26 revenue and PAT imply lower growth of about +17.7% and +7.3%, so the acceleration is less certain than it looks. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation is expensive at 24.0x for a 12.2% EBITDA margin, even though that is only P52 against a broad-market peer set rather than close auto peers; trailing P/E of 64.8x is well above the 18-30x OEM range, P/B of 12.7x is P89, and forward P/E of 31.0x assumes earnings roughly double. The biggest risk is that growth keeps needing debt-funded capital while thin margins and weak cash generation (H1FY27 operating cash flow Rs 143 cr, free cash flow Rs 14 cr, net debt Rs 2,732 cr) leave little room for error; the 14.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and was ignored, and the '2.7x H1 revenue' debt figure is wrong because Rs 2,732 cr is about 0.9x H1 revenue.

fundamental.thesis: BBTC is the Wadia Group's holding company with a controlling stake in Britannia Industries plus tea/coffee plantations and auto-electrical components — P/E comparison to pure FMCG operators is structurally misleading, and the correct yardstick here is P/B plus EV/EBITDA (sector card conglomerate guidance), not the 40–65× FMCG P/E benchmark. Using yfinance (Q1FY27 official PDF data is absent from the trend table), revenue grew +5.9% YoY to ₹2,959 cr, decelerating from +8.7% in Q1FY26, while PAT margin expanded sharply to ~9.7% (from 5.1% in Q1FY26) — though that expansion likely includes volatile Britannia dividend and investment income rather than structural operating improvement (note H1FY26 CFO/PAT was −0.02×, a poor cash-conversion signal for the operating businesses). On EV/EBITDA of 3.06× (P0 in broad market) and P/B of 1.42× with the stock at 14.6% of its 52-week range, BBTC appears deeply cheap by any metric — but a structural holding-company discount of 30–50% is normal and persistent, and the extreme D/E of 16.57 with US 10Y at 5.29% and rising is an offsetting overhang that explains why the discount exists. The biggest risk is that debt is likely collateralised against the Britannia stake, meaning a sustained FII-driven de-rating of Britannia under the current RISK_OFF regime could trigger a collateral squeeze at the BBTC level, amplifying downside disproportionately.

Minda Corporation is a mid-cap auto-components maker for Indian two-wheeler, passenger-vehicle and commercial-vehicle makers, supplying vehicle access systems, wiring harnesses and a growing range of electronics and EV parts. It has owned Minda-VAST as a subsidiary since April 1, 2026, so its headline growth is inflated. Q2FY27 revenue was a record ₹2,189 cr (+42.6% YoY) and H1FY27 revenue was ₹4,036 cr (+38.1%), but much of that comes from adding Minda-VAST, not organic growth. Q2 PAT was about ₹143 cr (H1 ₹349 cr minus Q1 ₹206 cr), a 6.5% margin. H1 PAT growth of +132.9% includes a one-off gain of ₹106 cr after tax; without it, H1 PAT is about ₹243 cr at a 6.0% margin, broadly in line with FY26 (5.8%) and FY25 (6.2%). EBITDA margin has been flat at around 11.6–11.8% after 14.2% in FY25, so margins are steady rather than expanding. Valuation is judged on the Auto sector card's P/E range plus EV/EBITDA: trailing P/E of 43.3x (higher still once the one-off gain is removed) and forward P/E of 29.2x are both above the 18–28x range for auto names. EV/EBITDA of 23.3x is only at the broad-market median, the stock sits at 88% of its 52-week range, and all 8 analysts rate it buy with estimates edging up (+5.8% over 90 days for next year). Overall the stock looks expensive, and the main risk is that growth slows sharply once the acquisition effect drops out from Q1FY28, which would hit a valuation priced near its highs.

fundamental.thesis: Olectra Greentech is a midcap maker of electric buses (Mobility division, about 86% of Q1FY27 revenue, partnered with BYD) and composite polymer insulators (Energy division), which puts it at the centre of India's public-transport electrification. On the official Q1FY27 filing, revenue grew 65.7% YoY to Rs 575.5 cr, faster than +10.6% a year earlier and +28.3% for FY26. But PAT rose only 2.4% to about Rs 27 cr: finance costs nearly doubled (Rs 12.0 cr to Rs 23.6 cr), EBITDA margin fell from 16.1% to 12.7%, and PAT margin fell from 7.5% to 4.6%. Earnings are also not turning into cash well: FY26 cash from operations was only 0.58x PAT and free cash flow was negative (Rs -55 cr). I graded valuation on trailing P/E because the EV/EBITDA (1066x), Debt/Equity (30.8) and Price/Sales (58x) figures in the snapshot look like data errors. At 56x trailing P/E, the stock is well above the 18-28x Auto OEM range, at the top of the 28-45x Industrials range, and in the top quarter of the broad market (P75 on P/E, P73 on P/B at 8.1x), so it is expensive. The 27.9x forward P/E assumes a sharp profit recovery that the latest quarter has not yet shown. The biggest risk is the Q2FY27 results on 9 Nov 2026: if margins keep shrinking or interest costs keep rising, a stock priced for growth could be cut down to a lower multiple.

On valuation we used P/E because the Auto card benchmarks OEMs and ancillaries that way, with EV/EBITDA as a check. Trailing P/E of 38.2x is well above the 18–28x auto band, so we grade it expensive. Forward P/E of 27.7x is only at the top of that band, and EV/EBITDA of 24.3x is roughly in line with the broad market (P53). P/B of 19.2x is at P96, which only the 43% ROE supports. The biggest risk is that the price assumes faster growth while margins are slipping, with rising crude and a reported 4.29 debt/equity adding pressure. That leverage figure does not fit the strong free cash flow and needs checking.

Rupee revenue growth improved from -3.0% in H1 FY26 to +6.6% in Q2 FY27 and PAT rose 37.5% to about Rs 160 cr (11.3% margin; the table's Rs 142 cr revenue and Rs 16 cr PAT look like unit errors), but constant-currency revenue fell 1.6% and EBITDA margin slipped from 16.0% to 15.2%, so currency and possibly non-operating items appear to be flattering the headline trend. The biggest risk is that this is a value trap: H1 order wins rose 15% to $285M but Q2 new wins were only $47M, and falling client numbers plus AI price deflation could keep underlying growth negative.

DOMS Industries is a leading Indian maker of branded stationery and art supplies, and it is building a newer hygiene business; its official filings put it closer to consumer goods than to the yfinance 'Industrials' tag. In Q2FY27, consolidated revenue rose 17.6% YoY to ₹668 cr, but PAT fell 37.0% YoY to ₹38 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 10.7% to 5.7%. Revenue growth has slowed every period, from +26.4% to +24.1% to +21.6% to +19.2% to +18.4% to +17.6%, and EBITDA margin has fallen from 17.3% in FY26 to 12.2% in H1FY27, partly because the low-margin hygiene segment (6.6% operating margin vs 13.5% for stationery) is pulling the average down. Using P/E against FMCG norms as the yardstick, the trailing P/E of 59.4x sits at the top of the 40–60x sector band and in the expensive top quartile against peers (P78 on P/E, P84 on P/B), while earnings are falling and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 11.5% in 30 days, so we grade it expensive despite the price sitting near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the market cuts the multiple further if margins do not recover while heavy capex (about 15.7% of revenue, H1 free cash flow of -₹106 cr) keeps eating cash.

fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini is one of India's largest integrated sugar makers, with 80,000 TCD of crushing, 1,050 KLPD of distillery (ethanol) capacity, 175.7 MW of saleable co-generation and a new 80,000 TPA PLA bioplastics plant. It is tagged FMCG, but it is really a seasonal, policy-driven, capital-intensive commodity business. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 12.3% YoY to ₹1,876 cr and PAT rose 81.6% to ₹104 cr (5.5% margin), helped by a weak base. Even so, H1 revenue growth slowed to +9.3% from +15.8% in FY26 and +22% in Q3 FY26, and EBITDA margin fell from 13.9% to 9.1%, though seasonality distorts quarter-to-quarter comparisons. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA rather than the FMCG P/E band because this is a commodity business: at 25.0× it sits slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3× (P56), which is rich for a sugar/ethanol producer. The 38× trailing P/E only looks fair against FMCG peers, and the 18.5× forward P/E plus rising analyst estimates (FY EPS +12.7% over 90 days) already assume a strong earnings recovery, likely from PLA and ethanol. So I rate it fair, with the stock at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the improvement depends on government-set sugar, cane and ethanol prices and on a smooth PLA ramp-up, while FY26 free cash flow was ₹-349 cr and leverage is meaningful.

C.E. Info Systems (MapmyIndia) is India's main homegrown digital-maps and location-tech provider, selling map data, navigation and IoT/telematics services mostly to auto makers, enterprises and government. H1FY27 consolidated revenue grew 15.3% YoY to ₹271.46 cr and PAT grew 32.1% to ₹84.99 cr, a clear pick-up from the +2.3% revenue growth and -9.2% PAT in FY26. However, nearly all of the growth came from the device segment (+161% YoY to ₹56.17 cr), while the core high-margin Map data & services business was almost flat (+0.66% to ₹215.29 cr), and the quarterly rows conflict with each other (Q1 PAT of about ₹50 cr implies only about ₹35 cr in Q2), which makes the PAT trend unreliable. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA together as the yardstick, trailing P/E of 36.9x is above the 22–30x IT services range but in line with the broad-market peer median (P53), forward P/E of 22.5x implies earnings growth, and EV/EBITDA of 29.1x is above the peer median (P64), so I grade it fair: not cheap despite trading near the bottom of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the flat core map business, a growing share of revenue from low-margin devices, and capex rising to 10.4% of revenue erode the margin profile that justifies the premium multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Torrent Power is a vertically integrated private utility operating licensed electricity distribution across Gujarat, Maharashtra, and UP (4.29M customers, India's lowest distribution-loss record) alongside 6.6 GW of gas, coal, and renewable generation capacity, with a further ~8.9 GWp under development including renewables, pumped storage, and coal. Q1FY27 revenue grew a modest +2.8% YoY to ₹8,124 Cr — decelerating from +10.0% in Q2FY26 and +4.3% in Q3FY26 — while Total Comprehensive Income fell 13.5% YoY to ₹639 Cr; PAT margins have contracted from ~10.5% (FY25) to ~8.3% (FY26) and an estimated ~7.9% in Q1FY27 as higher finance costs from the ₹3,632 Cr Nabha Power acquisition (June 2026, 1.4 GW supercritical coal with long-term Punjab PPAs) weigh on reported PAT despite stable EBITDA margins at ~20%. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card instruction), 15.03× vs a broad-market median of 23.3× places TORNTPOWER at the P25 cheapness rank; the trailing P/E of 30.25× sits above the 10–18× utility sector benchmark, but the forward P/E compressing to 23.1× signals the market is already pricing in earnings recovery from the commissioning pipeline, yielding a fair overall valuation grade. The CFO resignation (August 2026) is a governance red flag at a sensitive execution juncture for a midcap, compounded by elevated leverage from Nabha and LNG supply disruptions already suppressing thermal plant performance.

Zensar is an RPG-group mid-tier IT services firm with two businesses, Digital Services and Cloud Infrastructure, and it has a net cash position of ₹326 cr. Revenue is growing a little faster: H1FY27 revenue was ₹3,094 cr, up 10.2% YoY, compared with +7.5% to +8.7% through FY26, and Cloud Infrastructure grew 12.3%. Profit is not keeping up. H1 PAT of ₹374 cr rose only 2.7%, and PAT margin fell to 12.1% from 13.6% in FY26. Some of that drop is a one-off ₹24.9 cr Labour Code provision, but excluding it margin is still only about 12.9%. Cash conversion has also weakened, with CFO/PAT at 0.73x and only ₹22 cr of free cash flow because capex took up 8% of revenue, which is unusually high for an IT services firm. On valuation it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 12.6x against an IT sector band of 22–30x, EV/EBITDA is 8.2x (P7 across the market), and forward P/E of 11.2x is below trailing. Treat that discount with care, though. The stock is near its 52-week low, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by about 1.2–1.4% over 90 days, and the market may be pricing in AI-driven shrinkage of mid-tier IT revenue. The feed also has several conflicting numbers: the Q1 revenue figure differs between sources, the Q2FY26 row is off by a factor of 10, and D/E of 1.68 and a 351% dividend yield contradict the net-cash position. So read the cheap grade with somewhat less confidence.

fundamental.thesis: Emami is a mid-sized Indian FMCG company selling ayurvedic personal care and healthcare brands such as Navratna, BoroPlus and Zandu, and it is now buying its way into digital-first brands (60% of IncNut Digital, majority control of Axiom Ayurveda). Godfrey Phillips is a mid-cap cigarette-led business (Marlboro licensee, plus Four Square and Red & White) with smaller retail and confectionery arms, so it is a tobacco cash business rather than a typical FMCG name. In Q2FY27, reported revenue rose 157.2% YoY to ₹4,198 cr while PAT fell 37.7% to ₹190 cr, after a 44.3% drop in Q1FY27. PAT margin fell from about 19% in H1 FY26 to 4.5%. The revenue jump does not match the yfinance quarterly rows (₹762–1,115 cr), so it most likely reflects a change in how revenue is reported, such as duties included in the top line, rather than real demand. The falling profit is the real signal: earnings have dropped for two quarters in a row. Using P/E plus earnings direction (tobacco does not deserve the 40–65× FMCG multiple), the stock looks fair at 23.2× trailing and 20.3× forward, about 34% below the broad-market median, but that discount is offset by falling profits and weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT of 0.34x in FY26). The biggest risk is that the profit drop reflects lasting tax or volume pressure on cigarettes and keeps going.

PAT margin rose to 21.9% from 19.2%, EBITDA margin held steady at about 55%, and mobile ARPU climbed from ₹252 (FY26) to ₹259 (Q1FY27) to ₹264 (Q2FY27). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the measure the sector card uses: at 15.4x it is well above the 9–12x norm for Indian mobile operators, so the stock is expensive even though it sits near its 52-week low; trailing P/E of 41.4x is inside the 35–60x telecom band and forward P/E of 22.4x assumes further earnings growth. The main concern is that growth now comes almost entirely from higher ARPU: mobile customers fell by 16k net this quarter, churn is 2.6%, and analysts have trimmed FY EPS estimates by 2.7% over 90 days despite the strong print. That leaves the stock dependent on the next industry tariff hike, and there was also a board and management change on results day.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Chemicals is a diversified chemicals conglomerate (soda ash, bicarb, salt via Living Essentials; agrochemicals via Rallis India in Farm Essentials; industrial chemicals in Industrial Essentials) operating across India, US, UK, and Kenya — a global price-taker in soda ash, its largest earnings driver historically. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +14.4% YoY to ₹4,255 crore (reversing four consecutive quarters of -1% to -2.5% decline), but PAT fell -81% YoY to ₹60 crore and EBITDA contracted -14.5% to ₹555 crore, as the Industrial Essentials segment swung from +₹131 crore profit to -₹70 crore loss — revenue growth is not flowing to earnings; PAT margin stands at just 1.4% vs 4.3% in the comparable prior period. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card for this capital-intensive commodity name, at 14.5× vs sector peer median 17.9× (P40 rank), the stock screens modestly below peer median, but the sector card's own 5–8× mid-cycle commodity benchmark and a negative TTM ROE of -7.7% mean the current multiple implies significant recovery — graded fair, with limited margin of safety on a structurally depressed EBITDA base. The central risk is that China's elevated soda ash inventories (~1.8 million tonnes), sustained price-dumping into Asian markets, and structurally uncompetitive US operations (already requiring ₹1,837 crore goodwill impairment in FY26) keep Industrial Essentials loss-making well beyond Q1FY27, with EPS estimates cut -21.8% over 90 days and a pending NSE exchange clarification (2026-09-29) and auditor change in UK subsidiaries (2026-09-26) adding governance uncertainty.
